uni-bcom-cost-accounting.title: B.Com · Cost Accounting (full paper)
uni-bcom-cost-accounting.description: The complete Cost Accounting paper unit by unit: cost concepts and the cost sheet, material control with EOQ and stock levels, labour remuneration and overheads, job, contract and process costing, operating costing and reconciliation of cost and financial accounts, with solved numericals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Com programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Cost concepts, classification and the cost sheet
courses.summary: Meaning, scope and objectives of cost accounting, cost units and cost centres, classification of costs by element, behaviour, function and relevance, preparation of a cost sheet from raw data, and preparing a quotation or tender price from past cost relationships.
outcomes: Distinguish cost accounting from financial accounting
Classify costs by element, behaviour, function and decision relevance
Prepare a cost sheet showing prime cost, works cost, cost of production and cost of sales
Prepare a quotation using overhead rates from a previous period

scenes.text: A Tiruppur garment unit earns an overall profit but cannot say whether T-shirts or trousers make money.
Cost accounting traces costs to each product, job and department.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Cost**: the amount of expenditure (actual or notional) incurred on, or attributable to, a given thing.
- **Costing**: the technique and process of ascertaining costs.
- **Cost accounting**: the process of accounting for cost from the point of incurrence to its final allocation to cost objects, including control and reporting for decisions.

steps.title: Objectives and advantages
steps.body:
- Ascertain cost per unit, job, process or service
- Fix selling prices and prepare tenders
- Control costs (material, labour, overhead) and reduce waste
- Provide data for decisions: make or buy, shut down, pricing in recession
- Identify profitable and unprofitable activities

steps.title: Cost vs financial accounting
steps.body:
| Basis | Financial | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | true and fair view to outsiders | cost ascertainment and control for managers |
| Coverage | whole business | products, jobs, departments |
| Compulsion | statutory | voluntary (except cost audit/records where notified) |
| Periodicity | annual | continuous, as needed |
| Items | actual figures | actual, estimated and standard figures |

steps.title: Cost unit and cost centre
steps.body:
- **Cost unit**: unit of product or service in which costs are expressed – per tonne (steel), per kWh (power), per passenger-km (transport), per bed-day (hospital), per 1,000 bricks.
- **Cost centre**: location, person or item of equipment for which costs are collected – production centres (machining, assembly) and service centres (stores, maintenance).
- **Profit centre** / **investment centre**: responsible also for revenue / capital employed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a department a cost unit (it is a cost centre).
- Saying cost accounting replaces financial accounting – both coexist.
- Using per-unit costs for transport (it should be a composite unit such as passenger-km).

activity.prompt: Match each industry to a suitable cost unit type.

quiz.q: A cost centre is:
options: a location or function for which costs are collected
quiz.why: A cost centre is a location, person or equipment used to accumulate costs.

quiz.q: Suitable cost unit for a hospital:
quiz.why: A hospital's service is measured by patient-days or bed-days.

quiz.q: Cost accounting is generally:
options: voluntary, except where cost records are prescribed
quiz.why: Cost accounting is mainly a management tool; cost records are compulsory only for notified industries.

quiz.q: A department responsible for both cost and revenue is a:
quiz.why: A profit centre is accountable for revenue and costs, hence profit.

story.title: Rent does not change, steel does

scenes.text: A furniture maker's factory rent stays ₹50,000 a month whether it makes 100 or 300 chairs.
But the wood cost doubles when output doubles – behaviour matters for decisions.

steps.title: By element
steps.body:
- **Direct material, direct labour, direct expenses** → together **prime cost**
- **Overheads** (indirect material, indirect labour, indirect expenses): factory, office and administration, selling and distribution

steps.title: By behaviour
steps.body:
- **Fixed**: total stays constant within a relevant range; per-unit falls as output rises (rent, salaries)
- **Variable**: total varies in direct proportion; per-unit constant (direct material)
- **Semi-variable**: part fixed, part variable (telephone, power with fixed charge)
- **Step cost**: fixed over a range, then jumps (supervisors)

steps.title: For decisions and control
steps.body:
- **Controllable vs uncontrollable** by a given manager
- **Sunk cost**: already incurred, irrelevant to decisions
- **Opportunity cost**: benefit forgone from the next best alternative
- **Relevant cost**: future cost that differs between alternatives
- **Normal vs abnormal**; **product vs period** costs

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying fixed cost per unit is constant (it falls as output rises).
- Including sunk costs in a decision analysis.
- Treating a semi-variable cost as wholly variable.

activity.prompt: Maintenance cost is ₹45,000 at 10,000 units and ₹57,000 at 14,000 units. Using the high–low method, what is the fixed element (₹)?

quiz.q: Fixed cost per unit:
quiz.why: The same total is spread over more units, so cost per unit falls.

quiz.q: Prime cost equals:
options: direct material + direct labour + direct expenses
quiz.why: Prime cost is the total of all direct costs.

quiz.q: A cost already incurred and unrecoverable is a:
quiz.why: Sunk costs are past and cannot be changed by any decision.

quiz.q: Telephone bill with fixed rental plus call charges is:
quiz.why: It has a fixed rental and a usage-based variable component.

scenes.text: A soap maker produced 10,000 cartons last quarter.
A cost sheet builds up cost stage by stage – from raw materials to the cost of sales.

steps.title: Format
steps.body:
1. Materials consumed = Opening RM + Purchases (+ carriage inwards) − Closing RM
2. + Direct wages + Direct expenses = **Prime cost**
3. + Factory overheads + Opening WIP − Closing WIP = **Works (factory) cost**
4. + Office and administration overheads = **Cost of production**
5. + Opening FG − Closing FG = **Cost of goods sold**
6. + Selling and distribution overheads = **Cost of sales (total cost)**
7. + Profit = **Sales**

steps.title: Solved: cost sheet
steps.body:
Opening RM 20,000; purchases 1,50,000; closing RM 30,000; direct wages 80,000; direct expenses 10,000; factory overheads 46,000; opening WIP 12,000; closing WIP 8,000; office overheads 30,000; opening FG 25,000; closing FG 35,000; S&D overheads 20,000; profit 20% on sales; 10,000 units produced.

- Materials consumed 1,40,000 → **Prime cost 2,30,000**
- + 46,000 + 12,000 − 8,000 → **Works cost 2,80,000**
- + 30,000 → **Cost of production 3,10,000** (₹31 per unit)
- + 25,000 − 35,000 → **COGS 3,00,000**
- + 20,000 → **Cost of sales 3,20,000**
- Profit 20% on sales = 25% on cost → **Sales 4,00,000; profit 80,000**

steps.title: Items excluded from cost accounts
steps.body: Purely financial items are excluded: interest received, dividend, profit/loss on sale of fixed assets, income-tax, donations, goodwill written off, discount on shares or debentures, transfers to reserves.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adjusting WIP after office overheads (WIP is normally adjusted at works cost).
- Converting '20% on sales' as 20% on cost.
- Including income-tax or interest on capital in the cost sheet.

activity.prompt: Opening raw materials ₹15,000; purchases ₹1,05,000; carriage inwards ₹2,000; closing raw materials ₹22,000; direct wages ₹60,000; direct expenses ₹8,000. Prime cost (₹)?

quiz.q: WIP is normally adjusted at the stage of:
quiz.why: WIP carries materials, labour and factory overheads, so it is adjusted in arriving at works cost.

quiz.q: Cost of sales ₹4,80,000; profit 20% on sales. Sales:
Which is excluded from the cost sheet?
quiz.why: Income-tax is an appropriation of profit, not a cost of production or sale.

quiz.q: Cost of production + opening FG − closing FG =
quiz.why: Adjusting finished goods stock gives the cost of goods actually sold.

scenes.text: A municipal corporation invites tenders for 500 steel benches.
The firm estimates materials and labour, then adds overheads at last year's rates and its profit margin.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
From last period's cost sheet compute:
- Factory overheads as % of direct wages (or of prime cost)
- Office overheads as % of works cost
- S&D overheads as % of works cost or cost of production, or per unit

Apply these to the estimated direct costs of the new job, adjusting for expected price changes, then add the desired profit.

steps.title: Solved: tender price
steps.body:
Last year: materials 2,00,000; wages 1,50,000; factory overheads 60,000; office overheads 41,000.
- FOH % of wages = 60,000 ÷ 1,50,000 = **40%**
- Works cost = 4,10,000; office OH % of works cost = **10%**

New job: materials 30,000; wages 20,000.
- FOH = 8,000 → works cost 58,000
- Office OH = 5,800 → total cost 63,800
- Profit 20% on selling price → **Tender price = 63,800 ÷ 0.8 = ₹79,750**

steps.title: Adjust for changes
steps.body: If material prices are expected to rise 10% or wages 5%, adjust the estimates before applying overhead percentages. Fixed overheads that will not change with one extra job may be excluded in a marginal-cost quotation during idle capacity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying factory overhead % to prime cost when it was computed on wages.
- Adding profit on cost when the question says on selling price.
- Forgetting expected price changes.

activity.prompt: Factory overheads are 50% of direct wages and office overheads are 20% of works cost. A job needs materials ₹40,000 and wages ₹20,000. Profit is 25% on cost. Quotation price (₹)?

quiz.q: Last year FOH ₹90,000 on wages ₹1,80,000. FOH rate on wages:
Total cost ₹72,000; profit 10% on selling price. Price:
Office overheads are normally related to:
quiz.why: Office and administration overheads are usually expressed as a percentage of works cost.

quiz.q: If material prices are expected to rise, the estimator should:
options: adjust estimated material cost before computing overheads
quiz.why: Estimates should reflect expected prices, and overheads based on them change accordingly.

questions.q: Cost accounting mainly serves:
questions.why: Its main purpose is cost ascertainment and control for managers.

questions.why: Bricks are costed in lots of 1,000.

questions.q: Direct material ₹50,000, direct wages ₹30,000, direct expenses ₹5,000, FOH ₹15,000. Prime cost:
Cost ₹12,000 at 4,000 units, ₹15,000 at 5,500 units. Variable cost per unit:
Opportunity cost is:
options: the benefit forgone from the next best alternative
the cost of buying an opportunity
questions.why: It measures what is given up by choosing one option over another.

questions.q: Works cost ₹2,00,000; office OH ₹20,000; opening FG ₹10,000; closing FG ₹30,000. COGS:
Profit 25% on cost equals what % on sales?
questions.why: Cost 100, profit 25, sales 125: 25 ÷ 125 = 20%.

options: interest on debentures (if treated as finance item)
questions.why: Factory depreciation is a factory overhead; the others are financial items.

questions.q: Prime cost ₹1,50,000; FOH ₹30,000; opening WIP ₹10,000; closing WIP ₹15,000. Works cost:
FOH 60% of wages, office OH 15% of works cost. Job: materials ₹10,000, wages ₹5,000. Total cost:
Total cost ₹60,000; profit 20% on selling price. Selling price:
Supervisor salary that rises only when a new shift is added is a:
questions.why: It stays fixed within a range then jumps, which is a step cost.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Material cost control
courses.summary: Purchase and store procedures with documents, selective inventory control (ABC, VED, JIT), economic order quantity, stock levels, pricing of material issues by FIFO and weighted average, material turnover and the treatment of normal and abnormal losses.
outcomes: Describe purchase and store procedure and its documents
Compute EOQ and the associated ordering and carrying costs
Compute re-order, minimum, maximum and average stock levels
Price issues and value closing stock by FIFO and weighted average
Compute material turnover and treat material losses correctly

scenes.text: A pump factory halts production because ₹300 bearings ran out, while its stores are full of slow-moving castings.
Proper purchase procedure and selective control prevent both stock-outs and dead stock.

steps.title: Purchase procedure and documents
steps.body:
1. **Purchase requisition** – from stores or department
2. Inviting quotations, selecting supplier
3. **Purchase order** to the supplier
4. Receiving and inspection – **goods received note (GRN)**, inspection report
5. Checking and passing the invoice for payment

Stores issue against a **material requisition note**; excess returns via **material return note**; transfers via **material transfer note**. Bin cards (quantity, kept by storekeeper) and stores ledger (quantity and value, kept by cost department).

steps.title: Selective control
steps.body:
- **ABC analysis**: A items – few items, high value (e.g. ~10% items, ~70% value) – tight control; C items – many items, low value – simple control
- **VED**: vital, essential, desirable (for spares)
- **FSN**: fast, slow, non-moving
- **JIT**: materials arrive just when needed, minimising stock
- **Perpetual inventory** with continuous stock verification

steps.title: Solved: ABC classification
steps.body:
10 items. Items P and Q (20% of items) account for ₹7,00,000 of ₹10,00,000 annual usage (70%); items R, S, T (30%) for ₹2,00,000 (20%); the other 5 (50%) for ₹1,00,000 (10%).

- **A**: P, Q – weekly review, exact EOQ
- **B**: R, S, T – monthly review
- **C**: rest – bulk ordering, periodic checks

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Classifying ABC by number of units instead of annual value.
- Confusing bin card (quantity only) with stores ledger (quantity and value).
- Ignoring cheap but vital spares – VED handles these.

activity.prompt: Which department or person normally keeps or raises the document?

quiz.q: A bin card records:
quiz.why: The bin card is kept by the storekeeper and shows quantities received, issued and in hand.

quiz.q: 'A' items in ABC analysis are:
quiz.why: A few items account for most of the annual consumption value.

quiz.q: The document authorising stores to issue material is the:
quiz.why: Departments draw materials from stores against a material requisition.

quiz.q: JIT aims to:
quiz.why: Just-in-time minimises stock by timing deliveries to production needs.

scenes.text: Ordering often means many delivery and paperwork costs; ordering in bulk ties up cash and space.
EOQ finds the order size where the two costs balance.

steps.title: EOQ formula
steps.body:
**EOQ = √(2AO ÷ C)**
- A = annual demand (units)
- O = cost per order
- C = carrying cost per unit per year (often % of unit price)

At EOQ, annual ordering cost = annual carrying cost.
Ordering cost = (A ÷ Q) × O; carrying cost = (Q ÷ 2) × C.

steps.title: Stock levels
steps.body:
- **Re-order level** = Maximum usage × Maximum lead time
- **Minimum level** = ROL − (Normal usage × Normal lead time)
- **Maximum level** = ROL + ROQ − (Minimum usage × Minimum lead time)
- **Average level** = (Minimum + Maximum) ÷ 2, or Minimum + ½ ROQ
- **Danger level** = Average (or minimum) usage × emergency lead time

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using monthly demand with annual carrying cost in EOQ.
- Forgetting that carrying cost given as a % must be multiplied by unit price.
- Using normal usage instead of maximum usage for the re-order level.

activity.prompt: Annual demand 20,000 units; ordering cost ₹250 per order; unit price ₹50; carrying cost 20% of unit price per year. EOQ (units)?

quiz.q: At EOQ:
quiz.why: Total cost is minimised where annual ordering and carrying costs are equal.

quiz.q: Maximum usage 400 units/week, maximum lead time 6 weeks. Re-order level:
Minimum level 500, ROQ 1,200. Average stock (alternative formula):
quiz.why: Minimum + ½ ROQ = 500 + 600 = 1,100.

scenes.text: A fabricator bought steel at ₹20, ₹22 and ₹25 per kg in one month.
Which price should a job be charged when steel is issued?

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
- **FIFO**: issues priced at earliest prices; closing stock at latest prices
- **Weighted average**: new average after each receipt = total value ÷ total units
- **Simple average**, **standard price**, **replacement price**, **specific price** (for special jobs)
- **LIFO** appears in older syllabi; it is **not permitted under AS 2** for inventory valuation in financial statements.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Recomputing the weighted average after an issue (it changes only on receipts).
- Pricing FIFO issues at the latest price.
- Stating LIFO is acceptable under AS 2.

activity.prompt: Receipts: 400 units @ ₹10, then 600 units @ ₹12. Issue: 700 units. Using FIFO, what is the value of the issue (₹)?

quiz.q: In rising prices, FIFO gives closing stock at:
quiz.why: Earliest units go out first, so remaining stock carries the latest prices.

quiz.q: Weighted average price changes after:
quiz.why: A new receipt changes the total value and units, so a new average is computed.

quiz.q: Which method is not permitted by AS 2?
quiz.why: AS 2 (revised) does not allow LIFO for inventory valuation.

quiz.q: 200 units @ ₹15 and 300 units @ ₹20 in stock. Weighted average price:

scenes.text: A chemical unit loses 2% of solvent through evaporation every month, and once loses a full drum to theft.
The two losses are treated very differently in the cost accounts.

steps.title: Material turnover ratio
steps.body:
**Turnover ratio = Cost of materials consumed ÷ Average stock**
Average stock = (Opening + Closing) ÷ 2
**Days held = 365 ÷ Turnover ratio**

High turnover = fast-moving; low turnover = slow-moving or overstocking.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Opening stock 20,000; closing 30,000; consumed 2,00,000.

- Average stock = 25,000
- **Turnover = 8 times**
- Days = 365 ÷ 8 ≈ **45.6 days**

steps.title: Losses
steps.body:
- **Wastage / normal loss** (evaporation, shrinkage): absorbed by good units – raises their cost
- **Abnormal loss** (theft, fire, careless handling): valued at cost and charged to **Costing P&L A/c**
- **Scrap**: residue with small value – sale value credited to the job/process or to overheads
- **Spoilage** (damaged units beyond rectification) and **defectives** (rectifiable)

steps.title: Solved: normal loss
steps.body:
1,000 kg bought at ₹50 = ₹50,000; normal loss 4%.

- Good units = 960 kg
- **Cost per good kg = 50,000 ÷ 960 = ₹52.08**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Charging normal loss to Costing P&L.
- Using closing stock instead of average stock in the turnover ratio.
- Ignoring scrap sale value in the cost of the job or process.

activity.prompt: Opening material stock ₹36,000; closing stock ₹44,000; materials consumed ₹3,20,000. Material turnover ratio (times)?

quiz.q: Normal loss of material is:
quiz.why: Unavoidable loss is part of the cost of good output.

quiz.q: Abnormal loss is transferred to:
quiz.why: Avoidable losses should not inflate product cost, so they go to Costing P&L.

quiz.q: Turnover ratio 10 times means material is held for about:
Rectifiable faulty units are called:
quiz.why: Defectives can be brought up to standard with extra work.

questions.q: GRN stands for:
questions.why: The goods received note records materials received and inspected.

questions.q: VED analysis is mainly used for:
questions.why: VED classifies spares by criticality: vital, essential, desirable.

ROL 2,500; ROQ 3,000; minimum usage 100/day; minimum lead time 8 days. Maximum level:

Same data, weighted average price after both receipts:
Material bought 2,000 kg for ₹1,00,000; normal loss 5%. Cost per good kg:
Material turnover 6 times. Average holding period:
Theft of material is a:
questions.why: Theft is avoidable, so it is an abnormal loss.

questions.why: The stores ledger shows quantities and values and is kept by the costing department.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Labour cost and overheads
courses.summary: Time-keeping and time-booking, idle and overtime, labour turnover, time and piece rates with Halsey and Rowan incentive plans, overhead classification, allocation and apportionment with secondary distribution by the simultaneous-equation method, machine hour rate, and under- or over-absorption of overheads.
outcomes: Compute labour turnover by separation, replacement and flux methods
Compute earnings under time rate, piece rate, Halsey and Rowan plans
Apportion overheads to departments and redistribute service department costs
Compute a machine hour rate
Find and treat under- or over-absorbed overheads

lessons.title: Labour records, idle time and labour turnover

scenes.text: A Chennai auto-parts unit loses 20 trained workers in a year and must hire and train replacements.
Labour turnover figures show management how costly this churn has become.

steps.title: Time-keeping and time-booking
steps.body:
- **Time-keeping**: recording attendance (gate cards, biometric systems)
- **Time-booking**: recording time spent on each job (job cards) – so wages can be charged to jobs
- **Idle time**: paid time with no production. Normal idle time (tea breaks, tool setting) → factory overhead; abnormal idle time (power failure, strike, machine breakdown) → Costing P&L
- **Overtime premium**: if due to general pressure → overhead; if at customer's request for a job → charge to that job; if abnormal → Costing P&L

steps.title: Labour turnover
steps.body:
Average workers = (opening + closing) ÷ 2
- **Separation method** = Separations ÷ Average workers × 100
- **Replacement method** = Replacements ÷ Average workers × 100
- **Flux method** = (Separations + Replacements) ÷ Average workers × 100 (some texts use separations + total accessions)

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Workers: 380 at start, 420 at end → average 400. Separations 20; replacements 16; new hires for expansion 24.

- Separation = 20/400 = **5%**
- Replacement = 16/400 = **4%**
- Flux (separations + replacements) = 36/400 = **9%**
- Flux (separations + all accessions 40) = 60/400 = 15%

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting new hires for expansion as replacements.
- Charging abnormal idle time to the product.
- Using closing workers instead of the average.

activity.prompt: Workers on roll: 1,150 at the start and 1,250 at the end of the year. 60 workers left and 48 were replaced. Labour turnover by the separation method (%)?

quiz.q: Idle time due to power failure is:
quiz.why: A power failure is avoidable and irregular, so it is abnormal idle time.

quiz.q: Overtime premium for a rush order at a customer's request is charged to:
quiz.why: The customer caused the extra cost, so it is charged to the job.

quiz.q: Time-booking records:
quiz.why: Time-booking allocates paid time to jobs or activities.

lessons.title: Time rate, piece rate, Halsey and Rowan

scenes.text: A machinist is allowed 10 hours for a job but finishes in 8.
Incentive plans share the value of the saved time between worker and employer.

steps.title: Basic methods
steps.body:
- **Time rate**: Earnings = Hours worked × Rate. Simple; no incentive.
- **Straight piece rate**: Earnings = Units × Rate per unit. Incentive for speed; quality may suffer.
- **Taylor's differential piece rate**: lower rate (e.g. 83%) below standard, higher rate (e.g. 125%) at or above standard.

steps.title: Premium bonus plans
steps.body:
Let S = standard time, T = time taken, R = rate per hour.
- **Halsey**: Earnings = T × R + 50% × (S − T) × R
- **Rowan**: Earnings = T × R + [(S − T) ÷ S] × T × R

Both guarantee time wages. Under Rowan the bonus as a fraction of time wages equals (S − T) ÷ S, so it can never reach the full time wage, and the bonus amount falls once savings exceed 50%.

steps.title: Equal earnings point
steps.body: Halsey and Rowan give equal bonus when time saved is exactly 50% of standard time. Below 50% saving Rowan pays more; above 50% Halsey pays more.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using standard time instead of time taken in the Rowan multiplier.
- Forgetting the guaranteed time wage component.
- Applying Halsey at 100% of time saved.

activity.prompt: Standard time 12 hours, time taken 9 hours, rate ₹40 per hour. Total earnings under the Rowan plan (₹)?

quiz.q: Under Halsey, the worker receives what share of time saved?
quiz.why: The standard Halsey plan pays 50% of time saved at the hourly rate.

quiz.q: S = 8 h, T = 6 h, R = ₹30. Halsey earnings:
Time saved is 50% of standard. Compared with Rowan, Halsey bonus is:
quiz.why: At 50% saving, both formulas give the same bonus.

quiz.q: Straight piece rate earnings for 240 units at ₹2.50:

scenes.text: The factory canteen and maintenance shop serve the machining and assembly departments.
Their costs must be shared out fairly before products can be costed.

steps.title: Primary distribution
steps.body:
- **Allocation**: charging a whole item to one cost centre (supervisor's salary of one department)
- **Apportionment**: sharing common items on a suitable base:
  - Rent, rates, lighting → floor area
  - Power → horsepower × machine hours
  - Depreciation, insurance of plant → value of plant
  - Canteen, welfare, ESI → number of workers
  - Supervision → direct labour hours or number of workers

steps.title: Solved: apportionment
steps.body:
Rent ₹24,000; floor area: Production A 2,000 sq ft, Production B 3,000, Service S 1,000 (total 6,000).

- A = 24,000 × 2/6 = **8,000**; B = **12,000**; S = **4,000**

steps.title: Secondary distribution
steps.body:
Service department costs are redistributed to production departments:
- **Direct redistribution** – ignore services between service departments
- **Step (non-reciprocal)** – service departments closed one by one
- **Reciprocal**: repeated distribution, trial-and-error, or **simultaneous equations**

steps.title: Solved: simultaneous equations
steps.body:
Service X: own cost ₹9,000, receives 20% of Y's cost. Service Y: own cost ₹4,500, receives 50% of X's cost.

- X = 9,000 + 0.2Y; Y = 4,500 + 0.5X
- X = 9,000 + 0.2(4,500 + 0.5X) = 9,900 + 0.1X → 0.9X = 9,900 → **X = 11,000**
- **Y = 4,500 + 5,500 = 10,000**

These totals are then shared among production departments in the given percentages.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Apportioning rent on number of workers.
- Forgetting that the totals from simultaneous equations exceed own costs because of reciprocal services.
- Leaving a balance in a service department after redistribution.

activity.prompt: Power cost ₹36,000 is apportioned on horsepower × machine hours. Department P: 20 HP × 500 hours; Department Q: 10 HP × 800 hours. Power charged to P (₹)?

quiz.q: Most suitable base for apportioning canteen expenses:
quiz.why: Canteen benefits employees, so the number of workers is the fair base.

quiz.q: Charging the whole of an identifiable item to one department is:
quiz.why: Allocation charges a cost wholly to one cost centre.

quiz.q: Fire insurance on plant is usually apportioned on:
quiz.why: Insurance premium depends on the value insured.

quiz.q: Reciprocal services can be handled by:
quiz.why: Simultaneous equations account for services that departments give each other.

lessons.title: Absorption, machine hour rate and under/over-absorption

scenes.text: A tool room's CNC machine does work for many jobs.
Charging each job by machine hours used needs a machine hour rate.

steps.title: Absorption methods
steps.body:

- **Direct labour hour rate** = Overheads ÷ Direct labour hours
- **Machine hour rate** = Overheads ÷ Machine hours (best where machines dominate)
- Rate per unit of output

Pre-determined rate = Budgeted overheads ÷ Budgeted base.

steps.title: Solved: machine hour rate

- Depreciation = 20,000 ÷ 2,000 = 10.00 per hour
- Power = 30.00 per hour

- Absorbed = 55,000 × 5 = 2,75,000
- **Under-absorbed = ₹15,000**

Treatment: if due to normal causes and material – supplementary rate on WIP, finished stock and cost of sales; if abnormal (strike, idle capacity) – Costing P&L; if small – Costing P&L.

scenes.text: A Kolkata printer handles wedding cards, a school's annual magazine and posters – each order different.
Each order gets its own job number and cost sheet.

steps.title: Job costing
steps.body:
Used where work is done to customer specifications and each job is distinct (printing, furniture, repair workshops, interior design).

Procedure: production order → job number → materials via requisitions, labour via job cards, overheads at pre-determined rates → job cost sheet → profit on completion.

steps.title: Solved: job cost sheet
steps.body:
Job 214: materials ₹12,000; labour 80 hours at ₹50; factory overheads ₹40 per labour hour; administration overheads 10% of works cost; profit 20% on cost.

- Labour 4,000; FOH 3,200 → **works cost 19,200**
- Admin 1,920 → **total cost 21,120**
- Profit 4,224 → **price ₹25,344**

steps.title: Batch costing and EBQ
steps.body:
A batch of identical units is treated as one job; cost per unit = batch cost ÷ units (pharmaceuticals, garments, components).

**Economic batch quantity = √(2DS ÷ C)**
- D = annual demand, S = set-up cost per batch, C = carrying cost per unit per year

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Charging actual overheads (unknown until year end) to jobs instead of pre-determined rates.
- Using ordering cost in EBQ – it is set-up cost.
- Computing profit on selling price when it is stated on cost.

How much of the profit earned so far can be safely taken to P&L?

steps.title: Key terms
steps.body:
- **Work certified**: value of work approved by the architect/engineer (at contract price)
- **Work uncertified**: work done but not yet certified (at cost)
- **Retention money**: part of certified value withheld by the contractee
- **Notional profit** = (Work certified + Work uncertified) − Cost of work to date
- **Escalation clause**: allows the price to rise with input costs

steps.title: Profit on incomplete contracts (traditional rules)
steps.body:
Stage of completion = Work certified ÷ Contract price.
- Below 25%: no profit
- 25%–50%: ⅓ × Notional profit × Cash received ÷ Work certified
- 50%–90%: ⅔ × Notional profit × Cash received ÷ Work certified
- Near completion (90%+): Estimated total profit × Work certified ÷ Contract price (× cash ratio as per question)

Any expected loss is provided in full. (AS 7 revised uses the percentage-of-completion method in financial statements.)

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Contract price ₹20,00,000; work certified 12,00,000; uncertified 50,000; cost to date 9,50,000; cash received 9,60,000 (80% of certified).

- Notional profit = 12,50,000 − 9,50,000 = **3,00,000**
- Completion = 60% → ⅔ rule
- **Profit to P&L = ⅔ × 3,00,000 × 80% = ₹1,60,000**
- Reserve carried forward = 1,40,000

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Valuing uncertified work at contract price (it is at cost).
- Using cash ÷ contract price instead of cash ÷ work certified.
- Taking any profit when work is below 25% complete.

activity.prompt: Contract price ₹10,00,000; work certified ₹6,00,000; notional profit ₹2,40,000; cash received is 90% of work certified. Profit to be credited to P&L (₹)?

quiz.why: Uncertified work has not been approved, so it is carried at cost.

quiz.why: Below 25% completion no profit is recognised.

quiz.why: The contractee holds back a percentage until the work is satisfactorily completed.

quiz.why: Prudence requires full provision for foreseeable losses.

lessons.title: Process costing: normal loss, abnormal loss and gain

scenes.text: Cane passes through crushing, boiling and crystallising; some weight is always lost.
Expected losses raise unit cost; unexpected losses are isolated so they do not hide inefficiency.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- **Normal loss**: expected; credited to process at scrap value; cost absorbed by good units
- **Cost per unit** = (Total process cost − Scrap value of normal loss) ÷ (Input − Normal loss units)
- **Abnormal loss**: actual loss > normal; valued at cost per unit; transferred to Abnormal Loss A/c → scrap value credited → balance to Costing P&L
- **Abnormal gain**: actual loss < normal; valued at cost per unit; debited to process; Abnormal Gain A/c credited to Costing P&L after reducing for scrap value forgone

steps.title: Solved: abnormal loss
steps.body:
Input 1,000 units; total process cost ₹27,500; normal loss 10% with scrap value ₹5 per unit; output 850 units.

- Normal loss 100 units → scrap 500
- Cost per unit = (27,500 − 500) ÷ 900 = **₹30**
- Output 850 × 30 = **25,500**
- Abnormal loss 50 × 30 = **1,500**; scrap 50 × 5 = 250 → **net to Costing P&L ₹1,250**
- Check: 500 + 25,500 + 1,500 = 27,500 ✓

steps.title: Solved: abnormal gain
steps.body:
Same data but output 920 units.

- Abnormal gain = 920 − 900 = 20 units × 30 = **600** (debited to process)
- Scrap forgone 20 × 5 = 100 → **net gain to Costing P&L ₹500**
- Output value = 920 × 30 = 27,600

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Valuing abnormal loss at scrap value instead of cost per normal unit.
- Dividing by actual output rather than normal output.
- Forgetting to reduce abnormal gain by scrap value forgone.

activity.prompt: Input 2,000 units; total process cost ₹39,000; normal loss 5% with scrap value ₹10 per unit; actual output 1,920 units. Value of output transferred to the next process (₹)?

quiz.q: Normal loss units are credited to the process at:
quiz.why: Only the scrap value of normal loss is recovered; its cost falls on good units.

quiz.q: Abnormal loss is valued at:
options: cost of a normal good unit
quiz.why: It is valued as if it were good output, so the inefficiency is fully measured.

quiz.q: Input 500, normal loss 10%, output 460. This is:
quiz.why: Normal output is 450; actual 460 gives an abnormal gain of 10 units.

quiz.q: Net abnormal loss is finally transferred to:
quiz.why: After crediting scrap, the balance of abnormal loss is written off to Costing P&L.

lessons.title: Equivalent production, joint products and by-products

scenes.text: At month end, a paint plant has 2,000 litres with all pigments added but only half the mixing done.
Equivalent units let it compare finished and unfinished output on one scale.

steps.title: Equivalent units (no opening WIP)
steps.body:
EU = Completed units + (Closing WIP × % completion), computed separately for materials and conversion (labour + overheads).

Cost per EU = Cost of element ÷ EU of that element.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Introduced 10,000 units; completed 8,000; closing WIP 2,000 (materials 100%, conversion 50%). Materials ₹50,000; conversion ₹36,000.

- EU materials = 10,000 → ₹5
- EU conversion = 8,000 + 1,000 = 9,000 → ₹4
- Completed: 8,000 × 9 = **₹72,000**
- WIP: 2,000 × 5 + 1,000 × 4 = **₹14,000**
- Check: 86,000 ✓

steps.title: Joint products and by-products
steps.body:
- **Joint products**: two or more products of significant value from one process (petrol and diesel). Joint cost up to the split-off point apportioned by physical units, sales value at split-off, or net realisable value.
- **By-products**: minor value (molasses from sugar). Usually their net realisable value is credited to the main product's process account.

steps.title: Solved: joint cost
steps.body:
Joint cost ₹60,000. Product A: 2,000 units selling at ₹30 (₹60,000); B: 3,000 units at ₹20 (₹60,000).

- Sales value basis (1:1): **A 30,000; B 30,000**
- Physical units basis (2:3): **A 24,000; B 36,000**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using one EU figure for both materials and conversion when completion differs.
- Apportioning costs incurred after split-off as joint costs.
- Treating a by-product's sales as main revenue instead of a cost reduction.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Operating costing, reconciliation and modern techniques
courses.summary: Service (operating) costing for transport and similar services using composite units, reconciliation of profit shown by cost and financial accounts, activity-based costing with cost pools and drivers, and an overview of integrated and non-integrated accounts, cost audit, uniform and target costing.
outcomes: Compute composite cost units such as passenger-km and tonne-km
Prepare a memorandum reconciliation statement
Assign overheads using activity-based costing
Distinguish integrated and non-integrated cost accounting systems and describe other cost-management tools

scenes.text: A private operator runs a 50-seat bus between two towns 100 km apart.
To set a fare, it needs the cost per passenger-kilometre.

steps.title: Meaning and cost units
steps.body:
Operating costing is used for services: transport, hospitals, hotels, power, canteens. Composite units combine two factors:
- Passenger-km (bus, airline), tonne-km (goods transport)
- Bed-day / patient-day (hospital), room-day (hotel), kWh (power)

Costs are grouped as **standing (fixed) charges** – driver salary, insurance, garage rent, road tax; **running (variable) charges** – fuel, oil, tyres, depreciation linked to use; **maintenance charges** – repairs, overhaul.

steps.title: Solved: passenger-km
steps.body:
Bus: 50 seats, 80% average occupancy, 2 round trips a day of 100 km each way, 25 days a month. Monthly cost ₹1,60,000.

- Km per month = 2 × 200 × 25 = 10,000
- Passenger-km = 10,000 × 50 × 80% = **4,00,000**
- **Cost per passenger-km = ₹0.40**

steps.title: Solved: tonne-km
steps.body:
Lorry: A→B 120 km with 6 t; B→C 80 km with 4 t; C→A 100 km empty.

- **Absolute tonne-km** = 6 × 120 + 4 × 80 = **1,040**
- **Commercial tonne-km** = average load × total km = (6 + 4 + 0) ÷ 3 × 300 = **1,000**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to double one-way distance for round trips.
- Applying occupancy to kilometres instead of to seats.
- Using commercial tonne-km when absolute is asked.

lessons.title: Reconciliation of cost and financial accounts

scenes.text: The cost department reports a profit of ₹1,20,000; the financial accounts show ₹1,14,000.
A reconciliation statement explains every rupee of difference.

steps.title: Reasons for difference
steps.body:
1. **Items only in financial accounts**: incomes (interest, dividend, rent received, profit on sale of assets) and charges (interest paid, preliminary expenses written off, donations, fines, loss on sale of assets, goodwill written off)
2. **Items only in cost accounts**: notional charges (notional rent, interest on capital)
3. **Under/over-absorption of overheads** in cost accounts
4. **Different stock valuation** methods
5. **Different depreciation** methods

steps.title: Rule of thumb
steps.body:
Starting from **costing profit**:
- **Add** items that make financial profit higher: financial-only incomes, over-absorbed overheads, notional costs, higher stock values in financial books (closing) …
- **Deduct** items that make financial profit lower: financial-only expenses, under-absorbed overheads, lower closing stock in financial books …

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Costing profit ₹1,20,000. Factory overheads under-absorbed ₹8,000; administration overheads over-absorbed ₹3,000; interest received ₹5,000 (not in cost books); preliminary expenses written off ₹4,000; closing stock valued ₹2,000 higher in cost books.

- 1,20,000 − 8,000 + 3,000 + 5,000 − 4,000 − 2,000
- **Profit per financial accounts = ₹1,14,000**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding under-absorbed overheads (actual costs were higher, so financial profit is lower).
- Including income-tax as a reconciling item without noting it is an appropriation – check the question.
- Reversing the sign for opening stock differences (an opening stock overvaluation in financial books reduces financial profit).

activity.prompt: Costing profit ₹2,50,000. Dividend received ₹10,000 (financial books only). Donation ₹6,000 (financial books only). Factory overheads over-absorbed in cost books ₹12,000. Depreciation: ₹50,000 in financial books, ₹44,000 in cost books. Profit per financial accounts (₹)?

quiz.why: Actual overheads exceeded those charged in cost books, so financial profit is lower.

quiz.q: Interest received appearing only in financial books is:
quiz.why: It raises financial profit without appearing in cost books.

quiz.q: Notional rent charged only in cost books is, from costing profit:
quiz.why: Financial books have no such charge, so financial profit is higher.

quiz.q: Which is a purely financial item?
quiz.why: Goodwill write-off is an appropriation-type financial charge excluded from cost accounts.

story.title: The small orders that cost a lot

scenes.text: A components maker absorbs all overheads on labour hours and finds its tiny custom orders look profitable.
ABC shows that each small order needs many set-ups and inspections that labour hours ignore.

steps.title: Concept
steps.body:
**ABC** assigns overheads to activities (cost pools) and then to products by the products' use of **cost drivers**.

Steps:
1. Identify activities (set-ups, purchasing, inspection, material handling)
2. Collect cost of each activity into a pool
3. Choose a driver for each pool (number of set-ups, purchase orders, inspections, moves)
4. Rate = Pool cost ÷ Total driver volume
5. Charge products = Rate × Driver units used

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Set-up pool ₹60,000; total set-ups 30 → **₹2,000 per set-up**.
Inspection pool ₹40,000; inspections 200 → **₹200 per inspection**.

Product X: 10 set-ups, 50 inspections → 20,000 + 10,000 = **₹30,000**
Product Y: 20 set-ups, 150 inspections → 40,000 + 30,000 = **₹70,000**

steps.title: When ABC helps
steps.body: High overheads relative to direct costs, diverse product range, many small batches, or products using support activities very differently. Traditional volume-based absorption tends to over-cost high-volume products and under-cost low-volume, complex ones.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using one plant-wide rate and calling it ABC.
- Choosing a driver that does not cause the cost (e.g. labour hours for set-ups).
- Dividing pool cost by units of output instead of driver volume.

quiz.why: Purchasing effort grows with the number of orders handled.

lessons.title: Integrated accounts, cost audit and cost management tools

story.title: One set of books or two?

scenes.text: A mid-sized manufacturer keeps separate cost and financial ledgers and spends days reconciling them.
Integrated accounts record both in one system, so no reconciliation is needed.

steps.title: Non-integrated vs integrated
steps.body:
- **Non-integrated (cost ledger) system**: separate cost books with a **Cost Ledger Control A/c** (or General Ledger Adjustment A/c) representing the financial ledger; needs reconciliation.
- **Integrated system**: one set of accounts serves both purposes; no reconciliation; saves time; requires clear coding.

Main control accounts: Stores Ledger Control, WIP Control, Finished Goods Control, Wages Control, Overhead Control.

steps.title: Cost audit and cost records
steps.body: Under Section 148 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Central Government may require specified classes of companies to maintain cost records and, where thresholds are met, to have them audited by a cost accountant. Cost audit verifies cost records and checks adherence to costing principles.

steps.title: Other techniques
steps.body:
- **Uniform costing**: common costing methods in an industry (association members)
- **Inter-firm comparison** using uniform data
- **Target costing**: target cost = target price − desired profit; design to meet it
- **Life-cycle costing**: total cost over a product's life
- **Kaizen costing**: continuous small improvements in the production phase

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying cost audit is compulsory for every company.
- Confusing target costing (price-led) with cost-plus pricing.
- Thinking integrated accounts still need a reconciliation statement.

courses.summary: Formula sheet for the whole Cost Accounting paper, a practical on a complete cost sheet with per-unit figures and stock of finished goods, a practical on a process account with abnormal loss, previous-year-style questions with answer plans, and a 15-question paper-level exam.
outcomes: Recall all key cost formulas and treatments

scenes.text: Kabir lists every formula from the cost accounting paper on one page.
He tests himself until each one comes without looking.

steps.title: Cost sheet and classification
steps.body:
- Prime cost = DM + DL + DE
- Works cost = Prime + FOH + Opening WIP − Closing WIP
- Cost of production = Works + Office OH
- COGS = COP + Opening FG − Closing FG; Cost of sales = COGS + S&D
- High–low: variable rate = Δcost ÷ Δactivity
- 20% on sales = 25% on cost

steps.title: Materials and labour
steps.body:
- EOQ = √(2AO ÷ C); EBQ = √(2DS ÷ C)
- ROL = Max usage × Max lead time
- Min = ROL − Normal usage × Normal lead time
- Max = ROL + ROQ − Min usage × Min lead time
- Turnover = Consumed ÷ Average stock
- Halsey = TR + 50%(S − T)R; Rowan = TR + (S − T)/S × TR
- Separation rate = Separations ÷ Average workers

steps.title: Overheads and methods
steps.body:
- MHR = Hourly overheads (depreciation, power, repairs, standing charges)
- Under-absorbed = Actual − Absorbed (if positive)

- Process: Cost per unit = (Cost − scrap of normal loss) ÷ normal output
- EU = completed + WIP × % complete
- Reconciliation: from costing profit, add financial-only incomes and over-absorption; deduct financial-only expenses and under-absorption

uni-bcom-e-commerce.title: B.Com — E-commerce, unit by unit
uni-bcom-e-commerce.description: E-commerce for commerce students: business models, web and mobile infrastructure, electronic payments and security, digital marketing and metrics, logistics and CRM, and the legal and tax framework in India, with worked metric calculations. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Com programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Introduction to e-commerce and business models
courses.summary: Meaning, evolution, benefits and limitations of e-commerce; transaction types B2B, B2C, C2C, C2B, B2G and D2C; revenue models with marketplace arithmetic; and Indian structures — marketplace vs inventory models and ONDC.
outcomes: Define e-commerce and distinguish it from e-business
Classify transactions as B2B, B2C, C2C, C2B, B2G or D2C
Explain commission, subscription, advertising, freemium and transaction-fee revenue models
Compute marketplace revenue from GMV and take rate
Distinguish marketplace and inventory models under India's FDI policy

scenes.text: A Varanasi silk weaver sold only to walk-in customers for 30 years.
Now she lists on a marketplace and ships to buyers in Bengaluru and Dubai.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **E-commerce**: buying and selling of goods and services, and transfer of money and data, over electronic networks, mainly the internet.
- **E-business** is broader: all business processes done electronically — procurement, HR, supply chain, CRM — not just selling.
- Evolution: EDI and EFT (1970s–80s) → the web (1990s) → online marketplaces → mobile and app commerce → social and voice commerce.

steps.title: Benefits and limitations
steps.body:
**To firms**: global reach, lower costs, 24×7 operation, data on customers, low entry barriers.
**To consumers**: convenience, wider choice, price comparison, reviews.
**To society**: digital inclusion, employment in logistics, less travel.

**Limitations**: security and privacy risks, lack of touch-and-feel, returns and logistics costs, digital divide, trust issues, regulatory uncertainty.

steps.title: Traditional vs e-commerce
steps.body:
| Aspect | Traditional | E-commerce |
|---|---|---|
| Hours | Fixed | 24×7 |
| Reach | Local | Global |
| Set-up cost | High (rent) | Lower |
| Customer data | Limited | Detailed analytics |
| Inspection | Physical | Images, reviews, returns |

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using e-commerce and e-business as exact synonyms.
- Assuming online always means cheaper — logistics and returns can raise costs.

activity.prompt: Is each item a benefit or a limitation of e-commerce?

quiz.q: E-business differs from e-commerce in that it:
options: covers all business processes done electronically
quiz.why: E-business includes internal processes like procurement and HR, not just online transactions.

quiz.q: EDI was an early form of:
quiz.why: Electronic Data Interchange let firms exchange standardised business documents electronically.

quiz.q: A major limitation of e-commerce is:
quiz.why: Online transactions expose data and payments to cyber threats.

scenes.text: A steel maker buys spare parts on a B2B portal, while a student sells her old cycle on a classifieds app.
The same week, a contractor bids on the government's GeM portal.

steps.title: Classification by parties
steps.body:
- **B2B**: business to business — bulk orders, procurement portals, IndiaMART-style marketplaces.
- **B2C**: business to consumer — online retail, food delivery.
- **C2C**: consumer to consumer — classifieds, resale platforms.
- **C2B**: consumer to business — freelancers, influencers, reverse auctions.
- **B2G / G2B**: business with government — e-procurement, **GeM** (Government e-Marketplace).
- **G2C**: government services online — e-filing of tax returns.
- **D2C**: brands selling directly to consumers through their own sites/apps.

steps.title: By channel
steps.body: - **M-commerce** (mobile), **social commerce** (shopping inside social apps), **quick commerce** (10–30 minute delivery from dark stores), **voice commerce**, **live-stream commerce**.

steps.title: Indian examples
steps.body: B2B: wholesale portals for kirana stores. B2C: large marketplaces and vertical sites. C2C: resale apps for used goods. B2G: GeM. G2C: income-tax e-filing portal and DigiLocker.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling freelancers selling services to firms C2C — that is C2B.
- Treating every marketplace as B2C — many are B2B.

story.title: How does the app make money?

scenes.text: A food-delivery app charges restaurants a commission, customers a delivery fee and brands for ads.
Each stream is a different revenue model.

steps.title: Models
steps.body:
- **Commission / take rate**: % of GMV (marketplaces).
- **Sales / margin**: buy low, sell high (inventory retailers).
- **Subscription**: recurring fee (OTT, membership programmes).
- **Advertising**: sponsored listings, display ads.
- **Freemium**: free basic tier, paid premium.
- **Transaction fee**: per-transaction charge (payment gateways).
- **Affiliate**: commission for referring sales.

**GMV** (gross merchandise value) = total value of goods sold through the platform.

steps.title: Solved: marketplace revenue
steps.body:
GMV ₹10 crore a month; average take rate 15%; advertising income ₹40 lakh.

- Commission revenue = 10 × 0.15 = **₹1.5 crore**
- Total revenue = 1.5 + 0.4 = **₹1.9 crore**

steps.title: Solved: subscription
steps.body:
20,000 subscribers at ₹199 a month.

- Monthly recurring revenue = ₹39,80,000
- Annual = 39,80,000 × 12 = **₹4.776 crore**
- If 5% churn each month and no new sign-ups, subscribers after 1 month = 19,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reporting GMV as a marketplace's revenue — revenue is only its commission and fees.
- Ignoring churn when projecting subscription revenue.

quiz.why: Viewers pay a recurring fee for access to content.

quiz.why: GMV measures gross sales passing through the platform before commissions and returns.

quiz.why: Freemium gives basic features free and charges for advanced ones.

lessons.title: Marketplace vs inventory models and ONDC

scenes.text: On a marketplace, thousands of independent sellers own the goods; the platform only connects buyers and sellers.
With ONDC, a buyer on one app can buy from a seller listed on a different app.

steps.title: Marketplace vs inventory
steps.body:
- **Marketplace model**: platform provides an IT platform to connect buyers and sellers; does not own inventory.
- **Inventory model**: the e-commerce entity owns the stock and sells directly.
- India's FDI policy permits **100% FDI under the automatic route in the marketplace model**; FDI is **not permitted in the inventory-based model** of B2C e-commerce.
- Press Note 2 (2018) tightened rules, e.g. marketplaces cannot control sellers' inventory or influence prices.

steps.title: ONDC
steps.body: **Open Network for Digital Commerce** (launched 2022, a DPIIT initiative) is an open protocol, not an app. Buyer apps and seller apps interoperate, so small sellers can be discovered across networks — similar in spirit to how UPI made payments interoperable.

steps.title: Solved: seller's net payout
steps.body:
A seller lists a ₹1,000 kurta. Marketplace commission 18%, fixed closing fee ₹20, shipping ₹60, GST on fees ignored for simplicity.

- Deductions = 180 + 20 + 60 = ₹260
- **Net payout = ₹740** (before tax-related deductions like TCS)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling ONDC a shopping app — it is a network protocol.
- Assuming foreign-owned platforms may hold their own inventory for B2C sales in India.

quiz.why: India's FDI policy permits automatic-route FDI only in the marketplace model of e-commerce.

quiz.why: ONDC lets buyer and seller apps on different platforms transact through open protocols.

quiz.q: In the inventory model, the stock is owned by:
quiz.why: The platform itself buys and holds goods before selling them.

questions.why: Both parties are consumers.

questions.why: Government provides a service to citizens online.

questions.why: An individual supplies services to businesses.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Internet infrastructure, websites and m-commerce
courses.summary: Internet, intranet and extranet; how the web works — IP addresses, DNS, HTTP/HTTPS and hosting; planning and designing an e-commerce website; and mobile commerce with app-based business, including uptime and traffic calculations.
outcomes: Distinguish internet, intranet and extranet with business uses
Explain IP addressing, DNS resolution and HTTPS in simple terms
List the steps and components of building an e-commerce website
Apply usability principles to e-commerce site design
Compute uptime, downtime and bandwidth for a website

scenes.text: A distributor's staff check leave balances on the intranet.
Its dealers log in to an extranet to place orders, while customers browse the public website on the internet.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Internet**: global public network of networks using TCP/IP.
- **Intranet**: private network inside an organisation using internet technologies — HR portals, internal documents.
- **Extranet**: part of an intranet opened securely to selected outsiders — suppliers, dealers, banks.
- **WWW**: system of linked web pages accessed over the internet via browsers; email, FTP and VoIP are other internet services.

steps.title: Business uses
steps.body:
- Internet: marketing, online sales, customer support.
- Intranet: knowledge sharing, workflow, training.
- Extranet: supply-chain coordination, order tracking, EDI-like exchanges, dealer portals.

steps.title: Security
steps.body: Intranets and extranets are protected by **firewalls**, user authentication and often **VPNs** (virtual private networks) that create encrypted tunnels over the public internet.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the web and the internet the same thing — the web is one service running on the internet.
- Thinking an extranet is open to the public.

activity.prompt: Which network best fits each use?

items.text: Supplier portal to view purchase orders
Dealer login to check stock and place orders

quiz.q: An extranet is accessible to:
quiz.why: An extranet extends parts of the intranet to authorised suppliers, dealers or customers.

quiz.q: The internet uses the protocol suite:
quiz.why: TCP/IP is the foundational communication protocol suite of the internet.

quiz.q: A VPN provides:
options: an encrypted tunnel over a public network
quiz.why: VPNs encrypt traffic so remote users can securely access private networks.

lessons.title: How the web works: IP, DNS, HTTP and hosting

scenes.text: Priya types shop.example.com in her browser.
In milliseconds, DNS finds the server's IP address and the browser fetches the page securely over HTTPS.

steps.title: Building blocks
steps.body:
- **IP address**: numeric address of a device (IPv4 like 192.168.1.10; IPv6 for a much larger address space).
- **Domain name**: human-readable name (example.com); registered with a registrar; top-level domains such as .com, .in, .org.
- **DNS**: the internet's directory that translates domain names into IP addresses.
- **HTTP/HTTPS**: protocol for requesting web pages; HTTPS adds **TLS encryption** (padlock icon).
- **URL** = protocol + domain + path, e.g. https://shop.example.com/cart.

steps.title: Hosting and stack
steps.body:
- **Web hosting**: shared, VPS, dedicated, **cloud** (scalable, pay-as-you-use).
- **CDN** (content delivery network) caches content near users to speed up pages.
- Front end (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) vs back end (server code, database).
- Ready platforms: hosted store builders and open-source CMS with shopping plugins.

steps.title: Solved: bandwidth
steps.body:
Average page weight 2 MB; 10,000 visitors a day each viewing 5 pages.

- Daily transfer = 2 × 5 × 10,000 = 1,00,000 MB ≈ **100 GB/day** (using 1 GB = 1,000 MB)
- Monthly (30 days) ≈ **3,000 GB = 3 TB** — a CDN and image compression would cut this sharply.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking HTTPS makes a site trustworthy — it encrypts the connection but says nothing about the seller's honesty.
- Confusing domain registration with hosting.

activity.prompt: Page weight 1.5 MB, 4 pages per visit, 20,000 visits a day. Daily data transfer in GB (1 GB = 1,000 MB)?

quiz.q: DNS converts:
quiz.why: DNS works like a phone book, mapping names to numeric IP addresses.

quiz.q: HTTPS differs from HTTP by:
quiz.why: HTTPS encrypts data between browser and server using TLS.

quiz.q: A CDN helps by:
options: serving content from servers close to users
quiz.why: Caching content near users reduces latency and server load.

scenes.text: A shopper adds shoes to the cart, then sees a surprise ₹150 delivery fee and a seven-field sign-up form.
She closes the tab. Good design could have saved that sale.

steps.title: Steps to build
steps.body:
1. Define goals, target customers and product range
2. Choose domain name and hosting/platform
3. Design structure: home, category, product, cart, checkout, account, policies
4. Integrate payment gateway, shipping and tax settings
5. Add security (TLS certificate), privacy policy, terms, grievance officer details
6. Test (devices, browsers, load) → launch → monitor analytics → improve

steps.title: Design principles
steps.body:
- **Mobile-first** responsive layout
- Fast loading (compressed images, caching)
- Clear navigation and search with filters
- High-quality product images, specifications, reviews
- **Transparent pricing**: show taxes, delivery charges and return policy early
- Short checkout, guest checkout, multiple payment options
- Accessibility: readable fonts, alt text for images, contrast
- Trust signals: secure badge, contact details, easy returns

steps.title: Solved: uptime
steps.body:
Host promises **99.9%** uptime.

- Hours in 30 days = 720
- Allowed downtime = 0.1% × 720 = 0.72 h = **43.2 minutes per month**
- At 99.99%: 4.32 minutes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Hiding delivery fees until the last step.
- Forcing account creation before checkout.

activity.prompt: Uptime guarantee 99.5% over a 30-day month. Maximum downtime in hours?

quiz.why: Most Indian shoppers browse on phones, so layouts start from the mobile experience.

quiz.why: Surprise fees at the last step make many shoppers abandon the purchase.

quiz.q: Alt text on images improves:
options: accessibility for screen-reader users and search visibility
quiz.why: Alt text describes images for visually impaired users and helps search engines.

scenes.text: A tea-stall owner in Assam orders stock, pays suppliers by UPI and checks prices — all on a budget smartphone.
Cheap data and smartphones made India a mobile-first e-commerce market.

steps.title: M-commerce
steps.body:
**M-commerce**: commercial transactions through mobile devices — shopping apps, mobile banking, ticketing, UPI payments, mobile wallets.

Features: ubiquity, personalisation, location awareness, instant connectivity, push notifications.

Technologies: 4G/5G, mobile apps, mobile web, **QR codes**, NFC, SMS, USSD.

steps.title: Native app vs mobile web vs PWA
steps.body:
- **Native app**: installed from store; fast, uses device features, needs updates and storage.
- **Mobile website**: no install; reachable via search.
- **PWA** (progressive web app): web app with app-like features (offline, add to home screen).

Apps give better retention; mobile web gives wider reach.

steps.title: Challenges
steps.body: Small screens, network variability, device diversity, security (lost phones, malicious apps), app fatigue, regional-language needs. Vernacular interfaces and voice search help reach new users.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Building only an app and ignoring mobile web discovery.
- Assuming all users have fast 5G connections.

Can send push notifications by default

quiz.why: Progressive web apps run in the browser but can work offline and be added to the home screen.

quiz.q: Location-based offers are a feature of:
quiz.why: Mobile devices know the user's location, enabling local offers.

quiz.q: Vernacular interfaces help to:
options: reach users who prefer regional languages
quiz.why: Many new Indian internet users are more comfortable in regional languages.

questions.q: An intranet is:
options: a private network using internet technology
questions.why: Intranets serve an organisation's internal users.

questions.q: The web is:
options: a service running on the internet
questions.why: The WWW is an information system accessed over the internet.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Electronic payments and e-commerce security
courses.summary: Electronic payment systems — cards, net banking, wallets, UPI, BNPL — and the payment-gateway flow with merchant charges; security threats; encryption, digital signatures, certificates and TLS; and fraud prevention practices.
outcomes: Trace an online card or UPI payment through gateway, acquirer and issuer
Compute gateway charges, GST on fees and chargeback ratios
Identify common e-commerce security threats and their controls
Distinguish symmetric and asymmetric encryption and count keys required
Explain digital signatures, certifying authorities and TLS

scenes.text: Arjun clicks 'Pay now' for a ₹2,000 order and enters an OTP.
In two seconds, his bank, the merchant's bank, a card network and a gateway have all exchanged messages.

steps.title: Modes
steps.body:
- **Cards**: credit, debit, prepaid; networks such as RuPay, Visa, Mastercard; two-factor authentication (OTP) for online use in India.
- **Net banking**: redirect to the bank's site.
- **UPI**: real-time bank-to-bank via VPA/QR, operated by NPCI.
- **Prepaid payment instruments (wallets)**: regulated by the RBI.
- **BNPL** (buy now pay later), **EMI** options, **cash on delivery** (COD).
- **Card tokenisation**: merchants store tokens instead of card numbers (RBI mandate).

steps.title: Payment flow
steps.body:
1. Customer enters details on the merchant's checkout
2. **Payment gateway** encrypts and forwards to the **acquiring bank** (merchant's bank) or **payment aggregator**
3. Card network routes to the **issuing bank** (customer's bank)
4. Issuer authenticates (OTP) and approves/declines
5. Response returns; funds settle to the merchant later (e.g. T+1) after fees

**MDR** (merchant discount rate) = fee charged to the merchant per transaction.

steps.title: Common threats
steps.body:
- **Phishing / vishing / smishing**: fake emails, calls or SMS to steal credentials
- **Malware**: viruses, trojans, ransomware, keyloggers
- **DoS/DDoS**: flooding servers to make sites unavailable
- **SQL injection** and **cross-site scripting (XSS)**: exploiting weak website code
- **Man-in-the-middle**: intercepting unencrypted traffic
- **Identity theft**, **card skimming**, **account takeover**
- **Insider threats** and data breaches

steps.title: Security goals and controls
steps.body:
Goals (CIA+): **confidentiality, integrity, availability**, plus **authentication** and **non-repudiation**.

Controls: TLS everywhere, strong passwords and **multi-factor authentication**, patching, firewalls and WAF, input validation, PCI-DSS compliance for card data, backups, access control, staff training, incident response (report to CERT-In as required).

scenes.text: Anyone can drop a letter into a locked box through the slot (public key), but only the owner has the key to open it (private key).
That is the idea behind public-key cryptography.

steps.title: Encryption
steps.body:
- **Encryption** converts plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and a key; decryption reverses it.
- **Symmetric** (secret key): same key encrypts and decrypts; fast (e.g. AES); key distribution is the problem.
- **Asymmetric** (public key): a **public key** to encrypt, a **private key** to decrypt (e.g. RSA, ECC); slower but solves key exchange.
- TLS uses asymmetric cryptography to agree on a session key, then symmetric encryption for speed.

steps.title: Digital signatures and certificates
steps.body:
- **Hash function**: produces a fixed-length digest; any change in the message changes the digest.
- **Digital signature**: hash of the message encrypted with the sender's **private key**; the receiver verifies with the sender's **public key** ⇒ authentication, integrity, non-repudiation.
- **Digital certificate**: binds a public key to an identity, issued by a **Certifying Authority (CA)**.
- In India, CAs are licensed by the **Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA)** under the IT Act, 2000; **Digital Signature Certificates (DSC)** are used for MCA and tax filings.

steps.title: Solved: number of keys
steps.body:
10 traders want to communicate privately in pairs.

- Symmetric: each pair needs its own key ⇒ n(n − 1)/2 = 10 × 9/2 = **45 keys**
- Asymmetric: each person needs one key pair ⇒ 2n = **20 keys** (10 public + 10 private)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a digital signature is created with the receiver's public key — it uses the sender's private key.
- Thinking hashing is reversible encryption — a hash cannot be decrypted.

steps.title: Channels
steps.body:
- **SEO** (search engine optimisation): improving organic ranking — relevant keywords, quality content, fast mobile pages, backlinks, structured data.
- **SEM / PPC**: paid search ads; pay per click; bidding on keywords.
- **Social media marketing**: organic posts, paid ads, reels, communities.
- **Email and push/WhatsApp marketing** (with consent): newsletters, cart reminders.
- **Affiliate marketing**: partners earn commission on referred sales.
- **Influencer marketing**: creators promote products; disclosures required under ASCI guidelines.
- **Display and retargeting** ads to past visitors.

steps.title: Funnel
steps.body: **Awareness → Interest → Consideration → Purchase → Loyalty/Advocacy**. Different channels work at different stages: influencers and display for awareness, search for consideration, email and retargeting for conversion and loyalty.

steps.title: Owned, paid, earned
steps.body: **Owned** media: your website, app, email list. **Paid**: ads. **Earned**: reviews, shares, press coverage. Strong owned and earned media reduce dependence on paid ads.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting instant results from SEO — it builds over months.
- Messaging customers without consent, which hurts trust and may breach data-protection rules.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Conversion rate** = orders / sessions (visitors)
- **AOV** = revenue / orders
- **CTR** = clicks / impressions; **CPC** = ad spend / clicks
- **ROAS** = revenue from ads / ad spend
- **CAC** = marketing spend / new customers
- **Cart abandonment rate** = 1 − (completed purchases / carts created)
- **CLV** (simple) = AOV × purchases per year × years retained × gross margin
- Healthy rule of thumb: CLV/CAC ≥ 3

steps.title: Solved: dashboard

- ROAS = **5×**
- CAC = 3,00,000/600 = **₹500**

- CLV = 1,500 × 4 × 3 × 0.20 = **₹3,600**; CLV/CAC = 7.2 ✓

steps.title: E-CRM

**Electronic customer relationship management** uses digital tools to acquire, retain and grow customers.

- Components: customer database, analytics, campaign management, service desk (chat, email, WhatsApp, chatbots), loyalty programmes.
- **Segmentation**: by demographics, behaviour (RFM — recency, frequency, monetary value), location.
- **Personalisation**: recommendations, dynamic content, personalised offers.
- Benefits: higher retention, cross-selling and up-selling, better service.
- Retaining an existing customer usually costs less than acquiring a new one.

courses.summary: The Information Technology Act, 2000; consumer protection rules for e-commerce; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; GST provisions for e-commerce operators; ethical issues; and a whole-subject revision sheet with the final exam.
outcomes: Explain the legal recognition of electronic records and signatures and key cyber offences under the IT Act

scenes.text: A Delhi supplier signs a contract with a digital signature and emails it.
Under the IT Act, that electronic contract is as valid as one on paper.

steps.title: Objectives and scope
steps.body:
The **Information Technology Act, 2000** (amended 2008) provides:

- **Legal recognition of electronic records** and **electronic/digital signatures**
- Validity of contracts formed electronically
- Electronic filing with government
- Licensing of **Certifying Authorities** through the Controller (CCA)
- Penalties and offences for cyber wrongs
- Adjudication and appeals

steps.title: Key offences and provisions
steps.body:
- **Section 43**: penalty/compensation for unauthorised access, downloading, introducing viruses, damage to computer systems
- **Section 66**: computer-related offences (dishonest or fraudulent acts under s.43)
- **Section 66C**: identity theft (fraudulent use of passwords, electronic signatures)
- **Section 66D**: cheating by personation using computer resources
- **Section 79**: safe harbour for **intermediaries** that observe due diligence (detailed in the IT Rules, 2021)
- **CERT-In** is the national agency for cyber-incident response.

steps.title: Interaction with criminal law
steps.body: Cyber frauds may also attract offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (which replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024), for example cheating, along with IT Act provisions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking electronic contracts are invalid without paper — the IT Act recognises them.
- Believing intermediaries are immune in all cases — safe harbour depends on due diligence and acting on lawful orders.

steps.title: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and E-Commerce Rules, 2020
steps.body:
- Apply to marketplace and inventory e-commerce entities offering goods/services to consumers in India.
- Display **legal name, address, contact details** and the **grievance officer**; acknowledge complaints within **48 hours** and redress within **one month**.
- Show seller details, return/refund/exchange policies, warranty, payment methods and **country of origin** where applicable.
- No manipulation of prices, no fake reviews, no unfair trade practices; consent must be explicit (not pre-ticked boxes).
- **Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA)** can act against unfair practices, including **dark patterns** (guidelines issued in 2023).

steps.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
steps.body:
- **Data principal**: the individual whose data it is. **Data fiduciary**: entity deciding purpose and means of processing. **Data processor**: processes on behalf of a fiduciary.
- Processing on **consent** (free, specific, informed, unambiguous) or certain legitimate uses.
- Duties: notice, purpose limitation, security safeguards, breach intimation, erase data when purpose ends.
- Rights: access, correction and erasure, grievance redressal, nomination.
- Special care for children's data (verifiable parental consent).
- **Data Protection Board of India** adjudicates; penalties can go up to **₹250 crore** per instance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a pre-ticked consent box valid consent.
- Confusing the data fiduciary (decides purpose) with the data processor (acts on instructions).

Hiding the seller's identity from buyers

story.title: The TCS line in the payout

scenes.text: A seller's monthly marketplace statement shows a deduction labelled 'TCS'.
It is tax collected at source under GST, which she can claim as credit in her own returns.

steps.title: GST provisions
steps.body:
- **E-commerce operator (ECO)**: person who owns/operates a digital platform for e-commerce.
- **Section 52 of the CGST Act**: ECOs must **collect tax at source (TCS)** on the **net value of taxable supplies** made through them by other suppliers, at the notified rate, and deposit it; sellers claim it in their electronic cash ledger.
- **Section 9(5)**: for notified services (e.g. passenger transport, accommodation, restaurant services through the platform) the ECO itself pays GST.
- Income-tax also requires TDS by ECOs on payments to e-commerce participants (section 194-O) at notified rates.

*Rates have changed over time — always check the current notification.*

steps.title: Solved: TCS at an assumed rate
steps.body:
Assume a TCS rate of 1% (illustrative).

Taxable supplies through the platform in a month ₹10,00,000; returns ₹1,00,000.

- Net taxable supplies = ₹9,00,000
- **TCS = ₹9,000**, credited to the seller's cash ledger after the ECO files its statement.

steps.title: Ethical issues
steps.body: Privacy and surveillance, fake reviews, counterfeit goods, predatory pricing, gig-worker welfare, environmental cost of packaging and fast returns, accessibility, algorithmic bias. Responsible platforms publish clear policies and audits.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing TCS on gross supplies without deducting returns.
- Treating TCS as an extra cost — the seller can use it to pay GST liability.

quiz.why: The base is the net value of taxable supplies made through the operator.

quiz.q: Under section 9(5), for notified services the GST is paid by the:
quiz.why: For notified services the ECO is treated as liable to pay the tax.
