questions.q: Order ₹8,000; fee 2% + 18% GST on fee. Merchant receives:
A platform's AOV ₹1,000, 6 orders/year, 3 years, 15% margin; CAC ₹900. CLV/CAC =

uni-bcom-financial-accounting.title: B.Com · Financial Accounting (full paper)
uni-bcom-financial-accounting.description: The complete Financial Accounting paper unit by unit: accounting framework and standards, journal to trial balance, rectification, depreciation and BRS, final accounts with adjustments, incomplete records, partnership, consignment, joint venture and hire purchase, with solved numericals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Com programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Accounting framework and the accounting process
courses.summary: Meaning and users of accounting, GAAP concepts and conventions, accounting standards (AS and Ind AS) in India, the double-entry process from journal and subsidiary books to ledger and trial balance, and the location and rectification of errors including the suspense account.
outcomes: Explain the main accounting concepts and conventions with examples
Describe the role of ICAI accounting standards and Ind AS
Journalise transactions and post them to ledger accounts
Prepare a trial balance and state its limitations
Classify errors and pass rectification entries, with and without a suspense account

scenes.text: Two textile firms in Surat report profit; one counts orders received, the other counts goods delivered. A bank cannot compare them.
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles and accounting standards give everyone the same yardstick.

steps.title: Meaning and users
steps.body:
Accounting is the process of **identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising, analysing and communicating** financial information to users.

- Internal users: owners, managers, employees
- External users: lenders, investors, suppliers, government (tax), customers

Book-keeping is only the recording part; accounting includes interpretation.

steps.title: Concepts (assumptions)
steps.body:
- **Business entity** – business separate from owner
- **Money measurement** – only money-measurable events
- **Going concern** – business will continue (so assets at cost, not break-up value)
- **Accounting period** – profit measured for a period (in India usually 1 April–31 March)
- **Cost** – assets recorded at acquisition cost
- **Dual aspect** – every transaction has two equal sides: A = L + C
- **Realisation / revenue recognition** – revenue when earned (goods delivered / service rendered)
- **Accrual** and **matching** – expenses matched with revenues of the same period

steps.title: Conventions
steps.body:
- **Consistency** – same methods year to year; changes disclosed
- **Prudence (conservatism)** – anticipate no profit, provide for all probable losses (e.g. closing stock at lower of cost or net realisable value)
- **Materiality** – insignificant items need not be shown separately
- **Full disclosure** – all material facts disclosed (notes to accounts)

steps.title: Accounting standards in India
steps.body:
- The **Accounting Standards Board of ICAI** formulates standards.
- **AS** (e.g. AS 2 Inventories, AS 10 Property, Plant & Equipment, AS 9 Revenue) apply to non-Ind AS entities.
- **Ind AS** (converged with IFRS) are notified by the Central Government under the Companies Act, 2013 and apply to listed companies and companies above prescribed net-worth thresholds, in phases from 2016.
- Benefits: comparability, reliability, reduced choice of methods.

steps.title: Solved: which concept?
steps.body:
1. Owner's household electricity paid from business cash is recorded as drawings → **business entity**.
2. Stock costing ₹50,000 with market value ₹45,000 valued at ₹45,000 → **prudence**.
3. A ₹300 stapler is expensed, not capitalised → **materiality**.
4. December salary paid on 5 January is still a December expense → **accrual/matching**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling conservatism 'understating profit deliberately' – it means not anticipating gains, not hiding profit.
- Mixing up consistency (same method over time) with comparability (across firms).
- Saying Ind AS apply to every company – they apply only to notified classes.

activity.prompt: Classify each as a concept (assumption) or a convention.

quiz.q: Fixed assets are shown at cost less depreciation rather than at sale value because of:
quiz.why: Under going concern the business is expected to continue, so assets are not valued at break-up or sale value.

quiz.q: Valuing closing stock at the lower of cost or net realisable value follows:
quiz.why: Prudence requires providing for probable losses, so stock is not carried above what it can realise.

quiz.q: In India accounting standards are formulated by the Accounting Standards Board of:
quiz.why: The Accounting Standards Board of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India formulates the standards.

quiz.q: Ind AS are converged with:
quiz.why: Ind AS are India's IFRS-converged standards notified under the Companies Act, 2013.

scenes.text: Meena keeps every bill of her tailoring unit in a shoebox and cannot say who owes her money.
She learns to journalise each transaction, post it to accounts, and keep separate day books for routine purchases and sales.

steps.title: Rules of debit and credit
steps.body:
**Modern approach**
- Assets, expenses, losses, drawings: Dr increase, Cr decrease
- Liabilities, capital, incomes, gains: Cr increase, Dr decrease

**Traditional (golden) rules**
- Personal: Dr the receiver, Cr the giver
- Real: Dr what comes in, Cr what goes out
- Nominal: Dr expenses and losses, Cr incomes and gains

steps.title: Solved: journal entries
steps.body:
1. Started business with cash ₹2,00,000: **Cash A/c Dr 2,00,000 / To Capital A/c 2,00,000**
2. Bought goods on credit from Raj ₹40,000: **Purchases A/c Dr / To Raj A/c 40,000**
3. Sold goods to Asha ₹25,000 at 10% trade discount on credit: record net ₹22,500 → **Asha A/c Dr / To Sales A/c 22,500** (trade discount is never recorded)
4. Paid Raj ₹39,200 in full settlement of ₹40,000: **Raj A/c Dr 40,000 / To Cash 39,200 / To Discount Received 800**
5. Goods ₹3,000 taken for personal use: **Drawings A/c Dr / To Purchases A/c 3,000**

steps.title: Subsidiary books
steps.body:
- **Purchases book** – credit purchases of goods only
- **Sales book** – credit sales of goods only
- **Purchase returns / sales returns books**
- **Cash book** – single column, double column (cash + bank) or triple column (cash, bank, discount); it is both a book of original entry and a ledger
- **Bills receivable / payable books**
- **Journal proper** – everything else: opening, closing, adjustment, rectification entries, credit purchase of assets

steps.title: Solved: posting and balancing
steps.body:
Cash A/c: Dr side – Capital 2,00,000, Sales 18,000; Cr side – Raj 39,200, Rent 6,000, Salaries 12,000.

- Dr total = 2,18,000; Cr total = 57,200
- Balance c/d on the Cr side = 2,18,000 − 57,200 = **₹1,60,800**, shown as balance b/d on the Dr side (a debit balance = cash in hand).

steps.title: Cash book contra entry
steps.body: Cash deposited into bank appears on both sides of a double-column cash book (Dr bank column, Cr cash column) and is marked **C** – contra. No ledger posting is needed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Entering credit purchase of furniture in the purchases book – it goes to journal proper.
- Recording trade discount in the books.
- Crediting 'Goods' for drawings instead of Purchases.
- Forgetting that discount columns of a cash book are memorandum and must be posted in totals.

activity.prompt: Goods with list price ₹60,000 sold on credit at 15% trade discount and 2% cash discount offered for payment within 7 days. The customer pays within 7 days. How much cash is received (₹)?

quiz.q: Credit purchase of machinery is recorded in the:
quiz.why: The purchases book records only credit purchases of goods, so a credit purchase of an asset goes to journal proper.

quiz.q: Discount received is:
quiz.why: Discount received is a gain, a nominal account, so it is credited.

quiz.q: A contra entry in a cash book is one that:
options: affects both cash and bank columns
quiz.why: A contra entry such as cash deposited into bank affects both the cash and bank columns and needs no ledger posting.

quiz.q: Goods withdrawn by owner for personal use are credited to:
quiz.why: Withdrawn goods reduce goods purchased for sale, so Purchases is credited and Drawings debited.

quiz.q: A ledger account with a credit balance for Raj (supplier) means:
quiz.why: A credit balance on a supplier's personal account shows the amount the business still owes him.

scenes.text: Karan balances every ledger account and lists the balances: debits on one side, credits on the other.
The totals agree – but his teacher warns that agreement does not prove the books are error-free.

steps.title: Meaning and objectives
steps.body:
A trial balance is a **statement** (not an account) of ledger balances on a date.

- Checks arithmetical accuracy of postings
- Basis for preparing final accounts
- Methods: **balance method** (most common), total method, total-and-balance method

steps.title: Which side?
steps.body:
**Debit side**: assets, expenses, losses, drawings, purchases, sales returns, debtors, opening stock

**Credit side**: capital, liabilities, incomes, gains, sales, purchase returns, creditors, provisions (e.g. provision for doubtful debts, provision for depreciation)

Closing stock normally does **not** appear (it appears only if adjusted purchases are given).

steps.title: Errors not disclosed
steps.body:
Trial balance agrees despite:
- **Errors of omission** (transaction completely omitted)
- **Errors of commission** that affect two accounts equally (posted to the wrong person's account)
- **Errors of principle** (capital vs revenue confusion)
- **Compensating errors**
- Wrong amount in the book of original entry

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting closing stock in the trial balance along with opening stock and unadjusted purchases.
- Placing provision for doubtful debts on the debit side.
- Calling a trial balance an account.

activity.prompt: A trial balance shows debit total ₹4,86,300 and credit total ₹4,83,900. What amount is put into the suspense account (₹)? (The suspense account will be credited.)

quiz.q: A trial balance is:
quiz.why: A trial balance is a statement listing ledger balances; it is not itself an account.

quiz.q: Which error is NOT revealed by a trial balance?
options: omitting one side of an entry
quiz.why: Debiting a revenue account instead of an asset account affects two debits equally, so the trial balance still agrees.

quiz.q: Provision for doubtful debts appears on the:
quiz.why: A provision is a credit balance set aside out of profits, so it appears on the credit side.

quiz.q: Sales returns appear on the:
quiz.why: Sales returns reduce income and carry a debit balance, so they go on the debit side.

lessons.title: Rectification of errors and suspense account

scenes.text: Nisha's trial balance is short by ₹2,400 on the credit side; she parks the difference in a suspense account and finishes the accounts.
Next month she finds the errors one by one and clears the suspense account to zero.

steps.title: Types of errors
steps.body:
- **One-sided errors** (affect one account only: wrong totalling, posting wrong amount, posting to wrong side) → rectified **through the suspense account** if found after the trial balance
- **Two-sided errors** (omission, principle, commission affecting two accounts, compensating) → rectified by a journal entry between the two accounts

Rule: write the **wrong entry**, write the **correct entry**, then pass the entry that turns one into the other.

steps.title: Solved: two-sided errors
steps.body:
1. Furniture ₹8,000 bought, debited to Purchases → **Furniture A/c Dr 8,000 / To Purchases 8,000**
2. Credit sale to Ram ₹2,000 posted to Shyam → **Ram A/c Dr 2,000 / To Shyam A/c 2,000**
3. Repairs to building ₹1,500 debited to Building → **Repairs A/c Dr 1,500 / To Building A/c 1,500**

steps.title: Solved: one-sided errors through suspense
steps.body:
1. Sales book overcast by ₹1,000 → Sales was credited ₹1,000 too much: **Sales A/c Dr 1,000 / To Suspense 1,000**
2. ₹750 paid to Mohan posted to his account as ₹570 → Mohan under-debited by 180: **Mohan A/c Dr 180 / To Suspense 180**
3. Discount allowed ₹600 not posted to discount account → **Discount Allowed A/c Dr 600 / To Suspense 600**
4. Purchases book undercast by ₹200 → **Purchases A/c Dr 200 / To Suspense 200**

If the opening suspense balance was Dr ₹1,980, these entries credit it 1,000 + 180 + 600 + 200 = 1,980 and close it.

steps.title: Effect on profit
steps.body:
An error rectified after final accounts that involves a nominal account changes profit:
- Overcast sales corrected → profit falls
- Purchase of asset debited to purchases corrected → profit rises

In the next year, use **Profit & Loss Adjustment A/c** in place of the nominal account.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using suspense for two-sided errors (no suspense needed when both sides are wrong equally).
- Reversing the direction: an overcast sales book needs Sales **Dr**, not Cr.
- Forgetting the suspense balance must become nil after all errors are found.

activity.prompt: Does the rectification need the suspense account?

items.text: Rent ₹900 posted as ₹90 in rent account
Credit sale to Anil entered in Sunil's account
Discount received not posted to discount account

quiz.q: Sales book overcast by ₹1,000 is rectified by:
quiz.why: Sales was over-credited, so debiting Sales and crediting Suspense removes the extra credit.

quiz.q: Wages paid for installing a new machine debited to Wages A/c is an error of:
quiz.why: Installation wages are capital expenditure, so charging them to wages violates accounting principle.

quiz.q: Purchase of machinery debited to purchases, rectified after final accounts, will:
quiz.why: Removing the amount from purchases reduces expenses, so the previously reported profit was understated and rises.

quiz.q: After rectifying all errors, the suspense account should:
quiz.why: The suspense account only holds the trial-balance difference, so once all errors are found it closes with no balance.

questions.q: The concept that every transaction has two equal effects is:
questions.why: The dual aspect concept says every debit has an equal credit, giving A = L + C.

questions.q: Trade discount is:
options: deducted from list price and not recorded
questions.why: Trade discount reduces the invoice price itself, so only the net amount is recorded.

questions.q: Assets ₹6,00,000 and liabilities ₹2,25,000 means capital is:
questions.why: Capital = Assets − Liabilities = 6,00,000 − 2,25,000 = ₹3,75,000.

questions.q: A credit purchase of goods is recorded in the:
questions.why: The purchases book records all credit purchases of goods meant for resale.

questions.q: Which appears on the credit side of a trial balance?
questions.why: Purchase returns reduce purchases and carry a credit balance.

questions.q: A trial balance can agree even when there is:
options: a casting error in one account
questions.why: Compensating errors cancel each other, so the totals still agree.

questions.q: Rent paid ₹4,500 posted to rent account as ₹5,400. Rectification:
questions.why: Rent was over-debited by ₹900, so Rent is credited and Suspense debited.

questions.q: Received ₹19,400 from a debtor in full settlement of ₹20,000. Discount allowed is:
questions.why: Discount allowed = 20,000 − 19,400 = ₹600, debited as an expense.

questions.q: Ind AS apply to:
options: notified classes of companies such as listed companies
questions.why: Ind AS apply to companies notified under the Companies Act, 2013, such as listed companies and those above net-worth thresholds.

questions.q: Purchases book undercast ₹300 and sales book undercast ₹300 together are:
options: errors of commission affecting one side
questions.why: An under-debit and an equal under-credit offset each other, so they are compensating errors.

questions.q: Goods ₹5,000 sold to Arun on credit were entered in the purchases book. The rectification entry is:
options: Arun Dr 10,000 / To Purchases 5,000, To Sales 5,000
questions.why: Arun was wrongly credited 5,000 and must be debited 5,000, so he is debited 10,000; Purchases is reversed and Sales credited.

questions.q: Cash A/c: Dr total ₹1,45,000, Cr total ₹1,62,000. This means:
options: an impossible balance indicating an error
questions.why: A cash account cannot have a credit balance since you cannot pay more cash than you have, so it signals an error.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Depreciation, provisions and bank reconciliation
courses.summary: Nature and causes of depreciation, straight-line and written-down-value methods, sale of assets and provision for depreciation account, provisions versus reserves with the provision for doubtful debts, and preparation of the bank reconciliation statement from either balance.
outcomes: Compute depreciation by SLM and WDV and record it
Find profit or loss on sale of a depreciated asset
Distinguish provisions from reserves and account for bad and doubtful debts
Prepare a bank reconciliation statement starting from cash book or pass book, including overdrafts

scenes.text: A bakery in Pune buys a van for ₹6,00,000 expecting to use it for 5 years.
Charging the full cost to year one would show a loss; spreading it over five years matches cost with the revenue the van helps earn.

steps.title: Meaning and causes
steps.body:
Depreciation is the **systematic allocation of the depreciable amount** of an asset over its useful life (AS 10 / Ind AS 16 language).

Causes: wear and tear, efflux of time (leases), obsolescence, depletion (mines).

Objectives: true profit (matching), true asset value in the balance sheet, funds retained for replacement.

steps.title: Straight-line method (SLM)
steps.body:
**Annual depreciation = (Cost − Residual value) ÷ Useful life**

Cost includes purchase price, freight, installation and other directly attributable costs.

Rate (%) = Annual depreciation ÷ Cost × 100.

Charge is equal every year; book value falls in a straight line to the residual value.

steps.title: Solved: SLM
steps.body:
Machine price ₹1,00,000, freight and installation ₹10,000, residual value ₹10,000, life 5 years.

- Cost = 1,10,000
- Depreciation = (1,10,000 − 10,000) ÷ 5 = **₹20,000 a year**
- Book value after 3 years = 1,10,000 − 60,000 = **₹50,000**

Entry: **Depreciation A/c Dr 20,000 / To Machinery A/c 20,000**; then **P&L A/c Dr / To Depreciation A/c**.

steps.title: Provision for depreciation method
steps.body:
The asset stays at original cost; accumulated depreciation is credited to **Provision for Depreciation A/c**.

- Depreciation A/c Dr / To Provision for Depreciation A/c
- Balance sheet: Machinery at cost less provision
- On sale, the accumulated provision on that asset is transferred to the Asset Disposal (or asset) account.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving installation cost out of the asset's cost.
- Charging a full year's depreciation for an asset bought mid-year when the question says 'time basis'.
- Treating depreciation as a cash outflow – it is a non-cash expense.

activity.prompt: An asset costs ₹2,50,000 with installation ₹10,000. Residual value ₹20,000, life 8 years. Annual SLM depreciation (₹)?

quiz.q: Depreciation is primarily a process of:
quiz.why: Depreciation allocates the depreciable amount of an asset over its useful life; it is not a valuation method.

quiz.q: Under SLM the depreciation charge each year is:
quiz.why: SLM charges the same amount every year because it is a fixed fraction of the depreciable amount.

quiz.q: Depletion is the cause of depreciation for:
quiz.why: Wasting assets such as mines lose value as the mineral is extracted, which is depletion.

quiz.q: Under the provision for depreciation method, the asset account shows:
quiz.why: Accumulated depreciation sits in a separate provision account, so the asset remains at original cost.

lessons.title: WDV method and sale of assets

scenes.text: A workshop sells a lathe midway through its third year.
To find the profit or loss, it must first depreciate the lathe up to the date of sale.

steps.title: Written-down-value (diminishing balance)
steps.body:
Depreciation = fixed rate × **opening book value** each year.

- Higher charge in early years, lower later – matches higher early efficiency and rising repairs
- Never reaches zero
- Also the method used for income-tax block-of-assets depreciation

steps.title: Solved: sale of an asset (SLM)
steps.body:
Machine bought 1 April 2023 for ₹1,00,000; SLM 10% p.a.; sold 30 September 2025 for ₹70,000. Books close 31 March.

- 2023-24: 10,000; 2024-25: 10,000; 2025-26 (6 months): 5,000
- Book value on sale = 1,00,000 − 25,000 = 75,000
- Loss = 75,000 − 70,000 = **₹5,000**

Entries: Cash Dr 70,000 / To Machinery 70,000; P&L Dr 5,000 / To Machinery 5,000 (loss on sale).

steps.title: Change of method
steps.body: Under AS 10 / Ind AS 16 a change in depreciation method is a **change in accounting estimate**: apply it prospectively from the date of change on the remaining book value. Older syllabi also show the retrospective approach – follow the question.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the WDV rate to original cost every year (that is SLM).
- Forgetting depreciation for the part-year before the sale.
- Showing loss on sale as a deduction from sales revenue instead of in P&L.

activity.prompt: An asset costing ₹4,00,000 is depreciated at 15% WDV. What is its book value at the end of year 2 (₹)?

quiz.q: Under WDV the rate is applied to:
quiz.why: WDV applies the fixed percentage to the reducing opening book value each year.

quiz.q: Machine cost ₹50,000, accumulated depreciation ₹20,000, sold for ₹34,000. Result:
quiz.why: Book value is 30,000, so selling at 34,000 gives a profit of ₹4,000.

quiz.q: Under AS 10 a change in depreciation method is treated as:
quiz.why: AS 10 and Ind AS 16 treat a change of depreciation method as a change in estimate applied prospectively.

quiz.q: WDV book value can reach zero:
quiz.why: A percentage of a positive balance always leaves a positive balance, so WDV never reaches zero.

scenes.text: A wholesaler's customer owing ₹5,000 shuts shop and cannot be traced.
The wholesaler writes the debt off and keeps a cushion for other customers who may not pay.

steps.title: Provision vs reserve
steps.body:
- **Provision**: charge against profit for a known liability or expected loss whose amount is uncertain (doubtful debts, depreciation, taxation). Must be made even if there is a loss.
- **Reserve**: appropriation of profit to strengthen the business (general reserve, capital reserve). Made only out of profit.
- **Secret reserve**: created by understating assets – not permitted for companies' published accounts.

steps.title: Solved: bad and doubtful debts
steps.body:
Trial balance: Debtors ₹1,05,000; Bad debts ₹2,000; Provision for doubtful debts (old) ₹3,000.
Adjustments: further bad debts ₹5,000; new provision 5% on debtors.

- Good debtors = 1,05,000 − 5,000 = 1,00,000; new provision = 5,000
- P&L charge = 2,000 + 5,000 + 5,000 − 3,000 = **₹9,000**
- Balance sheet: Debtors 1,00,000 less provision 5,000 = **₹95,000**

steps.title: Bad debts recovered and discount provision
steps.body:
- **Bad debts recovered**: Cash Dr / To Bad Debts Recovered A/c (an income) – not credited to the debtor, who was already written off.
- **Provision for discount on debtors** is computed on debtors **after** deducting the provision for doubtful debts.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing the new provision on debtors before deducting further bad debts.
- Crediting a recovered bad debt to the customer's account.
- Calling a provision an appropriation of profit.

activity.prompt: Debtors ₹82,000; further bad debts ₹2,000; old provision ₹5,000; bad debts in trial balance ₹1,500; new provision 5% on debtors. Net amount charged to P&L (₹)?

quiz.q: A provision differs from a reserve in that a provision is:
quiz.why: A provision is a charge against profit for an expected loss, while a reserve appropriates profit.

quiz.q: Bad debts recovered are credited to:
quiz.why: The debtor's account was closed on write-off, so the recovery is credited to an income account.

quiz.q: Provision for discount on debtors is calculated on:
options: debtors after provision for doubtful debts
quiz.why: Discount is only allowed to customers expected to pay, so it is computed after deducting doubtful debts.

quiz.q: General reserve is an example of:
quiz.why: General reserve is created out of revenue profits and is free for any purpose, so it is a revenue reserve.

scenes.text: Arif's cash book shows ₹20,000 in the bank, but his pass book shows ₹22,300.
Neither is wrong – some entries simply have not reached the other record yet.

steps.title: Causes of difference
steps.body:
Timing differences:
- Cheques **issued but not yet presented**
- Cheques **deposited but not yet cleared**
- Bank charges, interest on overdraft debited by bank only
- Interest credited, dividends collected, direct deposits by customers (bank only)
- Dishonoured cheques, standing instructions paid by bank

Plus errors in either record.

steps.title: Solved: favourable balance, from cash book
steps.body:
Cash book Dr ₹20,000. Cheques issued not presented ₹5,000; deposited not cleared ₹3,000; bank charges ₹200; interest credited by bank ₹500.

- 20,000 + 5,000 − 3,000 − 200 + 500 = **₹22,300 per pass book** ✓

steps.title: Solved: overdraft, from pass book
steps.body:
Overdraft per pass book ₹15,000. Cheques issued not presented ₹4,000; deposited not credited ₹6,000; bank charges ₹300 not in cash book.

Work in overdraft terms:
- Issued not presented: cash book already recorded payment → CB overdraft larger: +4,000
- Deposited not credited: CB already reduced overdraft → −6,000
- Bank charges only in PB → CB overdraft smaller: −300
- **Overdraft per cash book = ₹12,700**

steps.title: Amended cash book first
steps.body: When asked, first correct the cash book for items the bank knows but you don't (charges, interest, direct deposits, dishonours, errors in CB). Then the BRS needs only timing items (unpresented and uncleared cheques).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying 'add' and 'less' the same way for an overdraft as for a favourable balance.
- Including bank charges in the BRS after already amending the cash book (double count).
- Forgetting that a debit balance in the cash book equals a credit balance in the pass book.

activity.prompt: Starting from a favourable cash book balance, is each item added or deducted to reach the pass book balance?

items.text: Cheques issued but not yet presented
Cheques deposited but not yet cleared
Bank charges debited only in pass book

quiz.q: A debit balance in the cash book corresponds to a ___ balance in the pass book.
quiz.why: The bank records the customer's money as its liability, so a favourable cash-book debit is a pass-book credit.

quiz.q: Starting with cash book balance ₹10,000, cheques deposited but not cleared ₹2,000 are:
quiz.why: The cash book already includes the deposit but the bank has not credited it, so the pass book is lower.

quiz.q: Overdraft per pass book ₹15,000, cheques issued not presented ₹4,000, deposited not credited ₹6,000, bank charges ₹300. Overdraft per cash book:
Interest on overdraft charged by the bank, when not yet in the cash book, makes the pass book overdraft:
quiz.why: Interest charged adds to the debt to the bank, so the pass book overdraft is larger.

questions.q: Depreciation under SLM for cost ₹80,000, scrap ₹8,000, life 6 years:
Which is NOT a cause of depreciation?
questions.why: A rise in market price is not a cause of depreciation; depreciation allocates cost, it does not track market value.

questions.q: WDV 20% on ₹1,00,000: depreciation in year 3:
questions.why: Book values are 1,00,000, 80,000 and 64,000, so year-3 depreciation is 20% of 64,000 = ₹12,800.

questions.q: Machine cost ₹60,000 on 1 April 2024, SLM 10% p.a., sold 1 October 2025 for ₹54,000 (books close 31 March). Result:
questions.why: Depreciation for 18 months is 6,000 + 3,000 = 9,000, so book value is 51,000 and selling at 54,000 gives a profit of ₹3,000.

questions.q: Provision for doubtful debts is shown in the balance sheet as:
questions.why: The provision reduces debtors to the amount expected to be collected.

questions.q: A reserve is:
questions.why: A reserve is set aside out of profits to strengthen the business.

questions.q: Debtors ₹50,000, new provision 4%, old provision ₹3,000. Effect on P&L from the provision alone:
questions.why: New provision is 2,000 against old 3,000, so the excess 1,000 is written back as a credit to P&L.

questions.q: Cash book shows ₹8,000 favourable. Cheque of ₹1,200 deposited was dishonoured (only bank knows). Pass book balance (no other items):
questions.why: The bank has reversed the deposit, so the pass book is 8,000 − 1,200 = ₹6,800.

questions.q: Cheques issued ₹7,000; of these ₹2,500 presented. Starting from cash book balance ₹15,000, the adjustment is:
questions.why: Only the unpresented ₹4,500 creates a difference, and it is added to reach the pass book.

questions.q: Which method is followed for depreciation under the Income-tax Act's block of assets?
questions.why: Income-tax depreciation on blocks of assets uses the written-down-value method.

questions.q: Bad debts recovered ₹1,000 are:
questions.why: A recovered bad debt is an income credited to P&L via Bad Debts Recovered A/c.

questions.q: Overdraft per cash book ₹10,000; cheques deposited but not cleared ₹3,000. Overdraft per pass book:
questions.why: The cash book already reduced the overdraft by 3,000 but the bank has not, so the pass book overdraft is ₹13,000.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Final accounts and incomplete records
courses.summary: Capital and revenue items, the trading and profit and loss account, the balance sheet of a sole proprietor with common adjustments (outstanding and prepaid items, accrued income, depreciation, bad debts, goods lost, manager's commission), and ascertaining profit from incomplete records by the statement of affairs and conversion methods.
outcomes: Classify receipts and expenditure as capital, revenue or deferred revenue
Prepare a trading account and compute gross profit
Prepare P&L account and balance sheet with adjustments
Ascertain profit under single entry by the statement of affairs method
Derive missing figures such as credit sales and credit purchases from incomplete records

lessons.title: Capital vs revenue and the trading account

scenes.text: A godown owner spends ₹80,000 replacing a leaking tin roof with a new RCC slab, and ₹3,000 fixing a broken door.
One is capital expenditure that improves the asset; the other is a routine revenue repair.

steps.title: Capital vs revenue
steps.body:
- **Capital expenditure**: acquires or improves a fixed asset, or increases earning capacity, with benefit beyond one year (machinery, installation, extension of building).
- **Revenue expenditure**: maintains the business for the current period (wages, repairs, rent, salaries).
- **Deferred revenue expenditure**: revenue in nature but benefit spread over a few years (heavy advertising campaign) – largely restricted under current standards; note it if your syllabus asks.
- Capital receipts: loans, capital introduced, sale of fixed assets. Revenue receipts: sales, commission, interest.

steps.title: Trading account
steps.body:
Shows **gross profit** from buying and selling.

**Debit**: opening stock, purchases less returns, direct expenses (carriage inwards, freight, wages, fuel and power, octroi/import duty)
**Credit**: sales less returns, closing stock

GP = Net sales − Cost of goods sold
COGS = Opening stock + Net purchases + Direct expenses − Closing stock

steps.title: Solved: trading account
steps.body:
Opening stock 30,000; purchases 1,20,000; purchase returns 5,000; carriage inwards 3,000; wages 12,000; sales 2,00,000; sales returns 10,000; closing stock 40,000.

- Net purchases = 1,15,000
- COGS = 30,000 + 1,15,000 + 3,000 + 12,000 − 40,000 = **1,20,000**
- Net sales = 1,90,000
- **Gross profit = ₹70,000** (GP ratio 70,000 ÷ 1,90,000 = 36.8%)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting carriage outwards in the trading account (it is a selling expense in P&L).
- Deducting closing stock twice when 'adjusted purchases' are given.
- Treating installation wages of a new machine as revenue.

activity.prompt: Capital or revenue expenditure?

items.text: Wages paid for installing new machinery

quiz.q: Carriage outwards is shown in:
quiz.why: Carriage outwards is a selling and distribution expense, so it goes to P&L, not trading.

quiz.q: Opening stock 20,000, net purchases 80,000, direct expenses 5,000, closing stock 25,000. COGS:
Sale of old machinery is a:
quiz.why: Selling a fixed asset is not a normal operating income, so it is a capital receipt.

quiz.q: Gross profit equals:
quiz.why: Gross profit is net sales less the cost of goods sold.

lessons.title: P&L account and balance sheet with adjustments

scenes.text: Priya's March staff salary of ₹2,000 is paid only on 3 April.
Accrual says it still belongs to the year ending 31 March – it must appear as an expense and as a liability.

steps.title: The double effect of each adjustment
steps.body:
Every adjustment outside the trial balance appears **twice**:
- Closing stock → credit of trading A/c + current asset
- Outstanding expense → add to expense + current liability
- Prepaid expense → deduct from expense + current asset
- Accrued income → add to income + current asset
- Income received in advance → deduct from income + current liability
- Depreciation → P&L debit + deduct from asset
- Interest on capital → P&L debit + add to capital
- Interest on drawings → P&L credit + deduct from capital

steps.title: Solved: net profit with adjustments
steps.body:
GP 70,000. Salaries 24,000 (outstanding 2,000). Rent 12,000. Insurance 6,000 (prepaid 1,500). Commission received 3,000 (accrued 1,000). Depreciation on furniture 5,000.

- Expenses: 26,000 + 12,000 + 4,500 + 5,000 = 47,500
- Incomes: 70,000 + 4,000 = 74,000
- **Net profit = ₹26,500**

Balance sheet: outstanding salary 2,000 (liability); prepaid insurance 1,500 and accrued commission 1,000 (assets); furniture less 5,000.

steps.title: Balance sheet layout
steps.body:
Liabilities side (order of permanence): Capital (+ net profit + interest on capital − drawings), long-term loans, current liabilities (creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses).

Assets side: fixed assets (land, buildings, machinery, furniture), investments, current assets (stock, debtors less provision, bills receivable, prepaid, cash at bank, cash in hand).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Showing an adjustment only once (e.g. outstanding salary added in P&L but not shown as a liability).
- Deducting prepaid expenses from the liability side.
- Adding net profit to capital before deducting drawings and then deducting drawings again.

activity.prompt: Gross profit ₹80,000. Indirect expenses in the trial balance ₹45,000, which include prepaid rent ₹1,000. Salary ₹2,000 for March is outstanding and not recorded. Net profit (₹)?

quiz.q: Prepaid insurance appears in the balance sheet as:
quiz.why: Prepaid insurance is a benefit still to be received, so it is a current asset.

quiz.q: Income received in advance is:
quiz.why: Income received in advance is owed back as service still to be rendered, so it is a liability and is deducted from income.

quiz.q: Interest on capital is:
options: debited to P&L and added to capital
quiz.why: Interest on capital is an expense to the business and an addition to the proprietor's capital.

quiz.q: Closing stock given outside the trial balance appears:
quiz.why: An adjustment outside the trial balance has two effects: trading credit and current asset.

lessons.title: Special adjustments: goods lost, samples, manager's commission

scenes.text: A short circuit destroys goods costing ₹20,000 in a Kanpur warehouse; the insurer accepts a claim of ₹15,000.
The accountant must show the goods leaving trading, the claim as an asset, and the ₹5,000 loss in P&L.

steps.title: Solved: goods lost by fire
steps.body:
Cost ₹20,000; claim admitted ₹15,000 (not yet received).

- Trading A/c: credit 'By goods lost by fire 20,000'
- P&L A/c: debit loss 5,000
- Balance sheet: insurance claim receivable 15,000 (current asset)

Entry: Loss by Fire A/c Dr 20,000 / To Trading (Purchases) 20,000; Insurance Claim Dr 15,000, P&L Dr 5,000 / To Loss by Fire 20,000.

steps.title: Samples, drawings in goods, and charity
steps.body:
- Goods distributed as free samples: deduct from purchases (trading credit side), debit Advertisement in P&L.
- Goods taken by proprietor: deduct from purchases; add to drawings.
- Goods given as charity: deduct from purchases; debit Charity in P&L.

steps.title: Solved: manager's commission
steps.body:
Net profit before commission ₹1,10,000; manager gets 10%.

- On profit **before** charging commission: 10% × 1,10,000 = **₹11,000**
- On profit **after** charging commission: 1,10,000 × 10 ÷ 110 = **₹10,000**

Check: 1,10,000 − 10,000 = 1,00,000; 10% of 1,00,000 = 10,000 ✓. Outstanding commission is a current liability.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Debiting the whole fire loss to P&L while ignoring the insurance claim.
- Using 10% of profit when the clause says 'after charging such commission'.
- Recording samples at selling price instead of cost.

activity.prompt: Net profit before manager's commission is ₹2,52,000. The manager is entitled to 5% of net profit after charging such commission. Commission (₹)?

quiz.q: Goods costing ₹8,000 lost by fire, claim accepted ₹6,000. Amount debited to P&L:
quiz.why: Only the uninsured part, 8,000 − 6,000 = ₹2,000, is a loss to P&L.

quiz.q: Free samples distributed are debited to:
quiz.why: Free samples are a promotional cost, so they are charged to advertisement.

quiz.q: Profit ₹66,000 before commission; commission 10% after charging it:
Goods withdrawn by the proprietor are added to:
quiz.why: Goods taken for personal use are drawings, which reduce capital.

scenes.text: Shyam keeps only a cash diary and a list of who owes him money; he has no ledger.
To find his profit, his accountant compares what he was worth at the start and end of the year.

steps.title: Statement of affairs method
steps.body:
A **statement of affairs** lists assets and liabilities on a date; Capital = Assets − Liabilities.

**Profit = Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital − Opening capital**

Then adjust for items like depreciation, provision for doubtful debts and interest on capital if the question asks for a 'statement of profit'.

steps.title: Solved: statement of affairs
steps.body:
1 April: assets 1,50,000, liabilities 30,000 → opening capital 1,20,000.
31 March: assets 2,10,000, liabilities 40,000 → closing capital 1,70,000.
Drawings 24,000; fresh capital 10,000.

- Profit = 1,70,000 + 24,000 − 10,000 − 1,20,000 = **₹64,000**

steps.title: Solved: conversion – finding credit sales
steps.body:
Opening debtors 20,000; cash received from debtors 1,50,000; discount allowed 2,000; closing debtors 28,000.

Total debtors account: Dr opening 20,000 + credit sales ? = Cr cash 1,50,000 + discount 2,000 + closing 28,000
- Credit sales = 1,80,000 − 20,000 = **₹1,60,000**

Similarly prepare total creditors account to find credit purchases.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding additional capital instead of deducting it.
- Forgetting to include cash and bank balances in the statement of affairs.
- Calling single entry a 'system' – it is an incomplete form of double entry.

activity.prompt: Opening capital ₹1,60,000; closing capital ₹2,00,000; drawings ₹30,000; additional capital introduced ₹20,000. Profit for the year (₹)?

quiz.q: Under the statement of affairs method, additional capital is:
quiz.why: Fresh capital raised closing capital without being profit, so it is deducted.

quiz.q: A statement of affairs resembles a:
quiz.why: It lists assets and liabilities on a date, like a balance sheet, though from incomplete records.

quiz.q: Opening creditors 15,000; paid to creditors 90,000; closing creditors 25,000. Credit purchases:
Opening capital 50,000, closing capital 45,000, drawings 12,000, no fresh capital. Result:

questions.q: Wages in the trading account are:
questions.why: Wages for producing or handling goods are direct expenses charged to trading.

questions.q: Net sales ₹3,00,000, COGS ₹2,10,000. Gross profit ratio:
Outstanding rent appears in the balance sheet as:
questions.why: Rent owed but unpaid is a liability at the balance sheet date.

questions.q: Extension of a factory building is:
questions.why: It increases the asset and earning capacity beyond one year.

questions.q: Insurance paid ₹12,000 for the year from 1 July. Books close 31 March. Prepaid amount:
questions.why: April to June (3 months) of the next year is prepaid: 12,000 × 3 ÷ 12 = ₹3,000.

questions.q: Interest on drawings is:
options: credited to P&L and deducted from capital
questions.why: Interest on drawings is an income to the business charged to the proprietor.

questions.q: Goods ₹10,000 destroyed by fire, insurance claim ₹7,500 admitted. Trading account is credited with:
questions.why: The full cost of goods lost leaves the trading account; the claim and loss are shown separately.

questions.q: Net profit before commission ₹1,32,000, commission 10% after charging. Commission:
Opening capital ₹2,00,000; closing capital ₹2,40,000; drawings ₹36,000; fresh capital ₹50,000. Profit:
Opening debtors 40,000; closing debtors 55,000; cash collected 2,20,000; bad debts 3,000. Credit sales:
Commission received ₹9,000 includes ₹1,500 received in advance. Amount credited to P&L:
questions.why: Only the earned part, 9,000 − 1,500 = ₹7,500, is income this year.

questions.q: Assets are arranged in order of liquidity when shown:
options: from most permanent to most liquid
from most liquid to least liquid
questions.why: Order of liquidity starts with cash and ends with the most permanent fixed assets; order of permanence is the reverse.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Partnership accounts
courses.summary: Partnership deed and the default rules of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, profit and loss appropriation with interest on capital and drawings, fixed and fluctuating capitals, valuation of goodwill, admission, retirement and death of a partner, and dissolution through the realisation account.
outcomes: Prepare a P&L appropriation account with interest, salary and commission
Compute interest on drawings and choose fixed or fluctuating capital accounts
Value goodwill by average profit, super profit and capitalisation methods
Compute new, sacrificing and gaining ratios and record goodwill on admission and retirement
Prepare realisation, partners' capital and cash accounts on dissolution

scenes.text: Anjali invests ₹2,00,000 and Bilal ₹1,00,000 in a bakery; Bilal also runs the shop full-time.
Their partnership deed fixes interest on capital, a salary for Bilal and a 3:2 profit split – without it, the Act's default rules would apply.

steps.title: Partnership and the deed
steps.body:
Partnership is the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all (Indian Partnership Act, 1932).

The deed usually covers: capital, profit ratio, interest on capital/drawings, salaries, commission, admission/retirement rules, goodwill.

steps.title: Default rules (no deed or deed silent)
steps.body:
- Profits and losses shared **equally**
- **No interest on capital**; no interest on drawings
- **No salary or commission** to partners
- **Interest on partner's loan @ 6% p.a.**

These come from the provisions on mutual rights and duties in the 1932 Act.

steps.title: Fixed vs fluctuating capital
steps.body:
- **Fixed**: capital account shows only capital introduced/withdrawn permanently; interest, salary, share of profit and drawings go to a separate **current account**.
- **Fluctuating**: all these items pass through the capital account itself.

steps.title: Solved: interest on drawings
steps.body:
Drawings ₹60,000 made evenly at the middle of each month; rate 10% p.a.

Average period = 6 months → interest = 60,000 × 10% × 6/12 = **₹3,000**.

(At the beginning of each month: 6.5 months; at the end: 5.5 months.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Allowing interest on capital when the deed is silent.
- Charging partner's loan interest in the appropriation account – it is a charge against profit in P&L.
- Using 6 months for drawings made at the beginning of each month (it is 6.5).

activity.prompt: Partners P and Q share profits 3:2. Capitals ₹3,00,000 and ₹2,00,000; interest on capital 5%; Q's salary ₹30,000. Net profit ₹1,45,000. What is P's share of the remaining (divisible) profit (₹)?

quiz.q: If the deed is silent, interest on a partner's loan is allowed at:
quiz.why: The Partnership Act's default rule allows 6% p.a. interest on loans advanced by a partner.

quiz.q: In the absence of a deed, profits are shared:
options: in the ratio of time devoted
as decided by the eldest partner
quiz.why: Without an agreement, partners share profits and losses equally.

quiz.q: Under fixed capital method, a partner's salary is credited to his:
quiz.why: Under fixed capitals, all recurring items such as salary go to the current account.

quiz.q: Drawings ₹24,000 at the beginning of each month, 10% p.a. Interest on drawings:
quiz.why: Average period is 6.5 months, so 24,000 × 10% × 6.5/12 = ₹1,300.

lessons.title: Goodwill and admission of a partner

scenes.text: A and B, sharing 3:2, admit Chitra for a 1/5 share.
Since the firm already has a loyal customer base, Chitra pays for her share of goodwill, which goes to the partners who give up profit.

steps.title: Goodwill valuation
steps.body:
- **Average profit**: Goodwill = Average profit × No. of years' purchase
- **Super profit**: Super profit = Average profit − Normal profit (Capital employed × Normal rate); Goodwill = Super profit × years' purchase
- **Capitalisation of super profit**: Super profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate
- **Capitalisation of average profit**: (Average profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate) − Capital employed

steps.title: Solved: goodwill
steps.body:
Profits of last 3 years: 40,000; 50,000; 60,000 → average 50,000.

- 2 years' purchase of average profit = **₹1,00,000**
- Capital employed 4,00,000, normal rate 10% → normal profit 40,000; super profit 10,000; 3 years' purchase = **₹30,000**
- Capitalising super profit: 10,000 × 100/10 = **₹1,00,000**

steps.title: Solved: new and sacrificing ratio
steps.body:
A:B = 3:2; C admitted for 1/5.

- Remaining 4/5 shared 3:2 → A 12/25, B 8/25, C 5/25 → **new ratio 12:8:5**
- Sacrifice: A 3/5 − 12/25 = 3/25; B 2/5 − 8/25 = 2/25 → **sacrificing ratio 3:2**
- Goodwill 1,00,000 → C's share 20,000 brought in cash: **Cash Dr 20,000 / To Premium for Goodwill 20,000; Premium Dr / To A 12,000, To B 8,000**

steps.title: Revaluation on admission
steps.body: Changes in asset and liability values go through the **Revaluation A/c** (gains credit, losses debit); the balance is shared by **old partners in old ratio**. Existing reserves and accumulated profits are also distributed to old partners in old ratio. AS 26 permits only purchased goodwill to be recorded, so goodwill is adjusted through capital accounts rather than raised in the books.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Crediting premium to old partners in the old ratio when the sacrificing ratio differs.
- Distributing revaluation profit to the new partner too.
- Confusing normal profit with average profit.

activity.prompt: X and Y share 5:3. Z is admitted for a 1/4 share. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,60,000. How much premium for goodwill must Z bring (₹)?

quiz.q: Super profit is:
quiz.why: Super profit is the excess of average actual profit over the normal profit expected on capital employed.

quiz.q: Premium for goodwill brought by a new partner is credited to old partners in the:
quiz.why: Old partners are compensated for the share of profit they give up, so the sacrificing ratio applies.

quiz.q: Revaluation profit on admission is shared by:
quiz.why: The change in values arose before admission, so it belongs to the old partners in their old ratio.

quiz.q: A:B = 1:1; C admitted for 1/3 share taken equally from A and B. New ratio:
quiz.why: A and B each give 1/6, leaving each 1/3, so all three share equally.

lessons.title: Retirement and death of a partner

scenes.text: Charan, a partner with a 1/6 share, retires after 20 years.
The continuing partners pay him his share of goodwill in their gaining ratio and settle his capital, partly in cash and partly as a loan.

steps.title: Gaining ratio
steps.body: **Gaining ratio = New share − Old share** for each continuing partner. If nothing else is said, continuing partners keep the old ratio among themselves, so gaining ratio = their old ratio.

steps.title: Solved: retirement
steps.body:
A, B, C share 3:2:1. C retires. Firm's goodwill ₹60,000.

- C's share of goodwill = 60,000 × 1/6 = 10,000
- Gaining ratio A:B = 3:2 → **A's Capital Dr 6,000, B's Capital Dr 4,000 / To C's Capital 10,000**
- C's capital (after revaluation, reserves, goodwill) is paid in cash or transferred to **C's Loan A/c**.

steps.title: Solved: death – profit up to date of death
steps.body:
D (share 1/6) dies on 30 June. Last year's profit ₹1,20,000; books close 31 March.

- Time basis: 1,20,000 × 3/12 × 1/6 = **₹5,000**
- Entry: P&L Suspense A/c Dr 5,000 / To D's Capital A/c 5,000
- The balance is transferred to **D's Executors A/c**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Debiting goodwill to continuing partners in the new ratio instead of the gaining ratio.
- Forgetting the deceased partner's interest on capital up to date of death when the deed allows it.
- Paying the executors without crediting the share of reserves.

activity.prompt: P, Q, R share 2:2:1. R dies on 31 August. Average profit of the last three years is ₹90,000; books close 31 March. R's share of profit till death on time basis (₹)?

quiz.q: On retirement, the retiring partner's goodwill share is debited to continuing partners in the:
quiz.why: Continuing partners gain the retiring partner's share, so they compensate him in the gaining ratio.

quiz.q: A:B:C = 4:3:2; B retires; A and C continue in old ratio. Gaining ratio:
quiz.why: A and C keep their old ratio 4:2, i.e. 2:1, so the gaining ratio is 2:1.

quiz.q: Amount due to a deceased partner is transferred to:
quiz.why: The firm settles with the legal representatives, so the balance goes to the executors' account.

quiz.q: The deceased partner's share of profit up to date of death is debited to:
quiz.why: Since the year's books are not closed, the share is debited to P&L Suspense and adjusted later.

scenes.text: Three partners decide to close their electronics shop after losses.
Every asset is sold, every creditor paid, and the partners take what remains – through the realisation account.

steps.title: Realisation account
steps.body:
**Debit**: all assets at book value (except cash/bank and fictitious assets), liabilities paid, realisation expenses
**Credit**: all outside liabilities at book value, assets realised (cash or taken over by a partner)

Balance = profit or loss on realisation, shared in profit ratio. Fictitious assets (P&L debit balance) go directly to capital accounts.

Order of settlement: outside liabilities → partners' loans → partners' capitals.

steps.title: Solved: profit or loss on realisation
steps.body:
Assets (other than cash) ₹2,00,000 realise ₹1,70,000. Creditors ₹50,000 settled for ₹48,000. Realisation expenses ₹2,000.

- Debit: 2,00,000 + 48,000 + 2,000 = 2,50,000
- Credit: 50,000 + 1,70,000 = 2,20,000
- **Loss on realisation = ₹30,000**, shared in profit ratio.

steps.title: Garner v Murray
steps.body: If a partner is insolvent and no agreement exists, the solvent partners bear his capital deficiency in the ratio of their **capitals before dissolution** (not their profit ratio), after bringing in cash for their own share of realisation loss.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Transferring cash/bank balance to the realisation account.
- Debiting a partner's loan to realisation (it is paid separately before capitals).
- Using profit ratio to share an insolvent partner's deficiency under Garner v Murray.

activity.prompt: On which side of the realisation account does each item go?

items.text: Cash received from sale of stock
Asset taken over by a partner

quiz.q: On dissolution, the first payment out of realised cash is to:
quiz.why: Outside liabilities are settled before any partner's loan or capital.

quiz.q: Book value of assets 1,50,000, realised 1,35,000; creditors 30,000 paid in full; expenses 1,000. Realisation loss:
Under Garner v Murray, an insolvent partner's deficiency is borne by solvent partners in:
quiz.why: The rule apportions the deficiency in the ratio of solvent partners' capitals before dissolution.

quiz.q: A partner taking over a stock item is debited to his capital and credited to:
quiz.why: Taking over an asset is a realisation of that asset, so Realisation A/c is credited.

questions.q: The Indian Partnership Act was enacted in:
questions.why: Partnerships are governed by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.

questions.q: In the absence of a deed, partners get interest on capital at:
questions.why: No interest on capital is allowed unless the deed provides for it.

questions.q: Drawings ₹36,000 at the end of each month, interest 10% p.a.:
questions.why: Average period is 5.5 months, so 36,000 × 10% × 5.5/12 = ₹1,650.

questions.q: Average profit ₹80,000, normal profit ₹60,000, goodwill at 3 years' purchase of super profit:
Super profit ₹15,000, normal rate 12.5%. Goodwill by capitalisation of super profit:
A:B = 3:1; C admitted for 1/4 share. New ratio (if old partners keep their ratio):
questions.why: A gets 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16, B gets 3/16 and C 4/16, giving 9:3:4.

questions.q: Reserves existing at the time of admission are credited to:
questions.why: Reserves were built before admission, so they belong to old partners in the old ratio.

questions.q: Interest on a partner's loan is:
questions.why: Loan interest is payable whether or not there is profit, so it is charged in P&L.

questions.q: X:Y:Z = 5:3:2; Y retires. Goodwill ₹50,000 (not in books). Amount debited to X if X and Z continue in old ratio:
questions.why: Y's share is 15,000; gaining ratio is 5:2, so X bears 15,000 × 5/7 = ₹10,714 (rounded).

questions.q: On dissolution, a partner's loan is paid:
options: after outside creditors but before capitals
questions.why: Partners' loans rank after outside liabilities and ahead of capital repayments.

questions.q: Profit on realisation is shared among partners in:
questions.why: Realisation profit or loss is an ordinary profit or loss shared in the profit-sharing ratio.

questions.q: Fixed capital method requires:
questions.why: Fixed capitals keep a capital account for permanent capital and a current account for recurring items.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Consignment, joint venture, hire purchase and branch accounts
courses.summary: Accounting for consignments with valuation of unsold stock, joint ventures by the memorandum method, hire purchase from the hire purchaser's side with interest calculation, and dependent branch accounts under the debtors system.
outcomes: Prepare consignment account and value stock on consignment
Record a joint venture and settle co-venturers by the memorandum method
Split hire purchase instalments into principal and interest and record them
Compute branch profit under the debtors system

scenes.text: A Ludhiana manufacturer sends 100 shawls to an agent in Delhi who will sell them for a 5% commission.
Ownership stays with the manufacturer until sale, so unsold shawls are still his stock.

steps.title: Meaning and documents
steps.body:
- **Consignor**: owner who sends goods; **consignee**: agent who sells them for commission.
- Relationship is principal–agent; ownership does not pass to the consignee.
- **Proforma invoice** shows goods sent; **account sales** is the consignee's periodic statement of sales, expenses, commission and balance due.
- **Del credere commission**: extra commission for which the consignee bears bad debts.

steps.title: Valuing stock on consignment
steps.body:
Unsold stock = **Cost of unsold goods + proportionate non-recurring expenses** (consignor's freight, insurance in transit, consignee's unloading, octroi).

Recurring expenses (godown rent, selling expenses, salesmen's salary) are **not** added to stock.

steps.title: Abnormal loss
steps.body: Goods lost by accident or theft are valued like stock (cost + proportionate non-recurring expenses up to that point), credited to the Consignment A/c, and the net loss after any insurance claim is debited to P&L. Normal loss (evaporation) is absorbed by increasing the cost of the remaining units.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including godown rent or selling expenses in stock valuation.
- Treating goods sent on consignment as sales.
- Forgetting to load stock with consignee's non-recurring expenses.

activity.prompt: 200 units costing ₹300 each sent on consignment. Consignor's freight ₹3,000; consignee's unloading ₹1,000; consignee's selling expenses ₹2,000. 50 units remain unsold. Value of stock on consignment (₹)?

quiz.q: The relationship between consignor and consignee is:
quiz.why: The consignee sells on behalf of the consignor, so they are agent and principal.

quiz.q: Del credere commission is paid to the consignee for:
quiz.why: Del credere commission compensates the consignee for guaranteeing collection from credit customers.

quiz.q: Which is added to the value of unsold stock?
quiz.why: Freight brings goods to their sale location, a non-recurring cost that attaches to every unit.

quiz.q: The statement sent by the consignee is called:
quiz.why: The account sales reports sales, expenses, commission and amount due to the consignor.

scenes.text: Amit in Raipur buys rice; Bhavna in Kolkata sells it. They agree to share profit equally on this one deal.
When the deal ends, they settle and the venture is over.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: A joint venture is a **temporary partnership** for a specific project, without a firm name, ending when the project ends. Methods: separate set of books, each venturer records all transactions, or **memorandum joint venture method** (each records only his own transactions in a 'Joint Venture with B' personal account; a Memorandum JV A/c finds the profit).

steps.title: Solved: memorandum method
steps.body:
A buys goods ₹40,000 and pays expenses ₹2,000. B sells all goods for ₹60,000 and pays expenses ₹3,000. Profit shared equally.

- Memorandum JV: Dr 40,000 + 2,000 + 3,000 = 45,000; Cr sales 60,000 → **profit ₹15,000**, each 7,500
- A is owed his outlay + profit = 42,000 + 7,500 = **₹49,500**
- B's cash after his own expenses = 60,000 − 3,000 = 57,000; he keeps his profit 7,500 and remits **₹49,500** ✓

steps.title: How to check settlement
steps.body: Amount due to a venturer = his outlay + his share of profit. The other venturer's net cash after his own payments, less his own profit share, must equal that amount; always cross-check both sides.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Deducting a venturer's expenses twice when computing the remittance.
- Recording the other venturer's transactions in your own books under the memorandum method.
- Treating a JV as a continuing partnership.

activity.prompt: Memorandum JV: X buys goods ₹30,000 and pays freight ₹1,000. Y sells the goods for ₹45,000 and pays selling expenses ₹2,000. Profit shared equally. How much does Y remit to X to settle (₹)?

quiz.q: A joint venture is:
options: a temporary partnership for a specific venture
quiz.why: A JV is formed for one project and ends when it is completed.

quiz.q: Under the memorandum method, each venturer opens in his books:
options: Joint Venture with the other venturer A/c
quiz.why: Each records only his own transactions in a personal account with the co-venturer.

quiz.q: JV profit is shared in:
quiz.why: The venturers' agreement governs; without one, profits are shared equally as in partnership.

quiz.q: Goods costing ₹20,000 sold for ₹28,000; total JV expenses ₹3,000. JV profit:

scenes.text: A farmer acquires a tractor with a down payment and three yearly instalments.
He uses it from day one, but ownership passes only after the last instalment.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body:
Under a hire purchase agreement the hirer gets **possession immediately**, pays instalments that include interest, and becomes **owner only on payment of the last instalment**. If he defaults, the vendor can repossess (contrast: in an instalment sale, ownership passes at once).

- Cash price + total interest = hire purchase price
- Interest is calculated on the **outstanding cash price** each period

steps.title: Solved: interest schedule
steps.body:
Cash price ₹1,00,000; down payment ₹40,000; balance ₹60,000 repaid in 3 equal annual principal parts of ₹20,000 plus interest at 10% on the outstanding balance.

| Year | Opening balance | Interest | Principal | Instalment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 60,000 | 6,000 | 20,000 | 26,000 |
| 2 | 40,000 | 4,000 | 20,000 | 24,000 |
| 3 | 20,000 | 2,000 | 20,000 | 22,000 |

Total interest = ₹12,000.

steps.title: Entries in the hirer's books (full cash price method)
steps.body:
- On signing: **Asset A/c Dr (full cash price) / To Vendor A/c**
- Down payment: Vendor Dr / To Bank
- Interest due: **Interest A/c Dr / To Vendor A/c**
- Instalment paid: Vendor Dr / To Bank
- Depreciation on full cash price: Depreciation Dr / To Asset
- Interest and depreciation transferred to P&L.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Capitalising the asset at hire purchase price (including interest).
- Charging interest on the original cash price every year.
- Charging depreciation only on amounts paid so far.

activity.prompt: Cash price ₹2,00,000; down payment ₹50,000; balance repaid in 3 equal annual principal parts plus 12% interest on the outstanding balance. Interest for year 2 (₹)?

quiz.q: Under hire purchase, ownership passes:
options: on payment of the last instalment
quiz.why: The hirer becomes owner only after all instalments are paid.

quiz.q: The hirer records the asset at:
quiz.why: Under the full cash price method the asset is capitalised at its cash price; interest is a separate expense.

quiz.q: Interest in a hire purchase instalment is calculated on:
quiz.why: Interest is charged on the balance of cash price still owed at the start of each period.

quiz.q: Cash price ₹50,000; total instalments including down payment ₹58,000. Total interest:
quiz.why: Total interest = hire purchase price − cash price = ₹8,000.

scenes.text: A Mumbai head office sends goods to its Nagpur branch and pays the branch's rent and salaries.
The branch remits all its cash daily and keeps no full books – the head office measures branch profit itself.

steps.title: Dependent branch, debtors system
steps.body:
Head office opens one **Branch A/c** (a nominal-cum-real account).

**Debit**: opening branch assets (stock, debtors, petty cash, furniture), goods sent, cash sent for expenses, closing branch liabilities
**Credit**: opening branch liabilities, cash remitted by branch, goods returned to HO, closing branch assets

Balance: credit side larger = **profit**.

steps.title: Solved: branch profit
steps.body:
Opening: stock 10,000, debtors 5,000. Goods sent 50,000. HO paid branch expenses 4,000. Remittances 60,000. Closing: stock 12,000, debtors 8,000.

- Dr: 10,000 + 5,000 + 50,000 + 4,000 = 69,000
- Cr: 60,000 + 12,000 + 8,000 = 80,000
- **Branch profit = ₹11,000**

steps.title: Goods sent at invoice price
steps.body: If goods are invoiced to the branch above cost, eliminate the loading: debit Branch A/c with loading on closing stock and credit it with loading on opening stock and goods sent (net of returns), using a 'Stock Reserve' or loading entries. Loading on cost of 25% = 20% of invoice price.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Entering branch credit sales or expenses paid out of branch cash in the Branch A/c (they are already reflected in remittances and closing figures).
- Forgetting to remove the loading on stock at invoice price.
- Mixing 25% on cost with 25% on invoice.

activity.prompt: Branch A/c: opening stock ₹8,000, opening debtors ₹4,000, goods sent ₹40,000, cheques sent by HO for branch salaries ₹3,000, cash remitted by branch ₹50,000, closing stock ₹9,000, closing debtors ₹6,000. Branch profit (₹)?

quiz.q: Under the debtors system, cash remitted by the branch is:
quiz.why: Remittances are amounts received by HO from the branch, credited to the Branch A/c.

quiz.q: Goods invoiced at cost + 25%; invoice price ₹1,000. Loading:
quiz.why: Cost is 1,000 ÷ 1.25 = 800, so loading is ₹200, i.e. 20% of invoice price.

quiz.q: Branch closing debtors appear in the Branch A/c on the:
quiz.why: Closing branch assets are credited to bring the Branch A/c balance to profit.

quiz.q: A dependent branch is one that:
options: does not maintain full books and depends on HO
quiz.why: A dependent branch keeps only basic records; head office maintains the accounts.

questions.q: Goods sent on consignment are credited to:
questions.why: The consignor credits Goods Sent on Consignment and debits Consignment A/c; it is not a sale.

questions.q: Consignee's godown rent is:
options: a recurring expense not added to stock
questions.why: Godown rent recurs with time and does not attach to goods, so it is excluded from stock valuation.

questions.q: 500 units costing ₹40 each; consignor's freight ₹2,000; 100 unsold. Stock value:
Sales ₹80,000; ordinary commission 5% and del credere 2% on sales. Total commission:
Memorandum JV A/c is prepared to:
options: ascertain profit or loss of the venture
questions.why: It combines both venturers' transactions solely to find the venture's result.

questions.q: A buys goods ₹50,000; B sells for ₹70,000 and pays expenses ₹4,000; profit equal. B remits to A:
In hire purchase the hirer charges depreciation on:
questions.why: The asset is capitalised at full cash price and depreciated on that amount.

questions.q: Cash price ₹90,000, down payment ₹30,000, interest 10% on outstanding. Interest for year 1:
questions.why: Outstanding after down payment is 60,000, so interest is ₹6,000.

questions.q: The main difference between hire purchase and instalment sale is:
questions.why: In instalment sale ownership passes at once; under hire purchase it passes on the last payment.

questions.q: Under the debtors system, branch profit appears as:
options: excess of credits over debits in Branch A/c
questions.why: When credits exceed debits in the Branch A/c, the difference is profit transferred to General P&L.

questions.q: Goods ₹60,000 at invoice price (cost + 50%). Loading included:
Abnormal loss on consignment, after insurance claim, is debited to:
questions.why: The net abnormal loss is not part of normal trading, so it is charged to the general P&L.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Revision, practicals & exam
courses.summary: A one-page formula and key-point sheet for the whole paper, a full final-accounts practical with adjustments, a computerised-accounting voucher practical, previous-year-style questions with model approaches, and a 15-question paper-level exam.
outcomes: Recall the key formulas and rules of every unit
Prepare complete final accounts with adjustments and check that the balance sheet tallies
Classify transactions into the voucher types used in accounting software
Plan answers to long numerical questions within exam time

scenes.text: Rohan has one evening before his Financial Accounting paper.
Instead of re-reading everything, he works through one sheet of rules and formulas.

steps.title: Process and errors
steps.body:
- A = L + C
- Debit: assets, expenses, drawings; Credit: liabilities, capital, incomes
- One-sided errors → suspense; two-sided → direct entry
- Trial balance does not reveal omission, principle, commission (two-sided) or compensating errors

steps.title: Depreciation, BRS, provisions
steps.body:
- SLM = (Cost − Scrap) ÷ Life; WDV = Rate × Opening book value
- Profit/loss on sale = Sale price − Book value on date of sale
- New provision on debtors after further bad debts; P&L charge = bad debts + new provision − old provision
- BRS: from favourable CB balance, add unpresented cheques, deduct uncleared deposits

steps.title: Final accounts and single entry
steps.body:
- COGS = Opening stock + Net purchases + Direct expenses − Closing stock
- Each adjustment appears twice
- Commission after charging = Profit × r ÷ (100 + r)
- Profit (single entry) = Closing capital + Drawings − Fresh capital − Opening capital

steps.title: Partnership and special accounts
steps.body:
- Default: equal profits, no interest on capital, no salary, 6% on partner's loan
- Drawings interest periods: beginning 6.5, middle 6, end 5.5 months
- Super profit = Average − Normal profit; capitalisation = Super profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate
- Sacrificing = Old − New; Gaining = New − Old
- Stock on consignment = cost + proportionate non-recurring expenses
- Loading: 25% on cost = 20% on invoice; 50% on cost = 33⅓% on invoice

steps.title: Exam technique
steps.body:
- Show working notes for every adjusted figure.
- In final accounts, tick each adjustment twice as you use it.
- Always check that the balance sheet tallies before moving on; if it does not, look for one-sided adjustments first.

items.text: Crediting premium for goodwill brought by a new partner
Debiting continuing partners for a retiring partner's goodwill
Compensating partners who give up share on admission
Sharing a deceased partner's goodwill among survivors

Loading of 33⅓% on cost equals what percentage of invoice price?
quiz.why: Cost 3, loading 1, invoice 4, so loading is 1/4 = 25% of invoice price.

quiz.q: Drawings at the end of each month carry interest for an average of:
quiz.why: The first drawing earns 11 months, the last 0, averaging 5.5 months.

quiz.why: Sale price exceeds book value by ₹3,500, a profit on sale.

scenes.text: You are handed the trial balance of Meera Traders and four adjustments.
Your task: trading account, P&L account and a balance sheet that tallies.

steps.title: Trial balance as on 31 March
steps.body:
**Debit**: Drawings 20,000; Opening stock 25,000; Purchases 1,50,000; Wages 15,000; Salaries 30,000; Rent 12,000; Debtors 60,000; Machinery 1,00,000; Cash 88,000 → **5,00,000**

**Credit**: Capital 2,00,000; Sales 2,60,000; Creditors 40,000 → **5,00,000**

Adjustments: closing stock 35,000; depreciate machinery 10%; salaries outstanding 3,000; rent prepaid 2,000.

steps.title: Step 1: Trading account
steps.body:

- Cr: Sales 2,60,000 + Closing stock 35,000 = 2,95,000
- **Gross profit = ₹1,05,000**

steps.title: Step 3: Balance sheet
steps.body:
**Liabilities**: Capital 2,00,000 + NP 52,000 − Drawings 20,000 = 2,32,000; Creditors 40,000; Outstanding salaries 3,000 → **2,75,000**

**Assets**: Machinery 90,000; Closing stock 35,000; Debtors 60,000; Prepaid rent 2,000; Cash 88,000 → **2,75,000** ✓

steps.title: Variation to try
steps.body: Add one more adjustment: provision for doubtful debts 5% on debtors. Recompute net profit (₹49,000) and the balance sheet total (₹2,72,000), and confirm both sides still agree.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to deduct depreciation from the machinery figure in the balance sheet.
- Adding prepaid rent to liabilities.
- Deducting drawings from net profit in the P&L account.

scenes.text: In the B.Com computer lab, Sana enters a week of transactions into accounting software.
Choosing the right voucher type decides which books the software updates.

steps.title: Common voucher types
steps.body:
Most Indian accounting packages use the same voucher families:
- **Payment** – money goes out (cash/bank credited)
- **Receipt** – money comes in (cash/bank debited)
- **Contra** – between cash and bank, or bank to bank
- **Sales** / **Purchase** – trading of goods or services (with GST where applicable)
- **Credit note / Debit note** – sales returns / purchase returns
- **Journal** – non-cash adjustments: depreciation, outstanding expenses, credit purchase of assets

steps.title: Ledger grouping
steps.body: Software asks you to place each ledger in a group (e.g. Capital Account, Sundry Debtors, Sundry Creditors, Fixed Assets, Direct Expenses, Indirect Expenses, Sales Accounts). The group decides where the ledger appears in the trial balance, P&L and balance sheet – so a wrong group gives wrong final accounts even if entries are right.

steps.title: Practical procedure
steps.body:
1. Create the company with financial year 1 April.
2. Create ledgers under correct groups with opening balances.
3. Enter vouchers date-wise.
4. View trial balance, P&L and balance sheet reports.
5. Compare with your manual answer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a payment voucher for cash deposited into bank (it is contra).
- Putting wages under indirect expenses (they normally go under direct expenses).
- Entering credit purchase of furniture as a purchase voucher of goods.

activity.prompt: Which voucher type should be used?

quiz.q: Cash withdrawn from bank for office use is entered as a:
quiz.why: Movement between cash and bank is a contra entry.

quiz.q: Depreciation is recorded through a:
quiz.why: Depreciation involves no cash, so it is a journal adjustment.

quiz.q: A sales return is usually recorded with a:
quiz.why: The seller issues a credit note to the customer for goods returned.

quiz.q: Placing a ledger in the wrong group mainly affects:
options: where the item appears in final accounts
quiz.why: The group decides whether the ledger shows in trading, P&L or the balance sheet.

scenes.text: The paper has one long final-accounts question and several shorter ones.
A plan for each question type saves time and marks.

steps.title: Q1 (theory, 5 marks): Distinguish provision and reserve
steps.body: Model points: charge vs appropriation of profit; made even in loss vs only from profit; for known liabilities vs strengthening finances; shown as deduction from asset or liability vs under capital/reserves; reduces divisible profit vs retains profit.

steps.title: Q2 (numerical, 10 marks): Depreciation with sale
steps.body: Plan: draw a year-wise table (opening, purchase, depreciation, sale, closing) per asset lot; compute depreciation to the date of sale; transfer book value; find profit/loss; prepare the Machinery A/c for each year. Always state the method and the closing date assumed.

steps.title: Q3 (numerical, 15 marks): Admission of a partner
steps.body: Plan: (1) new and sacrificing ratio, (2) revaluation account, (3) goodwill entry, (4) reserves distribution, (5) capital accounts, (6) new balance sheet. Working notes first; final statements second.

steps.title: Q4 (short numerical): Credit purchases
steps.body:
Opening creditors 30,000; closing creditors 45,000; cash paid 2,10,000; discount received 5,000; purchase returns 8,000.

Credit purchases = 2,10,000 + 5,000 + 8,000 + 45,000 − 30,000 = **₹2,38,000**.

steps.title: Time plan
steps.body: Allocate minutes in proportion to marks (about 1.6 minutes per mark in a 3-hour, 100-mark paper), leaving 10 minutes to check the balance sheet and totals.

In an admission question, which is computed first?
quiz.why: Goodwill and other entries depend on the ratios, so they come first.

quiz.q: A provision, unlike a reserve, is made:
options: even when there is a loss
quiz.why: A provision is a charge against profit for a known loss, so it is required even in a loss year.

quiz.why: 180 minutes over 100 marks is about 1.8; leaving checking time gives roughly 1.6 minutes per mark.

questions.why: The default rule allows 6% p.a. on partner's loans: ₹3,000.
