uni-bcom-financial-management.title: B.Com — Financial Management, unit by unit
uni-bcom-financial-management.description: Financial Management for commerce students: goals of the firm and time value of money, capital budgeting, cost of capital, leverage and capital structure, dividend policy and working capital management, with fully solved numericals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Com programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Nature of financial management and time value of money
courses.summary: Scope and functions of financial management, profit versus wealth maximisation and agency problems, and the time value of money: compounding, discounting, annuities, perpetuities, sinking funds and loan amortisation.
outcomes: Explain the three finance decisions and the role of the finance manager
Argue why wealth maximisation is superior to profit maximisation
Compute future and present values of single sums
Value ordinary annuities, annuities due, perpetuities and growing perpetuities
Compute sinking-fund deposits and build a loan amortisation schedule

lessons.title: Scope and objectives of financial management

scenes.text: The CFO of a Pune auto-parts maker faces three questions this year: which plant to build, how to fund it, and how much dividend to pay.
Each decision should raise the value of the shareholders' stake.

steps.title: Meaning and scope
steps.body:
**Financial management** is the planning, organising, directing and controlling of financial activities — procurement and use of funds.

Three core decisions:
1. **Investment decision** (capital budgeting, working capital)
2. **Financing decision** (debt–equity mix, sources)
3. **Dividend decision** (pay-out vs retention)

Plus the **liquidity decision** (managing current assets).

steps.title: Profit vs wealth maximisation
steps.body:
**Profit maximisation** — criticisms: vague (which profit?), ignores **timing** (time value), ignores **risk**, may encourage short-termism.

**Wealth (value) maximisation** — maximise the **market value of shares** / NPV of the firm: uses cash flows, accounts for time value and risk, aligns with shareholders' long-term interest. Widely accepted as the goal.

steps.title: Agency problem
steps.body: Managers (agents) may pursue their own goals — perks, empire-building — rather than shareholders' (principals'). **Agency costs**: monitoring, bonding, residual loss. Remedies: performance-linked pay, ESOPs, independent directors, audits, market for corporate control.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating wealth maximisation with maximising EPS — EPS ignores risk and timing.
- Forgetting that the finance manager also manages liquidity, not just long-term funds.

activity.prompt: Classify each choice by the finance decision it belongs to.

items.text: Whether to buy a new CNC machine
Take a term loan from a bank
Announce a buy-back instead of dividend

quiz.q: The goal most widely accepted in financial management is:
quiz.why: Wealth maximisation considers time value and risk through market value, unlike plain profit.

quiz.q: Profit maximisation ignores:
options: the timing and risk of returns
quiz.why: It treats ₹1 today and ₹1 in five years as equal and ignores uncertainty.

quiz.q: An ESOP helps reduce:
quiz.why: Giving managers equity aligns their interests with shareholders'.

scenes.text: Nikhil is offered ₹10,000 now or ₹13,000 after three years.
At 10% interest, ₹10,000 grows to ₹13,310 — so the money now is worth more.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Future value**: FV = PV × (1 + r)^n
- **Present value**: PV = FV / (1 + r)^n
- Multiple compounding: FV = PV × (1 + r/m)^(m·n)
- **Effective annual rate (EAR)** = (1 + r/m)^m − 1
- **Rule of 72**: years to double ≈ 72 / rate (%)

steps.title: Solved: semi-annual compounding and EAR
steps.body:
₹50,000 at 12% compounded half-yearly for 2 years.

- FV = 50,000 × 1.06^4 = 50,000 × 1.262477 = **₹63,124**
- EAR = 1.06² − 1 = **12.36%**
- Rule of 72 at 12%: doubles in ≈ 6 years (exact 6.12).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the annual rate with the number of half-years.
- Comparing amounts at different dates without discounting to the same date.

activity.prompt: PV of ₹50,000 receivable after 2 years at 10% (₹, nearest rupee)?

quiz.q: FV of ₹1,000 at 5% for 2 years:
EAR of 8% compounded quarterly:
By the Rule of 72, money at 9% doubles in about:
quiz.why: 72 / 9 = 8 years.

scenes.text: A retiring officer can take ₹10,000 a year for 5 years or ₹38,000 today.
At 10%, the annuity is worth ₹37,908 now — the lump sum is slightly better.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **PV of ordinary annuity**: PV = A × [1 − (1 + r)^(−n)]/r = A × PVIFA
- **FV of ordinary annuity**: FV = A × [(1 + r)^n − 1]/r = A × FVIFA
- **Annuity due** (payments at start): multiply ordinary value by (1 + r)
- **Perpetuity**: PV = A / r
- **Growing perpetuity**: PV = A1 / (r − g), r > g

steps.title: Solved: PV and FV of annuity

courses.title: Unit 2 · Capital budgeting
courses.summary: Nature and process of capital budgeting, estimation of after-tax cash flows, and the payback, discounted payback, ARR, NPV, profitability index and IRR methods, with one project worked through every technique.
outcomes: Estimate initial outlay and annual cash flows after tax
Compute payback and discounted payback periods
Compute the accounting rate of return
Compute NPV and profitability index and apply the decision rules

lessons.title: Nature of capital budgeting and cash-flow estimation

scenes.text: A small Coimbatore pump maker can buy a ₹1,00,000 machine expected to generate cash for four years.
Before deciding, the accountant estimates the after-tax cash flows year by year.

steps.title: Meaning and importance
steps.body:
**Capital budgeting** is the process of evaluating and selecting long-term investments whose benefits extend beyond one year.

Why it matters: large outlays, long-term effects, irreversibility, impact on risk and growth.

Process: idea generation → estimation of cash flows → evaluation → selection → implementation → **post-audit**.

Types of decisions: expansion, replacement, mutually exclusive, independent, capital rationing.

steps.title: Relevant cash flows
steps.body:
- Use **incremental, after-tax cash flows**, not accounting profit.
- **Initial outlay** = cost + installation + increase in working capital − sale proceeds of old asset (adjusted for tax).
- **Annual CFAT** = EBIT(1 − t) + depreciation, or (Revenue − Cash costs)(1 − t) + t × Depreciation.
- **Terminal cash flow** = salvage (after tax) + release of working capital.
- Ignore **sunk costs**; include **opportunity costs**; exclude financing costs (interest) — they are captured by the discount rate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Deducting interest when computing project cash flows.
- Including a feasibility study already paid for (sunk cost).
- Forgetting to recover working capital at the end.

activity.prompt: Profit before depreciation and tax ₹80,000; depreciation ₹30,000; tax 25%. Compute CFAT (₹).

quiz.q: Which is NOT a relevant cash flow?
options: sunk cost of a past survey
quiz.why: Sunk costs have already been incurred and do not change with the decision.

quiz.q: Depreciation affects cash flow because it:
quiz.why: Depreciation is non-cash but tax-deductible, so it creates a tax shield.

quiz.q: Interest on project loans is excluded from cash flows because:
options: financing cost is reflected in the discount rate
quiz.why: Including it in both the cash flows and the cost of capital would double-count financing cost.

steps.body: Cost ₹1,00,000; life 4 years; no salvage; straight-line depreciation ₹25,000; CFAT: Y1 30,000, Y2 40,000, Y3 50,000, Y4 20,000; cost of capital 10%.

steps.title: Solved: payback
steps.body:
Cumulative CFAT: 30,000 → 70,000 → 1,20,000.

- Recovered 70,000 after 2 years; need 30,000 more of Y3's 50,000.
- **Payback = 2 + 30/50 = 2.6 years**

Merits: simple, stresses liquidity. Limits: ignores time value and cash flows after payback.

steps.title: Solved: ARR
steps.body:
- Total CFAT = 1,40,000; total depreciation = 1,00,000 ⇒ total profit after tax = 40,000
- Average annual profit = 10,000
- Average investment = (1,00,000 + 0)/2 = 50,000
- **ARR = 10,000/50,000 = 20%** (on original investment: 10%)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Forgetting to add salvage to the average-investment formula: (Cost + Salvage)/2 (+ working capital).

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- **NPV = Σ CFt/(1 + k)^t − Initial outlay**; accept if NPV > 0.
- **PI = PV of inflows / Initial outlay**; accept if PI > 1.
- **Discounted payback**: time for cumulative discounted CFs to recover the outlay.

steps.title: Solved: discounted payback
steps.body:
Cumulative PV: 27,273 → 60,331 → 97,897 → 1,11,557.

- After 3 years 2,103 is still unrecovered; Y4 PV 13,660
- **Discounted payback = 3 + 2,103/13,660 = 3.15 years** (vs 2.6 simple)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Discounting the initial outlay at t = 0 (factor is 1).
- Treating PI > 0 as acceptance — the cut-off is 1.

The IRR is the rate at which the project's NPV becomes zero.

steps.title: Internal rate of return
steps.body:
IRR is the discount rate r at which **NPV = 0**. Accept if IRR > cost of capital.

Trial and error + **interpolation**: IRR = L + [NPV_L / (NPV_L − NPV_H)] × (H − L).

For even cash flows, start from PVIFA = Outlay / annual CF and find r in the annuity table.

steps.title: Solved: IRR of the unit project
NPV vs IRR
steps.body:
For independent conventional projects both give the same accept/reject decision. For **mutually exclusive** projects they may rank differently because of:
- **Size** differences, **timing** of cash flows, unequal lives
- Reinvestment assumption: NPV assumes reinvestment at k (more realistic); IRR at IRR
- Non-conventional flows can give multiple IRRs

When in conflict, **prefer NPV** (it maximises wealth).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Interpolating between rates whose NPVs have the same sign.
- Choosing the higher-IRR project when the other has a higher NPV.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Cost of capital
courses.summary: Meaning and significance of cost of capital; specific costs of debt, preference shares, equity (dividend-growth and CAPM) and retained earnings; and the weighted average cost of capital with book and market weights.
outcomes: Explain why cost of capital is the minimum required rate of return
Compute the after-tax cost of irredeemable and redeemable debt
Compute the cost of preference capital

Compute WACC using book-value and market-value weights

scenes.text: A project earning 11% looks good — until the CFO says money costs the firm 12.7%.
Cost of capital is the hurdle every project must clear.

steps.title: Meaning and significance
steps.body:
**Cost of capital** is the minimum rate of return a firm must earn on its investments to maintain the market value of its shares — the investors' required return.

- Used as the **discount rate/hurdle rate** in capital budgeting
- Guides capital structure and financing choices
- Basis for evaluating management performance

Components: explicit vs implicit cost; specific vs composite (WACC); historical vs future; marginal cost.

steps.title: Cost of debt
steps.body:
Interest is tax-deductible, so the **after-tax** cost is relevant.

- **Irredeemable debt**: Kd = I(1 − t) / NP, NP = net proceeds after flotation cost
- **Redeemable debt** (approximation): Kd = [I(1 − t) + (RV − NP)/n] / [(RV + NP)/2]
- Debt is usually the **cheapest** source: lower risk to lenders and a tax shield.

steps.title: Solved: redeemable debt
steps.body:
Same debentures redeemable at par after 5 years.

- Numerator = 8.4 + (100 − 95)/5 = 8.4 + 1 = 9.4
- Denominator = (100 + 95)/2 = 97.5
- **Kd = 9.4/97.5 = 9.64%**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the coupon rate as the cost of debt when debt is issued at a discount or premium.
- Applying the tax adjustment to the redemption premium/discount portion in the simplified formula.

activity.prompt: 10% irredeemable debentures, face ₹100, issued at ₹100 net, tax 25%. After-tax Kd (%)?

quiz.q: Debt is usually the cheapest source of finance because:
options: interest is tax-deductible and lenders face less risk
quiz.why: Lower risk for lenders and the tax shield on interest both reduce the effective cost.

quiz.q: Cost of capital is used in capital budgeting as the:
quiz.why: Projects are accepted only if they earn more than the cost of capital.

quiz.q: Issue at a discount makes Kd:
quiz.why: The firm receives less but pays full interest and redemption, raising the effective cost.

lessons.title: Cost of preference and equity capital

scenes.text: Equity holders get no fixed return — yet they expect more than lenders because they bear more risk.
Their expected return can be estimated from dividends and growth, or from market risk via CAPM.

steps.title: Preference capital
steps.body:
- Irredeemable: **Kp = D / NP**
- Redeemable: **Kp = [D + (RV − NP)/n] / [(RV + NP)/2]**
- No tax adjustment (preference dividend is paid out of post-tax profit).

steps.title: Equity capital
steps.body:
- **Dividend-growth (Gordon) model**: Ke = D1/P0 + g (for new issue use NP instead of P0)
- **CAPM**: Ke = Rf + β(Rm − Rf)
- **Earnings-price approach**: Ke = EPS/MP (assumes no growth)
- **Retained earnings**: Kr = Ke without flotation cost (opportunity cost to shareholders); some texts adjust for personal tax and brokerage.

steps.title: Solved: preference
steps.body:
10% preference shares of ₹100 issued at ₹98, redeemable at par after 5 years.

- Irredeemable view: 10/98 = **10.20%**
- Redeemable: [10 + 2/5]/[(100 + 98)/2] = 10.4/99 = **10.51%**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using D0 instead of D1 = D0(1 + g) in the Gordon model.
- Applying (1 − t) to preference dividends.
- Using Rm instead of the risk premium (Rm − Rf) in CAPM.

activity.prompt: CAPM: risk-free 6.5%, beta 1.5, market return 12.5%. Compute Ke (%).

quiz.q: In CAPM, β measures:
quiz.why: Beta captures sensitivity to market movements, the non-diversifiable risk.

quiz.q: Cost of retained earnings is usually:

quiz.why: Retained earnings avoid flotation costs, so their cost is a little below new equity.

lessons.title: Lab: weighted average cost of capital

scenes.text: The firm's capital is a mix of equity, retained earnings, preference shares and debt.
WACC blends their costs in proportion to their weights.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
**WACC = Σ (Wi × Ki)**, Wi = proportion of each source.

- **Book-value weights**: from the balance sheet; easy but historical.
- **Market-value weights**: current market values; theoretically superior.
- **Marginal weights**: proportions of new capital to be raised.

steps.title: Solved: market-value WACC
steps.body:
Equity + retained earnings have market value ₹12,00,000 (Ke 15%); debt ₹2,00,000 at 7%; no preference.

- Weights: 12/14 = 0.857, 2/14 = 0.143
- WACC = 0.857 × 15 + 0.143 × 7 = 12.86 + 1.00 = **13.86%**

Market weights give more weight to equity when shares trade above book value, raising WACC.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using before-tax cost of debt in WACC.
- Weights that do not add up to 1.

activity.prompt: Equity 60% at 16%, debt 40% at 8% after tax. WACC (%)?

quiz.q: In the book-value table, the largest contribution comes from:
quiz.why: Equity has the biggest weight and the highest cost, contributing 7.5 percentage points.

quiz.q: Market-value weights are preferred because:
quiz.why: Investors' required returns relate to current market values, not historical book values.

quiz.q: Adding more cheap debt (ignoring risk) tends to:
quiz.why: Replacing costlier equity with cheaper after-tax debt reduces the weighted average, until higher risk raises other costs.

lessons.title: Marginal cost of capital and practice

scenes.text: After the first ₹50 lakh of retained earnings is used up, the firm must issue new shares with flotation costs.
The marginal cost of capital steps up at that break point.

steps.title: Marginal cost of capital (MCC)
steps.body:
- MCC is the WACC of the **next rupee** of new capital.
- **Break point** = amount of a cheaper source available / its weight in the target structure.
- Beyond the break point, a costlier source replaces it and MCC rises.
- Accept projects (ranked by IRR) until IRR falls below MCC — the optimal capital budget.

steps.title: Solved: break point
steps.body:
Target: 60% equity, 40% debt. Retained earnings available ₹30 lakh (Kr 14%); new equity costs 16%; debt 7% after tax.

- Break point = 30/0.60 = **₹50 lakh** of total new capital
- MCC up to ₹50 lakh = 0.6 × 14 + 0.4 × 7 = **11.2%**
- MCC beyond = 0.6 × 16 + 0.4 × 7 = **12.4%**

steps.title: Practice
steps.body:
A firm's 11% debentures (₹100) trade at ₹110, irredeemable, tax 30%. Kd?

**Solution**: 11 × 0.7 / 110 = 7.7/110 = **7%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing available funds by the cost instead of by the weight to get the break point.
- Using a single WACC for any amount of new financing.

quiz.q: MCC rises after the break point because:
options: a costlier source replaces a cheaper one
quiz.why: Once cheaper funds like retained earnings are used up, the firm must use costlier new equity.

A firm should accept projects until:
quiz.why: Investing beyond that point would earn less than the cost of the extra funds.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Leverage and capital structure
courses.summary: Operating, financial and combined leverage; EBIT–EPS analysis and the indifference point; and the NI, NOI, traditional and Modigliani–Miller theories of capital structure, with valuation numericals.
outcomes: Compute DOL, DFL and DCL and interpret them

lessons.title: Lab: operating, financial and combined leverage

scenes.text: A firm's sales rise 10% and its EPS jumps 20%.
Fixed operating costs and fixed interest act like levers that magnify changes.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **DOL** = Contribution / EBIT = %ΔEBIT / %ΔSales
- **DFL** = EBIT / EBT = %ΔEPS / %ΔEBIT (with preference dividend: EBIT / [EBT − Dp/(1 − t)])
- **DCL** = DOL × DFL = Contribution / EBT = %ΔEPS / %ΔSales

High DOL ⇒ high business risk; high DFL ⇒ high financial risk.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Sales ₹10,00,000; variable cost 40%; fixed cost ₹2,00,000; interest ₹1,00,000.

- Contribution = 6,00,000; EBIT = 4,00,000; EBT = 3,00,000
- **DOL = 6/4 = 1.5**
- **DFL = 4/3 = 1.33**
- **DCL = 6/3 = 2.0**

Interpretation: a 10% rise in sales raises EBIT by 15% and EPS by 20%.

steps.title: Risky combinations
steps.body: A firm with both high DOL and high DFL is very risky. Firms with high operating leverage (airlines, steel) usually keep financial leverage moderate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using sales instead of contribution in DOL.
- Including interest in fixed costs for DOL — interest belongs to DFL.

activity.prompt: Contribution ₹5,00,000; fixed cost ₹3,00,000; interest ₹50,000. Compute DCL.

quiz.q: DOL = 2 and sales rise 5%. EBIT rises by:
quiz.why: %ΔEBIT = DOL × %ΔSales = 2 × 5% = 10%.

quiz.q: Financial leverage arises from:
quiz.why: Fixed interest (and preference dividends) magnify the effect of EBIT changes on EPS.

quiz.q: DOL 1.5 and DFL 2 give DCL of:
quiz.why: DCL = DOL × DFL = 3.

lessons.title: Lab: EBIT–EPS analysis and indifference point

scenes.text: A firm needs ₹10 lakh: all equity at ₹10 per share, or half equity and half 10% debt.
At expected EBIT of ₹2 lakh, which plan gives higher EPS?

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
EPS = [(EBIT − I)(1 − t) − Dp] / N, where N is the number of equity shares.

**Indifference point**: EBIT at which both plans give equal EPS:
(X − I1)(1 − t)/N1 = (X − I2)(1 − t)/N2

Above it, the more levered plan gives higher EPS; below it, the equity plan does.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting preference dividends are paid after tax.
- Choosing the levered plan without checking EBIT stability (risk).

activity.prompt: Plan X: 2,00,000 shares, no debt. Plan Y: 1,00,000 shares + interest ₹1,00,000. Tax 25%. Indifference EBIT (₹)?

quiz.q: Above the indifference EBIT, the plan with more debt gives:
quiz.why: Once EBIT exceeds the indifference point, fixed interest is covered and leverage magnifies EPS.

quiz.q: At EBIT ₹50,000 in the solved example, which plan is better?
quiz.why: ₹50,000 is below the ₹1,00,000 indifference point, so the all-equity plan gives higher EPS (₹0.35 vs ₹0).

quiz.q: EBIT–EPS analysis ignores:
quiz.why: It focuses on EPS and does not measure the effect of risk on share price.

scenes.text: Modigliani and Miller asked: does slicing a pizza differently change its size?
Without taxes, they said no; with corporate taxes, debt adds value through the tax shield.

steps.title: Assumptions and approaches
steps.body:
Common assumptions: only debt and equity; no taxes (initially); 100% payout; constant EBIT; no growth.

- **Net Income (NI)** (Durand): Kd and Ke constant ⇒ more debt lowers Ko and raises value; optimum at maximum debt.
- **Net Operating Income (NOI)**: Ko constant; Ke rises with leverage to offset cheaper debt ⇒ value independent of structure.
- **Traditional**: moderate debt lowers Ko up to a point, then rising Ke and Kd raise it ⇒ an **optimum** exists.
- **MM (1958, no taxes)**: Proposition I — value independent of leverage (arbitrage); Proposition II — Ke rises linearly with D/E.
- **MM with taxes (1963)**: **VL = VU + tD** — debt adds value via the tax shield.
- **Trade-off** and **pecking-order** theories add bankruptcy costs and information asymmetry.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying NI logic (constant Ke) under NOI.
- Ignoring bankruptcy and agency costs when recommending maximum debt under MM with taxes.

activity.prompt: MM with taxes: unlevered value ₹50 lakh, debt ₹20 lakh, tax 30%. Value of levered firm (₹ lakh)?

quiz.q: Under the NOI approach, the overall cost of capital:
quiz.why: NOI holds Ko constant, so value does not depend on capital structure.

quiz.q: MM Proposition II states that:
options: Ke rises linearly with the debt–equity ratio
quiz.why: Equity holders demand a higher return as financial risk rises with leverage.

quiz.q: The pecking-order theory says firms prefer:
options: internal funds, then debt, then equity
quiz.why: Information asymmetry makes internal funds cheapest and new equity the last resort.

scenes.text: A cement company with stable cash flows can carry more debt than a software start-up.
Managers weigh tax savings against the risk of financial distress.

steps.title: Features of an optimal structure
steps.body: - **Profitability** (maximise EPS/value), **solvency** (avoid excess debt), **flexibility**, **control** (avoid dilution), **conservatism**.

steps.title: Determinants
steps.body:
- Stability of sales and cash flows
- Cost of capital and tax rate
- Nature and size of business; asset tangibility (collateral)
- Control considerations, market conditions, legal and lender requirements (debt covenants)
- Interest coverage and debt-service coverage ratios

steps.title: Solved: interest coverage
steps.body:

- **Interest coverage = 4.0 times**

courses.title: Unit 5 · Dividend decisions, working capital, revision and exam
courses.summary: Walter, Gordon and Modigliani–Miller dividend models and practical dividend policy; working capital concepts and the operating cycle; inventory, receivables and cash management with EOQ and trade-credit cost; and a whole-subject revision sheet with the final exam.
outcomes: Value shares and choose payout ratios with the Walter and Gordon models

lessons.title: Lab: dividend theories — Walter, Gordon, MM

scenes.text: A fast-growing firm earns 15% on reinvested funds while shareholders expect only 12%.
Walter's model says it should retain everything — each rupee kept is worth more inside the firm.

steps.title: Relevance theories
steps.body:
**Walter**: P = [D + (r/ke)(E − D)] / ke
- r > ke (growth firm) ⇒ payout 0% maximises price
- r < ke (declining firm) ⇒ payout 100%
- r = ke (normal firm) ⇒ payout irrelevant

**Gordon**: P = E(1 − b) / (ke − br), b = retention ratio, g = br. 'Bird-in-hand' argument: investors value near dividends more under uncertainty.

steps.title: MM irrelevance
steps.body:
In perfect markets without taxes, value depends on earnings and investment policy, not on how earnings are split.

- **P0 = (D1 + P1) / (1 + ke)**
- New shares needed: m = (I − (E − nD1)) / P1

Criticisms: taxes, flotation costs, transaction costs, information content of dividends.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- In Walter's formula, multiplying (E − D) by r without dividing by ke.
- Using Gordon's model when br ≥ ke (price becomes undefined).

activity.prompt: Walter: E = ₹12, D = ₹6, r = 10%, ke = 8%. Share price (₹)?

quiz.why: Retained funds earn more than shareholders require, so retaining everything raises the share price.

quiz.why: MM assume perfect markets with no taxes or transaction costs.

scenes.text: A large FMCG company raises its dividend a little every year, even when profits dip.
Investors read a dividend cut as bad news about the future.

steps.title: Types of dividend policy
steps.body:
- **Stable dividend per share** (most common), **stable payout ratio**, **low regular plus extra**, **residual** (pay what is left after funding positive-NPV projects).
- **Lintner's model**: firms have a target payout and adjust dividends gradually towards it — dividend smoothing.

steps.title: Determinants and forms
steps.body:
- Determinants: earnings stability, liquidity, growth needs, access to capital, taxation, legal restrictions, debt covenants, shareholder preference, control.
- Forms: **cash dividend**, **bonus shares** (stock dividend), **share buy-back**, stock split (not a dividend).
- In India, dividends are taxable in the hands of shareholders (since the abolition of DDT from 1 April 2020).

steps.title: Information content
steps.body: A dividend increase is often read as management confidence in future earnings (signalling), which is why firms avoid cutting dividends.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a stock split a dividend — it only changes face value and number of shares.
- Thinking bonus shares transfer cash to shareholders.

quiz.why: Bonus shares convert reserves into share capital without any cash outflow.

quiz.q: Under a residual policy, dividends are paid:

quiz.why: The residual approach finances positive-NPV projects first and pays out what remains.

lessons.title: Lab: working capital and the operating cycle

story.title: Cash tied up in the cycle

scenes.text: A garment exporter buys fabric, stitches, stores, sells on credit and finally collects cash months later.
The longer that cycle, the more working capital it needs.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Gross working capital** = total current assets; **net working capital** = CA − CL.
- **Permanent** (minimum always needed) vs **temporary/fluctuating** working capital.
- Approaches to financing: **matching (hedging)**, **conservative**, **aggressive**.
- Excess WC ⇒ idle funds; inadequate WC ⇒ production stoppages, lost discounts.

steps.title: Operating cycle
steps.body:
**Gross operating cycle** = RM storage + WIP + FG storage + debtors' collection period
**Net operating (cash conversion) cycle** = Gross − creditors' payment period

- RM period = avg RM stock / daily RM consumption
- Debtors period = avg debtors / daily credit sales

steps.title: Solved: operating cycle
steps.body:
RM 30 days, WIP 15 days, FG 20 days, debtors 45 days, creditors 40 days.

- **Gross OC = 110 days**
- **Net OC = 70 days**
- If daily cash operating cost is ₹20,000, approximate WC need = 70 × 20,000 = **₹14 lakh**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding the creditors' period instead of deducting it.
- Using total sales instead of credit sales for the debtors' period.

quiz.why: NWC is current assets less current liabilities.

quiz.why: Matching aligns maturities: long-term needs with long-term sources.

quiz.q: Longer credit from suppliers makes the net operating cycle:
quiz.why: The creditors' period is subtracted, so more supplier credit shortens the net cycle.

scenes.text: A distributor uses 12,000 cartons a year; each order costs ₹200 to place and each carton costs ₹4.80 a year to store.
The EOQ formula balances ordering and carrying costs.

steps.title: Inventory
steps.body:
- **EOQ = √(2AO/C)**, A = annual demand, O = cost per order, C = carrying cost per unit per year.
- Reorder level = lead time × usage (+ safety stock).
- **ABC analysis**: tight control on high-value A items. JIT minimises stock.

steps.title: Receivables and cash
steps.body:
- Credit policy: standards (5 Cs), terms (e.g. 2/10 net 30), collection effort.
- **Cost of forgoing a cash discount** = [d/(100 − d)] × [365/(N − D)].
- Cash management motives: transaction, precautionary, speculative; tools: cash budgets, concentration banking, lock-box, sweep accounts.

steps.title: Solved: cost of trade credit
steps.body:
Terms 2/10 net 30.

- Cost = (2/98) × (365/20) = 0.020408 × 18.25 = **37.24% p.a.**
- If bank credit costs 12%, borrow and take the discount.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the unit price instead of the carrying cost per unit in EOQ.
- Dividing by N instead of (N − D) in the trade-credit formula.

uni-bcom-financial-markets-institutions.title: B.Com — Financial Markets & Institutions, unit by unit
uni-bcom-financial-markets-institutions.description: The Indian financial system for commerce students: structure and functions, money market instruments, primary and secondary capital markets with SEBI regulation, banking and non-banking institutions, mutual funds and financial services, with yield and valuation numericals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Com programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · The Indian financial system
courses.summary: Meaning, components and functions of a financial system; financial intermediation and the regulators of Indian finance; and the reforms since 1991 including financial inclusion.
outcomes: Identify the four components of a financial system
Explain how intermediaries transform maturity, size and risk
Classify markets as money/capital, primary/secondary, organised/unorganised
Name the regulator for each segment of Indian finance
Outline the major financial-sector reforms since 1991

lessons.title: Structure and functions of the financial system

scenes.text: A retired teacher in Kochi has ₹10 lakh of savings and wants safety and income.
A road builder in Gujarat needs ₹500 crore for 15 years. The financial system connects them.

steps.title: Components
steps.body:
A **financial system** is the set of institutions, markets, instruments and services that mobilise savings and allocate them to productive investment.

1. **Financial institutions**: banks, NBFCs, insurers, mutual funds, pension funds, DFIs
2. **Financial markets**: money market, capital market, forex market, derivatives, commodity
3. **Financial instruments**: deposits, T-bills, CPs, shares, bonds, units
4. **Financial services**: broking, merchant banking, leasing, factoring, credit rating, custodial services

steps.title: Functions
steps.body:
- Mobilisation of savings and **capital formation**
- Allocation of funds to efficient uses
- **Payment and settlement** mechanism
- **Risk sharing and transfer** (insurance, derivatives)
- **Liquidity** to investors through secondary markets
- **Price discovery** of assets and information production
- Monitoring borrowers and corporate governance

steps.title: Classification of markets
steps.body:
- **Money market**: short-term funds (up to one year) — call money, T-bills, CPs, CDs, repo.
- **Capital market**: long-term funds — equity and debt; **primary** (new issues) and **secondary** (trading of existing securities).
- **Organised** (regulated) vs **unorganised** (moneylenders, indigenous bankers, chit funds outside regulation).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the stock exchange as the whole capital market — it is only the secondary segment.
- Classifying a 6-month CP as a capital-market instrument — anything up to one year belongs to the money market.

activity.prompt: Place each instrument in its market.

quiz.q: The primary market deals with:
quiz.why: The primary market is where companies and governments raise fresh capital by issuing new securities.

quiz.q: Price discovery is a function of:
quiz.why: Trading between buyers and sellers in markets reveals the fair price of assets.

quiz.q: Chit funds outside regulation belong to the:
quiz.why: Unregistered chit funds and moneylenders operate outside formal regulation, so they are unorganised.

scenes.text: Thousands of savers each deposit small sums for short periods.
The bank pools them into large, long-term loans to factories — transforming size, maturity and risk.

steps.title: Why intermediaries?
steps.body:
Direct lending is costly: savers lack information, cannot diversify and want liquidity. Intermediaries provide:

- **Size transformation**: pooling small savings into large loans
- **Maturity transformation**: short-term deposits funding long-term loans
- **Risk transformation**: diversification across many borrowers
- **Reduced transaction and information costs** (screening, monitoring)
- **Liquidity** to savers

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Depository**: commercial and co-operative banks
- **Contractual**: insurance companies, pension and provident funds
- **Investment**: mutual funds, investment trusts
- **Non-banking finance companies**, housing finance companies, DFIs

**Disintermediation**: when borrowers go directly to markets (e.g. issuing bonds) instead of borrowing from banks.

steps.title: Solved: interest spread
steps.body:
A bank raises ₹100 crore of deposits at 6% and lends ₹80 crore at 10% (₹20 crore held as reserves/liquid assets earning 5%).

- Interest income = 8.0 + 1.0 = ₹9.0 crore
- Interest expense = ₹6.0 crore
- **Net interest income = ₹3.0 crore**; NIM on assets of ₹100 crore = **3%**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing spread as lending rate − deposit rate on all deposits, ignoring reserves that earn less.
- Thinking maturity transformation is risk-free — it creates liquidity and interest-rate risk.

activity.prompt: An NBFC borrows ₹50 crore at 8% and lends it all at 13%. What is its net interest income (₹ crore)?

quiz.q: Funding long-term loans with short-term deposits is:
quiz.why: Intermediaries convert short-term liabilities into long-term assets, which is maturity transformation.

quiz.q: A pension fund is a:
quiz.why: Pension funds receive regular contractual contributions and invest them long term.

quiz.q: Companies issuing bonds instead of taking bank loans is called:
quiz.why: Bypassing banks to raise funds directly from markets is disintermediation.

scenes.text: In 1991, India faced a balance-of-payments crisis and began sweeping financial reforms.
Today, separate regulators oversee banks, securities, insurance and pensions.

steps.title: Regulators
steps.body:
- **RBI**: banks, NBFCs, payment systems, money and forex markets, government securities market
- **SEBI** (statutory since 1992 under the SEBI Act): securities markets, mutual funds, intermediaries
- **IRDAI**: insurance (IRDA Act, 1999)
- **PFRDA**: pension funds and the National Pension System
- **IFSCA**: international financial services centres (GIFT City)
- **Ministry of Corporate Affairs**/NCLT for company law and insolvency matters
- **Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC)** for inter-regulatory coordination

steps.title: Major reforms since 1991
steps.body:
- **Narasimham Committees** (1991, 1998): lower CRR/SLR, deregulated interest rates, prudential norms (capital adequacy, NPA recognition), entry of private banks
- Repeal of the Capital Issues (Control) Act and free pricing of issues under SEBI
- Screen-based trading (NSE), dematerialisation (Depositories Act, 1996)
- Opening of insurance to private players (1999–2000)
- IBC 2016; GST and digital payments infrastructure
- **Financial inclusion**: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (2014), payments and small finance banks, UPI

steps.title: SEBI's three objectives
steps.body: Under its preamble, SEBI exists to **protect the interests of investors** in securities, **promote the development** of the securities market, and **regulate** it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying SEBI regulates banks — banks are regulated by the RBI.
- Dating SEBI to 1988 as a statutory body — it was set up in 1988 but got statutory powers in 1992.

activity.prompt: Which regulator oversees each entity?

quiz.q: SEBI got statutory status in:
quiz.why: The SEBI Act, 1992 converted SEBI into a statutory regulator.

quiz.q: PMJDY, launched in 2014, aims at:
quiz.why: Jan Dhan Yojana promotes financial inclusion through basic bank accounts for all households.

quiz.q: Dematerialisation was enabled by the:
quiz.why: The Depositories Act, 1996 allowed securities to be held in electronic form.

lessons.title: Lab: mapping the flow of funds

scenes.text: Trace ₹1 lakh saved by a household as it reaches a business through different channels.
Each channel involves a different institution, instrument and regulator.

steps.title: Channel 1: bank deposit
steps.body:
Household → FD in a bank (RBI-regulated) → bank lends to an MSME as a term loan.
**Instrument**: deposit / loan. **Risk to saver**: low (DICGC cover up to ₹5 lakh).

steps.title: Channel 2: mutual fund
steps.body:
Household → units of an equity mutual fund (SEBI-regulated) → fund buys shares of listed companies in the secondary market.
**Instrument**: units / shares. **Risk to saver**: market risk, no guarantee.

steps.title: Channel 3: direct IPO
steps.body:
Household → applies for shares in an IPO through ASBA/UPI → company receives capital in the primary market.
**Instrument**: equity. **Regulator**: SEBI (ICDR Regulations, 2018).

steps.title: Channel 4: life insurance
steps.body:
Household → premium to a life insurer (IRDAI) → insurer invests largely in government securities and infrastructure bonds.
**Instrument**: policy / bonds. **Horizon**: long term.

steps.title: Takeaway
steps.body: Direct channels (IPO, bonds) give higher potential returns but put risk on the saver; intermediated channels (banks, insurers) absorb more risk in return for a spread.

questions.why: Financial services such as broking and rating complete the system.

questions.why: Money market instruments are short term, up to one year.

questions.why: Intermediaries aggregate many small deposits into large loans.

questions.why: IRDAI regulates insurers.

questions.why: It advised lower reserve ratios, capital adequacy and NPA norms, and interest-rate deregulation.

courses.title: Unit 2 · The money market
courses.summary: Features and participants of the Indian money market; call, notice and term money; repo and TREPS; Treasury bills, commercial paper and certificates of deposit, with yield and price calculations.
outcomes: Describe the features, participants and functions of the money market
Distinguish call, notice and term money and explain repo transactions
Compute the price and yield of a Treasury bill
Compare commercial paper and certificates of deposit
Compute repo interest and discount-instrument yields

scenes.text: At 4 pm a bank finds it is ₹300 crore short of its CRR requirement for the day.
It borrows overnight from another bank in the call money market.

steps.title: Features and participants
steps.body:
- Market for **short-term funds** (overnight to one year); high liquidity, low risk, large deal sizes, mostly over-the-counter/electronic.
- Participants: RBI, commercial banks, primary dealers, mutual funds, insurers, corporates, NBFCs (in some segments).
- Functions: balance short-term liquidity, transmit monetary policy, finance working capital and government's short-term needs.

steps.title: Call, notice and term money
steps.body:
- **Call money**: overnight (1 day) borrowing/lending.
- **Notice money**: 2 to 14 days.
- **Term money**: 15 days to 1 year.
- Participants in call/notice money are restricted mainly to banks and primary dealers; trading on RBI's NDS-Call platform.
- The weighted average call rate is the **operating target** of monetary policy.

steps.title: Repo and TREPS
steps.body:
- **Repo** (repurchase agreement): sell securities today with an agreement to buy them back later at a higher price; it is collateralised borrowing.
- **Reverse repo**: the lender's side of the same deal.
- **TREPS** (Tri-party repo on government securities) is run by the Clearing Corporation of India; mutual funds and corporates use it heavily.
- RBI's repo with banks is the main channel of liquidity under the LAF.

steps.title: Solved: repo interest
steps.body:
A bank borrows ₹100 crore for 7 days at a repo rate of 6.5% (365-day basis).

- Interest = 100 × 0.065 × 7/365 = **₹0.1247 crore ≈ ₹12.47 lakh**
- Repurchase price ≈ **₹100.1247 crore**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a repo an outright sale — ownership returns at maturity.
- Mixing notice money (2–14 days) with term money (15 days–1 year).

activity.prompt: A bank borrows ₹200 crore for 14 days at 7.3% (365-day year) in a repo. Interest payable (₹ crore)?

quiz.q: Notice money has a maturity of:
quiz.why: Notice money covers borrowing for 2 to 14 days.

quiz.q: A repo is essentially:
quiz.why: The borrower sells securities and buys them back, so the securities act as collateral.

quiz.q: TREPS is operated by:
quiz.why: The Clearing Corporation of India Ltd runs the tri-party repo platform.

scenes.text: Every week the RBI auctions T-bills for the Government of India.
A bank bids ₹98.50 for a 91-day bill of face value ₹100. What is its yield?

steps.title: Features
steps.body:
- Short-term debt of the **Government of India**, issued at a **discount** and redeemed at face value.
- Tenors: **91, 182 and 364 days**; minimum ₹25,000 and in multiples.
- Issued through **auction** by the RBI (multiple-price or uniform-price).
- Zero default risk, highly liquid, eligible for SLR.
- **Cash management bills** are very short-term bills for temporary mismatches.

steps.title: Formulas (365-day year)
steps.body:
- **Yield** = (FV − P)/P × 365/n × 100
- **Price** = FV / (1 + y × n/365)
- n = days to maturity

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing discount by FV instead of price (that gives the discount rate, not yield).
- Using 360 days — Indian T-bill yields use 365.

activity.prompt: 182-day T-bill bought at ₹96.80 (FV ₹100). Yield % (2 decimals)?

quiz.q: T-bills are issued:
quiz.why: T-bills pay no coupon; the investor earns the difference between discounted price and face value.

quiz.q: Which tenor is NOT a regular T-bill?
quiz.why: T-bills are for less than a year; 730 days would be a dated security.

quiz.q: Higher auction price means:
quiz.why: Paying more for the same face value leaves a smaller discount and a lower yield.

lessons.title: Commercial paper and certificates of deposit

scenes.text: A highly rated FMCG company needs ₹500 crore for 90 days to buy raw materials.
Instead of a bank loan, it issues commercial paper to mutual funds at a lower rate.

steps.title: Commercial paper (CP)
steps.body:
- **Unsecured** short-term promissory note issued at a discount by corporates, NBFCs and all-India FIs.
- Maturity **7 days to 1 year**; requires a **credit rating**.
- Investors: mutual funds, banks, corporates, individuals.
- Issued in dematerialised form; IPA (issuing and paying agent) is a bank.
- Cheaper than bank credit for top-rated firms.

steps.title: Certificate of deposit (CD)
steps.body:
- **Negotiable** term deposit receipt issued at a discount by **banks** (7 days to 1 year) and select **FIs** (1 to 3 years).
- Minimum ₹5 lakh and multiples.
- Transferable, unlike an ordinary FD; no premature withdrawal by the issuing bank.
- Used by banks when deposit growth lags credit growth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying CPs are secured — they are unsecured, so rating matters.
- Treating CDs as non-transferable like FDs — CDs are negotiable.

quiz.why: Without collateral, investors demand strong credit ratings.

scenes.text: In the 1980s India's money market was narrow, dominated by call money and a few players.
Reforms added new instruments, platforms and market-based rates.

steps.title: Defects (traditional)
steps.body:
- Dichotomy between organised and unorganised sectors
- Lack of integration between segments
- Limited instruments and secondary market
- Seasonal stringency of funds (busy season)
- Volatility of call rates

steps.title: Reforms
steps.body:
- Introduction of **182-day and 364-day T-bills**, CPs, CDs (late 1980s–1990s; Vaghul Committee, 1987)
- **Liquidity Adjustment Facility** (2000) with repo/reverse repo; later MSF and SDF
- Call market limited to banks and primary dealers; corporates moved to repo/TREPS
- Electronic dealing platforms (NDS-OM, NDS-Call)
- Benchmarks such as **MIBOR** and the overnight rate administered by FBIL

steps.title: Solved: comparing options
steps.body:
A corporate treasurer has ₹10 crore for 91 days. Options: T-bill at 6.6% yield or bank CD at 7.1%.

- T-bill income ≈ 10 × 0.066 × 91/365 = **₹16.45 lakh**
- CD income ≈ 10 × 0.071 × 91/365 = **₹17.70 lakh**
- The CD pays ₹1.25 lakh more for slightly higher credit risk (bank vs sovereign).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring credit risk when comparing yields.
- Assuming all money market rates move independently — repo anchors them.

courses.title: Unit 3 · The capital market: primary and secondary
courses.summary: Methods of raising capital in the primary market including book building, rights issues and QIPs; stock exchanges, trading, clearing and depositories in the secondary market; SEBI's investor protection role; and stock indices with worked examples.
outcomes: Explain the methods of floating new issues and the book-building process
Compute the cut-off price and the theoretical ex-rights price
Describe trading, clearing, settlement and the role of depositories
Explain how free-float market capitalisation indices are built
Identify SEBI's investor protection measures

lessons.title: Primary market and methods of issue

scenes.text: A Bengaluru food-delivery start-up decides to raise ₹1,000 crore through its first public issue.
Merchant bankers file a draft red herring prospectus with SEBI and plan a book-built IPO.

steps.title: Methods of issue
steps.body:
- **Public issue**: **IPO** (first offer by an unlisted company) or **FPO** (further offer by a listed company).
- **Offer for sale (OFS)**: existing shareholders sell; money goes to them, not the company.
- **Rights issue**: offered to existing shareholders in proportion to holdings.
- **Bonus issue**: free shares from reserves (no fresh money).
- **Private placement** and **preferential allotment** to selected investors.
- **QIP** (qualified institutions placement): listed company issues to QIBs only.
- Governed by **SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2018**.

steps.title: Fixed price vs book building
steps.body:
- **Fixed price**: price stated in the offer document.
- **Book building**: price **band** announced (cap ≤ 120% of floor); investors bid quantity and price; the **cut-off price** is discovered from demand.
- Investor categories: QIBs, non-institutional investors (NIIs), retail individual investors (application up to ₹2 lakh), and employees.
- Applications through **ASBA** (application supported by blocked amount) and UPI — money stays in the investor's account until allotment.

steps.title: Solved: cut-off price
steps.body:
Issue size 10 lakh shares, band ₹100–110. Bids (lakh shares): ₹110: 3; ₹108: 4; ₹106: 5; ₹104: 6.

- Cumulative from the top: 110 → 3; 108 → 7; 106 → **12** ≥ 10
- **Cut-off price = ₹106**; oversubscription at cut-off = 12/10 = 1.2 times

steps.title: Solved: rights issue
steps.body:
Market price ₹120; rights 1 for every 4 held at ₹80.

- Theoretical ex-rights price (TERP) = (4 × 120 + 1 × 80)/5 = **₹112**
- Value of one right (per new share) = 112 − 80 = **₹32**, i.e. ₹8 per existing share.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking an OFS raises money for the company.
- Calling a bonus issue a source of finance — it only capitalises reserves.

activity.prompt: Market price ₹200; rights issue 1 for 3 at ₹140. Compute the theoretical ex-rights price (₹).

quiz.q: In an offer for sale, proceeds go to:
quiz.why: An OFS is a sale of existing shares, so the sellers receive the money.

quiz.q: ASBA means:
options: application money is blocked in the investor's account until allotment
quiz.why: Under ASBA the amount is only blocked and is debited if shares are allotted.

quiz.q: QIP is an issue to:
quiz.why: A qualified institutions placement is restricted to QIBs.

lessons.title: Secondary market: exchanges, trading and settlement

scenes.text: Riya buys 10 shares of a bank on her broker's app at 10:05 am.
The next working day, the shares appear in her demat account — T+1 settlement.

steps.title: Stock exchanges
steps.body:
- **BSE** (1875, Asia's oldest) and **NSE** (incorporated 1992; screen-based trading from 1994) are the main exchanges; others include MSE.
- Functions: liquidity, price discovery, safety via regulated trading, capital formation, economic barometer.
- Exchanges are **demutualised** — ownership separated from trading rights.
- Fully **screen-based, anonymous order-matching** (price-time priority).

steps.title: Trading cycle
steps.body:
1. Investor opens a **trading account** (broker) and **demat account** (depository participant) with KYC.
2. Order placed — market or limit order; matched electronically.
3. **Clearing corporation** (e.g. NSE Clearing, ICCL) becomes the central counterparty via novation and guarantees settlement.
4. Settlement on **T+1** (rolling) — shares to buyer's demat, funds to seller.
- **Depositories**: **NSDL** (1996) and **CDSL** (1999) hold securities electronically; DPs are their agents.

steps.title: Risk management and investor protection
steps.body:
- Margins (VaR, extreme-loss), circuit filters, market-wide circuit breakers
- Investor Protection Fund, SCORES grievance system, Online Dispute Resolution
- Ban on **insider trading** (SEBI PIT Regulations, 2015) and fraudulent/unfair trade practices

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing a trading account (for orders) with a demat account (for holding).
- Saying the broker guarantees settlement — the clearing corporation does.

activity.prompt: Who performs each role?

items.text: Places the client's order on the exchange
Acts as central counterparty to every trade
Credits shares to the investor's demat account

quiz.q: Indian equity markets settle on:
quiz.why: India moved all equity segments to T+1 rolling settlement by January 2023.

quiz.q: Novation by a clearing corporation means it:
options: becomes buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer
quiz.why: Through novation the CCP interposes itself and guarantees settlement.

quiz.q: The oldest stock exchange in Asia is:
quiz.why: BSE traces its origin to 1875 under a banyan tree in Mumbai.

scenes.text: The evening news says the Sensex rose 500 points. What does that measure?
An index tracks the weighted value of a basket of shares relative to a base.

steps.title: Indices
steps.body:
- **S&P BSE Sensex**: 30 stocks, base year 1978–79 = 100.
- **Nifty 50**: 50 stocks, base 3 November 1995 = 1,000.
- Both use **free-float market capitalisation** weighting: only shares available for trading (excluding promoter holdings etc.) count.
- **Index = current free-float m-cap / base m-cap × base value** (base m-cap adjusted for corporate actions via the divisor).
- Sectoral and thematic indices: Bank Nifty, Nifty IT, BSE Midcap.

steps.title: Solved: free-float m-cap
steps.body:
Company X: 100 crore shares, price ₹500, promoter holding 60%.

- Full m-cap = ₹50,000 crore
- Free-float factor = 0.40 ⇒ **free-float m-cap = ₹20,000 crore**

steps.title: Solved: 3-stock index
steps.body:
Base free-float m-cap ₹2,000 crore = index 1,000. Today: A ₹1,200 cr, B ₹900 cr, C ₹700 cr.

- Current m-cap = ₹2,800 crore
- Index = 2,800/2,000 × 1,000 = **1,400** (+40%)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating index points as rupees.
- Using total shares instead of free-float shares for weighting.

activity.prompt: Base m-cap ₹5,000 cr = 100. Current free-float m-cap ₹6,250 cr. Index value?

quiz.q: Nifty 50 base value is:
quiz.why: Nifty 50 was set at 1,000 on 3 November 1995.

quiz.q: Free-float excludes:
quiz.why: Shares held by promoters and strategic holders are not freely tradable, so they are excluded.

quiz.q: Sensex comprises:
quiz.why: The Sensex tracks 30 large, liquid BSE-listed companies.

scenes.text: A fund manager fears the market may fall before budget day.
She sells Nifty futures to protect her portfolio without selling shares.

steps.title: Debt market
steps.body:
- **Government securities (G-secs)**: dated securities and T-bills issued by the RBI on behalf of the Centre; **state development loans** by states.
- **Corporate bonds/debentures**: secured or unsecured, convertible or non-convertible (NCDs); credit-rated.
- Retail access: RBI Retail Direct, exchange platforms.
- Coupon, face value, maturity and yield-to-maturity are the key terms.

steps.title: Derivatives
steps.body:
- **Forward**: private OTC agreement to buy/sell later at a fixed price.
- **Futures**: standardised, exchange-traded forwards with daily mark-to-market.
- **Options**: right without obligation — **call** (to buy) and **put** (to sell); buyer pays a **premium**.
- **Swaps**: exchange of cash flows (e.g. fixed for floating interest).
- Uses: **hedging**, speculation, arbitrage.

steps.title: Solved: futures and option payoffs
steps.body:
**Futures**: sell 1 lot of 75 units at 22,000; index falls to 21,600. Gain = (22,000 − 21,600) × 75 = **₹30,000**.

**Call option**: strike 22,000, premium ₹150, lot 75. At expiry index = 22,400 ⇒ payoff per unit 400 − 150 = 250 ⇒ **₹18,750**. If the index ends below 22,000, loss is limited to the premium, ₹11,250. (Lot sizes are illustrative.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking an option buyer must exercise — it is a right, not an obligation.
- Forgetting the premium when computing option profit.

quiz.why: The call buyer may buy the underlying at the strike price.

quiz.q: Maximum loss of an option buyer is:
quiz.why: If the option expires worthless, the buyer loses only the premium.

questions.why: SEBI rules require the cap to be at most 120% of the floor price.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Financial institutions and financial services
courses.summary: Non-banking financial companies and development finance institutions; the structure, types and NAV of mutual funds with SIP averaging; and fund-based and fee-based financial services including leasing, hire purchase, factoring, venture capital and credit rating.
outcomes: Distinguish NBFCs from banks and describe India's DFIs
Explain the trust structure of a mutual fund and compute NAV
Show how SIPs achieve rupee-cost averaging
Compare leasing, hire purchase and factoring with cost calculations
Explain venture capital stages and the meaning of credit ratings

scenes.text: In a small town in Bihar, a vegetable seller buys a scooter on a loan from an NBFC, not a bank.
Meanwhile a DFI funds a 20-year highway project that banks find too long to finance.

steps.title: NBFCs
steps.body:
A **non-banking financial company** is a company registered under the Companies Act whose principal business is lending, investment, leasing, hire purchase etc., regulated by the **RBI** under the RBI Act, 1934.

**Differences from banks**
- Cannot accept **demand deposits** or issue cheques drawn on itself
- Not part of the payment and settlement system
- Deposit insurance (DICGC) is not available to NBFC depositors

RBI's **scale-based regulation** (2021) classifies NBFCs into base, middle, upper and top layers.

steps.title: Development finance institutions
steps.body:
- **NABARD** (1982): agriculture and rural development, refinance to banks.
- **SIDBI** (1990): MSME finance and refinance.
- **EXIM Bank** (1982): export–import finance.
- **NHB** (1988): housing finance regulation/refinance (regulation of HFCs later shifted to RBI).
- **NaBFID** (2021): National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development.
- Historic: IFCI (1948), ICICI and IDBI — later converted into banks.

steps.title: Why NBFCs matter
steps.body: NBFCs reach borrowers with thin credit histories — small businesses, used-vehicle buyers, gold-loan customers — using specialised local knowledge and faster processes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying NBFC deposits are insured by DICGC — they are not.
- Calling ICICI Bank a DFI today — it converted into a bank in 2002.

activity.prompt: Match each institution to its main focus.

quiz.q: NBFCs cannot:
quiz.why: Only banks can accept deposits repayable on demand and withdrawable by cheque.

quiz.q: SIDBI was set up to finance:
quiz.why: SIDBI is the principal institution for promotion and financing of micro, small and medium enterprises.

quiz.q: NBFCs are regulated by:
quiz.why: Chapter III-B of the RBI Act empowers the RBI to regulate NBFCs.

lessons.title: Lab: mutual funds, NAV and SIP

scenes.text: Kabir starts a ₹1,000 monthly SIP in an equity fund as soon as he gets his first job.
When markets fall, his ₹1,000 buys more units — that is rupee-cost averaging.

steps.title: Structure (SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996)
steps.body:
- **Sponsor** sets up the fund; **trust** holds assets for unitholders, supervised by **trustees**.
- **AMC** (asset management company) manages the money.
- **Custodian** keeps securities; **RTA** maintains unitholder records.
- Industry body: **AMFI**.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- By structure: **open-ended** (buy/sell any day at NAV), **close-ended** (fixed maturity, listed), **interval**.
- By asset: equity, debt, hybrid, solution-oriented, index funds and ETFs, fund of funds.
- **ELSS**: tax-saving equity fund with 3-year lock-in.
- **Direct** plans (no distributor commission) vs regular plans.
- **Expense ratio** is charged daily within SEBI limits; entry loads are banned since 2009.

steps.title: Solved: NAV
steps.body:
Market value of securities ₹100 crore, cash ₹5 crore, liabilities (expenses payable) ₹5 crore, units 8 crore.

- **NAV = (Assets − Liabilities)/Units = (105 − 5)/8 = ₹12.50**

steps.title: Solved: SIP averaging
steps.body:
₹1,000 a month at NAVs ₹10, ₹8, ₹12.50.

- Units: 100 + 125 + 80 = **305**
- Total invested ₹3,000 ⇒ **average cost = ₹9.84** per unit
- Average NAV = (10 + 8 + 12.5)/3 = ₹10.17 ⇒ SIP cost is lower than the average price.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a low NAV fund is 'cheaper' — NAV level does not indicate value.
- Ignoring exit loads and expense ratios when comparing returns.

activity.prompt: Fund assets ₹250 crore, liabilities ₹10 crore, units outstanding 12 crore. Compute NAV (₹).

quiz.q: The AMC of a mutual fund:
quiz.why: The AMC is the investment manager appointed by the trustees.

quiz.q: ELSS has a lock-in of:
quiz.why: Equity-linked saving schemes have a 3-year lock-in.

quiz.q: Rupee-cost averaging means:
options: buying more units when prices are low with a fixed amount
quiz.why: A fixed rupee amount buys more units at low prices and fewer at high prices, lowering average cost.

scenes.text: A small packaging firm needs a ₹20 lakh machine but lacks capital.
It can lease it, buy it on hire purchase, or free cash by factoring its receivables.

steps.title: Fund-based services
steps.body:
**Leasing**: lessor (owner) gives the right to use an asset to the lessee for rentals.
- **Finance lease**: transfers substantially all risks and rewards; long term, non-cancellable.
- **Operating lease**: short term, cancellable, lessor bears obsolescence risk.

**Hire purchase**: hirer pays instalments; ownership passes **after the last instalment**; hirer can claim depreciation.

**Factoring**: firm sells its receivables to a factor, who advances a % (usually 70–90%) and handles collection. With or without recourse. Governed by the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011.

**Forfaiting**: purchase of medium-term export receivables without recourse.

steps.title: Solved: cost of factoring
steps.body:
Receivables ₹10,00,000 for 90 days; advance 80%; interest 12% p.a. on advance; commission 1% of receivables.

- Advance = ₹8,00,000
- Interest = 8,00,000 × 0.12 × 90/365 = **₹23,671**
- Commission = **₹10,000**
- Total cost = ₹33,671; effective annual cost on funds received (8,00,000 − 33,671 = 7,66,329) ≈ 33,671/7,66,329 × 365/90 = **17.8%**

steps.title: Solved: flat-rate HP
steps.body:
Cash price ₹2,00,000; down payment ₹50,000; flat interest 10% p.a. on ₹1,50,000 for 3 years.

- Interest = 1,50,000 × 0.10 × 3 = ₹45,000
- Total instalments = 1,95,000 ⇒ monthly instalment = 1,95,000/36 = **₹5,416.67**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the lessee owns a leased asset at the end — ownership stays with the lessor unless a purchase option is exercised.
- Ignoring commission when computing factoring cost.

activity.prompt: Receivables ₹5,00,000; factor's commission 2% of receivables. Commission amount (₹)?

quiz.q: In hire purchase, ownership passes:
quiz.why: The hirer becomes owner only when all instalments are paid and the purchase option is exercised.

quiz.q: An operating lease is:
quiz.why: Operating leases are short-term and cancellable, with the lessor bearing obsolescence risk.

quiz.q: Factoring without recourse means the factor:
options: can recover bad debts from the client
quiz.why: In non-recourse factoring the factor absorbs losses from customer default.

lessons.title: Venture capital, merchant banking and credit rating

scenes.text: Two engineers in Pune build an ed-tech app but no bank will lend without collateral.
A venture capital fund invests ₹5 crore for a 20% equity stake.

steps.title: Venture capital and private equity
steps.body:
- Long-term **equity** finance for high-risk, high-growth unlisted firms, often with management support.
- Stages: **seed**, **start-up/early**, **expansion/growth**, **bridge/mezzanine**, buy-out.
- Exit routes: IPO, strategic sale, buy-back, secondary sale.
- Regulated under **SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012**.

steps.title: Merchant banking (fee-based)
steps.body:
- Issue management (lead manager to IPOs), underwriting, project counselling, loan syndication, M&A advisory, portfolio management.
- Registered with SEBI under the Merchant Bankers Regulations, 1992.

steps.title: Credit rating
steps.body:
- An opinion on the **relative ability and willingness** of an issuer to meet debt obligations on time — not a recommendation to buy.
- Agencies in India include **CRISIL** (1987), **ICRA** (1991), **CARE** (1993), India Ratings, Acuité, Brickwork; regulated by SEBI (CRA Regulations, 1999).
- Long-term scale: AAA (highest safety) → AA → A → BBB (lowest investment grade) → BB, B, C → D (default).

steps.title: Solved: VC valuation
steps.body:
A VC invests ₹5 crore for 20%.

- **Post-money valuation** = 5/0.20 = ₹25 crore
- **Pre-money valuation** = 25 − 5 = **₹20 crore**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a rating as a guarantee — it is an opinion that can change.
- Confusing pre-money with post-money valuation.

quiz.why: CRISIL, India's first credit rating agency, was set up in 1987.

questions.why: DICGC insurance applies to bank deposits, not NBFC deposits.

questions.why: NABARD was established in 1982.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Bond valuation, yields, revision and exam
courses.summary: Present-value valuation of coupon and zero-coupon bonds, current yield and approximate YTM, interest-rate risk and the yield curve, followed by a whole-subject revision sheet, practice problems and the final exam.
outcomes: Value coupon and zero-coupon bonds by discounting cash flows
Compute current yield and approximate yield to maturity
Explain the inverse price–yield relation and interest-rate risk
Interpret normal, flat and inverted yield curves
Solve mixed problems on money market, capital market and institutions

scenes.text: A 3-year, 10% coupon, ₹1,000 bond trades while similar bonds yield 12%.
Its fair price must be below ₹1,000 so a buyer earns the market's 12%.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Bond price** P = Σ C/(1 + y)^t + F/(1 + y)^n
- **Zero-coupon bond**: P = F/(1 + y)^n
- **Current yield** = annual coupon / market price
- **Approximate YTM** = [C + (F − P)/n] / [(F + P)/2]
- If coupon rate > required yield ⇒ bond trades at a **premium**; < ⇒ **discount**; = ⇒ par.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to add the face value in the final year.
- Using the coupon rate as the discount rate — discount at the market yield.

lessons.title: Interest-rate risk and the yield curve

scenes.text: When the RBI raises rates, a debt fund's NAV dips for a few days.
Old bonds with lower coupons become less attractive, so their prices fall.

steps.title: Price–yield relation
steps.body:
- Bond prices move **inversely** to yields.
- **Longer maturity** and **lower coupon** ⇒ greater price sensitivity.
- **Duration** measures this sensitivity (weighted average time to cash flows); modified duration ≈ % price change per 1% change in yield.
- **Reinvestment risk** moves opposite to price risk.

steps.title: Yield curve
steps.body:
Plot of yields against maturities for similar-credit bonds (usually G-secs).

- **Normal (upward sloping)**: longer bonds yield more — expected growth/inflation, term premium.
- **Flat**: similar yields — transition.
- **Inverted**: short yields above long — often read as a signal of slowdown.
- Theories: expectations, liquidity premium, market segmentation.

steps.title: Solved: price change estimate
steps.body:
Bond price ₹1,000, modified duration 4. Yield rises 0.5 percentage point.

- % change ≈ −4 × 0.5 = **−2%**
- New price ≈ **₹980**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking G-secs are risk-free in price — they have no default risk but do have interest-rate risk.
- Reading an inverted curve as a guarantee of recession.

uni-bcom-gst.title: Goods and Services Tax (GST)
uni-bcom-gst.description: India's GST from the ground up: constitutional basis, supply and levy, time, place and value of supply, input tax credit, registration, invoicing, e-way bills, returns, payment and compliance, with worked computations. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Com programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · GST Concept & Constitutional Framework
courses.summary: Why India moved to GST, the 101st Constitutional Amendment, dual GST structure (CGST, SGST/UTGST, IGST), the GST Council, taxes subsumed, rate structure and how input tax credit removes the cascading effect.
outcomes: Explain indirect taxation and the cascading problem GST solves
Describe Article 246A, 269A, 279A and the GST Council
Identify which taxes GST subsumed and which remain outside
Distinguish CGST, SGST, UTGST and IGST and when each applies
Compute tax under a value-added chain

lessons.title: From the old tax maze to GST

scenes.text: Before July 2017, trucks queued for hours at state check-posts paying entry tax and showing CST forms.
On 1 July 2017 GST replaced a dozen taxes and most check-posts disappeared.

steps.title: Indirect tax and cascading
steps.body: An indirect tax is collected by the supplier from the buyer and paid to the government; its burden is passed on. Under the pre-GST system, central excise and service tax credit could not be set off against state VAT, and CST was non-creditable, so tax was charged on tax — cascading. GST is a destination-based, multi-stage tax on the supply of goods and services, where tax paid at each stage is available as input tax credit (ITC) to the next.

steps.title: Taxes subsumed
steps.body: Central: central excise duty (except on specified petroleum and tobacco), additional excise and customs duties (CVD, SAD), service tax, central surcharges and cesses relating to goods and services. State: VAT, central sales tax, entry tax and octroi, purchase tax, luxury tax, entertainment tax (except by local bodies), taxes on advertisements, taxes on lotteries, betting and gambling.

steps.title: Outside GST
steps.body: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption (constitutionally excluded); five petroleum products — crude, petrol, diesel, ATF, natural gas — are within GST in law but not yet taxed until the Council recommends a date; electricity; basic customs duty; stamp duty.

steps.title: Worked example: value-added chain at 18%
steps.body: Manufacturer sells for ₹1,000 + GST 180. Wholesaler sells for ₹1,200 + GST 216; pays 216 − 180 = 36. Retailer sells for ₹1,500 + GST 270; pays 270 − 216 = 54. Total tax collected = 180 + 36 + 54 = ₹270 = 18% of the final price — no tax on tax.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying petrol is outside the GST law (it is within the definition but taxed at nil levy pending notification); calling GST origin-based (it is destination-based).

activity.prompt: Subsumed in GST or still outside?

quiz.q: GST was introduced on
quiz.why: GST came into force across India on 1 July 2017.

quiz.why: Tax revenue accrues to the state where goods or services are consumed.

quiz.q: In the chain example, the retailer pays in cash
quiz.why: The retailer's output tax of ₹270 less ITC of ₹216 leaves ₹54.

lessons.title: Constitutional basis and the GST Council

scenes.text: The Constitution (101st Amendment) Act 2016 gave both Parliament and state legislatures power to tax supply at the same time.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Key articles
steps.body: Article 246A: Parliament and state legislatures both have power to make laws on GST; Parliament exclusively for inter-state supply. Article 269A: IGST on inter-state supply levied and collected by the Centre, apportioned between Union and states as per Council recommendations. Article 279A: GST Council. Article 366(12A): 'goods and services tax' means any tax on supply of goods or services or both except alcoholic liquor for human consumption.

steps.title: GST Council
steps.body: Chaired by the Union Finance Minister; members include the Union Minister of State (Finance) and the Finance or nominated minister of each state. Decisions need three-fourths of weighted votes of members present and voting: the Centre's vote counts one-third, all states together two-thirds. Quorum: one-half of total members. It recommends rates, exemptions, thresholds, model laws and dispute resolution. The Supreme Court in Mohit Minerals (2022) held its recommendations persuasive, not binding.

steps.title: Worked example: voting arithmetic
steps.body: Centre's weight 33.33%; states' 66.67%. To pass, 75% is needed. Step 1: Centre alone (33.33%) cannot pass a proposal. Step 2: States alone (66.67%) cannot. Step 3: The Centre plus states carrying at least 41.67% weight are needed — a built-in consensus mechanism.

steps.title: Laws
steps.body: CGST Act 2017, IGST Act 2017, UTGST Act 2017, each state's SGST Act, and the GST (Compensation to States) Act 2017 (compensation cess).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying the Council's decisions are binding law; forgetting that IGST is levied only by Parliament.

activity.prompt: If the Centre votes in favour, what minimum percentage of total weighted votes must the states contribute for a proposal to pass?

quiz.q: Article dealing with the GST Council

quiz.why: Article 279A(2)(a) makes the Union Finance Minister the chairperson.

quiz.q: The Mohit Minerals judgement held Council recommendations are
quiz.why: The Supreme Court held they have persuasive value for Parliament and state legislatures.

lessons.title: Dual GST: CGST, SGST, UTGST, IGST

scenes.text: A Pune seller supplies a laptop to a Mumbai buyer (CGST + SGST) and another to a Bengaluru buyer (IGST).
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Which tax applies?
steps.body: Intra-state supply (location of supplier and place of supply in the same state): CGST + SGST (or UTGST in a union territory without legislature), each at half the rate. Inter-state supply, imports, exports, supplies to or by SEZ units: IGST at the full rate. Compensation cess was levied on specified luxury and demerit goods; it is being wound down as the compensation borrowing is repaid.

steps.title: Rate structure
steps.body: Original slabs: 0%, 5%, 12%, 18%, 28% plus special rates (3% on gold, 0.25% on rough diamonds). On the GST Council's September 2025 recommendation, from 22 September 2025 most goods and services moved to a two-rate structure of 5% and 18%, with a 40% rate for specified luxury and sin goods; nil, 3% and 0.25% rates continue. Always check the current notification for a specific item.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Taxable value ₹50,000 at 18%. Intra-state: CGST 9% = 4,500, SGST 9% = 4,500; invoice ₹59,000. Inter-state: IGST 18% = 9,000; invoice ₹59,000. The buyer's total cost is the same; only the split differs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Charging CGST + SGST on a supply to another state; charging IGST on a supply within the same state because the buyer's head office is elsewhere (place of supply rules decide).

steps.title: GSTIN structure
steps.body: 15 characters: first 2 digits = state code (e.g. 27 Maharashtra, 29 Karnataka, 07 Delhi, 33 Tamil Nadu); next 10 = PAN of the business; 13th = entity number for the same PAN in that state; 14th = 'Z' by default; 15th = check digit.

steps.title: GSTN and the portal
steps.body: Goods and Services Tax Network is the IT backbone running the common portal for registration, returns, payments and refunds. Supporting systems: e-invoice Invoice Registration Portal (IRN and QR code), e-way bill portal, GSTR-2B auto-drafted ITC statement.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: GSTIN 29ABCDE1234F2Z5: state Karnataka (29); PAN ABCDE1234F; second registration of the same PAN in Karnataka (2); Z default; 5 check digit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming one GSTIN for all states — registration is state-wise; ignoring the check digit when validating a supplier's GSTIN.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Supply, Levy, Time, Place & Value of Supply
courses.summary: Meaning and scope of supply (s.7), Schedules I–III, composite and mixed supply, levy and reverse charge (s.9), composition scheme (s.10), time of supply (ss.12–13), place of supply (IGST Act ss.10–13) and value of supply (s.15).
outcomes: Decide whether a transaction is a supply under s.7 and the Schedules
Distinguish composite and mixed supplies and apply the correct rate
Apply forward and reverse charge and composition rules
Determine time and place of supply
Compute transaction value under s.15

story.title: The free sample and the branch transfer

scenes.text: A company gives free samples to doctors and moves stock from its Pune unit to its Indore branch.
No sale price — is either a 'supply'?

steps.title: Section 7
steps.body: Supply includes all forms of supply of goods or services such as sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease or disposal, made for a consideration in the course or furtherance of business; import of services for consideration whether or not in business; activities in Schedule I even without consideration. Schedule II classifies activities as goods or services; Schedule III lists activities that are neither (e.g. services by an employee to employer, funeral services, sale of land and of a completed building, actionable claims other than specified lottery, betting, gambling, online gaming and casinos).

steps.title: Schedule I — supply without consideration
steps.body: (1) Permanent transfer or disposal of business assets on which ITC was availed; (2) supply between related persons or distinct persons (e.g. two GSTINs of the same PAN) in the course of business — gifts by employer to employee up to ₹50,000 a year are excluded; (3) supply between principal and agent in specified cases; (4) import of services from a related person or own establishment outside India.

steps.title: Composite vs mixed supply (s.8)
steps.body: Composite: two or more naturally bundled supplies with one principal supply — taxed at the rate of the principal supply (e.g. goods with packing, transport and insurance). Mixed: two or more individual supplies for a single price, not naturally bundled — taxed at the highest rate among them (e.g. a gift hamper of sweets, dry fruits and a toy).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Free samples to doctors: no consideration and not Schedule I → not a supply (but ITC on them must be reversed under s.17(5)(h)). Stock transfer Pune → Indore: distinct persons (different states) → Schedule I supply; value under Rule 28 (open market value / 90% of price to unrelated customer if recipient eligible for full ITC).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating every free item as a supply; treating a mixed supply at the principal item's rate.

buckets: Not a supply (Schedule III / no consideration)

scenes.text: A company receives a ₹1,00,000 bill from an advocate. The advocate charges no GST.
Under reverse charge, the company itself must pay the GST.

steps.title: Levy (s.9)
steps.body: CGST is levied on intra-state supplies on value determined under s.15 at rates notified on the Council's recommendation, maximum 20% CGST. Forward charge: supplier pays. Reverse charge s.9(3): recipient pays for notified supplies — e.g. services of an individual advocate or firm of advocates to a business entity, goods transport agency services (in specified cases), sponsorship services to a body corporate, director's services to the company, import of services. s.9(4): specified supplies from unregistered persons to notified classes. s.9(5): e-commerce operator pays for notified services (e.g. passenger transport via app, restaurant services).

steps.title: Composition scheme (s.10)
steps.body: Eligible: registered persons with aggregate turnover in the preceding year up to ₹1.5 crore (₹75 lakh in specified special category states). Rates (CGST + SGST total): manufacturers 1%, traders 1% (on taxable supply turnover), restaurants not serving alcohol 5%. Service providers can opt for s.10(2A) at 6% up to ₹50 lakh. Restrictions: no ITC, no inter-state outward supply, no supply through e-commerce operators who collect TCS (relaxations notified for some goods suppliers), cannot collect tax from customers, issue a bill of supply, file CMP-08 quarterly and GSTR-4 annually.

steps.title: Worked example: RCM
steps.body: Advocate fee ₹1,00,000 intra-state at 18%. Step 1: Company pays CGST 9,000 + SGST 9,000 in cash (RCM liability cannot be paid with ITC). Step 2: It may take ITC of ₹18,000 if used for business. Step 3: It must issue a self-invoice if the supplier is unregistered and a payment voucher.

steps.title: Worked example: composition
steps.body: Trader with turnover of taxable supplies ₹60,00,000 in a quarter... use annual: annual taxable turnover ₹1,20,00,000 at 1% = ₹1,20,000 tax (₹60,000 CGST + ₹60,000 SGST), paid from own pocket.

steps.body: Paying RCM tax through ITC; letting a composition dealer make inter-state sales; charging GST on a composition dealer's bill.
