story.title: Advance in March, invoice in April

scenes.text: A consultant receives a ₹2 lakh advance on 25 March and issues the invoice on 10 April after finishing work on 5 April.
In which month is GST due?

steps.title: Time of supply of goods (s.12)
steps.body: Earlier of (a) date of issue of invoice or the last date by which it should have been issued (s.31 — before or at removal/delivery), and (b) date of receipt of payment. However, GST on advances received for goods has been exempted by notification (No. 66/2017-CT), so for goods time of supply is effectively the invoice date. RCM goods: earliest of receipt of goods, payment, or 31 days after supplier's invoice.

steps.title: Time of supply of services (s.13)
steps.body: If invoice is issued within 30 days of completion of service: earlier of invoice date and payment date. If not issued within 30 days: earlier of date of completion of service and date of payment. Advances for services attract GST on receipt.

steps.title: Place of supply (IGST Act)
steps.body: Goods (s.10): where movement terminates for delivery; bill-to-ship-to — the principal place of business of the person on whose instruction goods are delivered; no movement — location of goods at delivery; installed goods — place of installation. Services (s.12, both parties in India): general rule — location of registered recipient; if unregistered, the recipient's address on record, else supplier's location. Specific rules: immovable property services — location of the property; restaurant and beauty services — where performed; event admission — where the event is held; passenger transport — where the passenger embarks.

steps.title: Worked example: consultant
steps.body: Service completed 5 April; invoice 10 April (within 30 days). Advance received 25 March → time of supply for ₹2,00,000 is 25 March (earlier of invoice and payment). GST is due in the March return.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Charging GST on advances for goods; using supplier's location as default place of supply for B2B services.

scenes.text: List price ₹1,00,000; 5% discount on invoice; packing ₹2,000; freight ₹3,000 charged to buyer; a ₹1,000 late-payment interest is later collected.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Transaction value
steps.body: Value = price actually paid or payable, where supplier and recipient are not related and price is the sole consideration. Include: taxes, duties, fees and charges other than GST (and compensation cess if charged separately); amounts the supplier is liable to pay but the recipient incurs; incidental expenses including commission and packing charged by the supplier; interest, late fee or penalty for delayed payment; subsidies directly linked to price except government subsidies. Exclude: discount given before or at the time of supply and recorded in the invoice; post-supply discount if established by an agreement in advance, linked to specific invoices and ITC is reversed by the recipient.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: List price 1,00,000 − 5% discount 5,000 = 95,000. Add packing 2,000 and freight 3,000 = 1,00,000. GST 18% = 18,000; invoice ₹1,18,000. Later interest of ₹1,000 is also value: GST 18% = ₹180 (via a debit note/invoice).

steps.title: Worked example: tax-inclusive price

Related persons: open market value; if the recipient is eligible for full ITC, invoice value is deemed open market value. Pure agent expenses (Rule 33) are excluded when conditions are met.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Input Tax Credit
courses.summary: Eligibility and conditions for ITC (s.16), blocked credits (s.17(5)), apportionment for exempt supplies (Rule 42), reversal for non-payment within 180 days, order of utilisation (s.49 and Rule 88A), and Input Service Distributor.
outcomes: List the conditions for taking ITC and the time limit
Identify blocked credits under s.17(5)
Apportion common credit between taxable and exempt supplies
Utilise IGST, CGST and SGST credit in the legal order
Compute net cash payable from ledgers

scenes.text: Ritu holds a valid tax invoice and has received the goods, but her supplier never filed GSTR-1.
The credit does not appear in her GSTR-2B. Can she claim it?

steps.title: Who can take ITC
steps.body: Every registered person may take credit of input tax charged on supply of goods or services used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of business (s.16(1)). Input tax includes CGST, SGST/UTGST, IGST on inward supplies, RCM tax paid, and IGST on imports.

steps.title: Conditions (s.16(2))
steps.body: (a) Possession of tax invoice or debit note; (aa) details furnished by the supplier in GSTR-1 and communicated (appear in GSTR-2B); (b) goods or services received (including bill-to-ship-to delivery to a third person on direction); (ba) not restricted in GSTR-2B under s.38; (c) tax actually paid to the government by the supplier; (d) return u/s 39 furnished by the recipient. Goods received in lots: credit on the last lot. Payment to supplier must be made within 180 days of invoice, else ITC is reversed with interest and can be re-availed on payment.

steps.title: Time limit (s.16(4))
steps.body: ITC for an invoice of a financial year cannot be taken after 30 November following the end of that year, or the date of filing the annual return, whichever is earlier. For FY 2025-26 invoices: 30 November 2026.

steps.title: Worked example: Ritu
steps.body: Step 1: Invoice and receipt satisfied. Step 2: Supplier did not file GSTR-1 → invoice not in GSTR-2B → condition (aa) fails. Step 3: No ITC until the supplier reports it and it reflects; she should follow up before the s.16(4) deadline.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Claiming ITC on the basis of purchase register alone; forgetting the 180-day payment condition; claiming capital goods depreciation on the tax component as well as ITC (s.16(3) bars both).

activity.prompt: Before booking ITC on an invoice, confirm:
items: Valid tax invoice or debit note in hand
Not a blocked credit under s.17(5)
Supplier to be paid within 180 days
Claimed before 30 November following the FY

quiz.q: ITC time limit for FY 2025-26 invoices
quiz.why: Section 16(4) as amended allows ITC until 30 November after the end of the financial year, or annual return filing if earlier.

quiz.q: Unpaid supplier after 180 days: recipient must
quiz.why: The second proviso to s.16(2) requires reversal, with interest, until payment is made.

quiz.q: Goods received in instalments: ITC is taken on
quiz.why: The first proviso to s.16(2) allows ITC on receipt of the last lot or instalment.

story.title: The office car and the staff party

scenes.text: A consulting firm buys a sedan for its partners and throws a staff Diwali party.
Both bills show GST, yet neither credit is allowed.

steps.title: Main blocked items
steps.body: (a) Motor vehicles for transport of persons with seating capacity of 13 or fewer (including driver), except when used for further supply of such vehicles, transport of passengers, training in driving, and their insurance/repair/servicing in those cases; vessels and aircraft similarly. (b) Food and beverages, outdoor catering, beauty treatment, health services, cosmetic and plastic surgery, life and health insurance, membership of clubs and fitness centres, travel benefits to employees on leave — unless used for the same category of outward supply or obligatory for employers under a law. (c)/(d) Works contract and goods/services for construction of immovable property on own account (other than plant and machinery), even if used in business. (e) Composition tax. (g) Personal consumption. (h) Goods lost, stolen, destroyed, written off or given as gifts or free samples. (i) Tax paid under ss.74, 129, 130 (fraud and detention demands).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Inward supplies with GST: raw material ₹1,80,000; sedan for directors ₹2,52,000; office repairs (revenue) ₹9,000; staff canteen catering (not mandated) ₹18,000; machinery ₹54,000; free samples ₹3,600.
Eligible = 1,80,000 + 9,000 + 54,000 = ₹2,43,000. Blocked = 2,52,000 + 18,000 + 3,600 = ₹2,73,600.

steps.title: Exceptions worth remembering
steps.body: A car dealer gets ITC on cars it buys for resale; a cab operator gets ITC on taxis; a caterer gets ITC on catering services it buys for its own outward catering; a factory required by the Factories Act to run a canteen gets ITC on canteen services.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Blocking ITC on goods trucks (goods transport vehicles are not blocked); blocking ITC on plant and machinery fixed to earth (allowed).

Cement for constructing the office building

story.title: The dairy with two product lines

scenes.text: A dairy sells fresh milk (exempt) and paneer and ghee (taxable). Common electricity and rent credit must be split.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Principle (s.17(1)–(2))
steps.body: ITC used partly for business and partly for other purposes, or partly for taxable and partly for exempt supplies, is restricted to the portion attributable to business and taxable supplies (zero-rated supplies count as taxable).

steps.title: Method (simplified Rule 42)
steps.body: Total ITC T. Remove T1 (exclusively non-business), T2 (exclusively exempt), T3 (blocked) → C1 = T − T1 − T2 − T3. Remove T4 (exclusively taxable) → common credit C2 = C1 − T4. Reversal for exempt D1 = (E ÷ F) × C2 where E = exempt turnover and F = total turnover of the period; for non-business D2 = 5% of C2. Eligible common credit C3 = C2 − D1 − D2. Monthly computation is finalised annually by the due date of the September return.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Total ITC ₹1,40,000: exclusively for exempt milk ₹10,000; exclusively for taxable ₹30,000; common ₹1,00,000; no non-business use. Turnover: exempt ₹20 lakh, taxable ₹80 lakh.
Step 1: T2 = 10,000 not allowed; T4 = 30,000 allowed.
Step 2: D1 = 20/100 × 1,00,000 = 20,000 reversed.
Step 3: Eligible ITC = 30,000 + 80,000 = ₹1,10,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating exports (zero-rated) as exempt; applying the ratio to exclusive credits.

activity.prompt: Common ITC ₹2,40,000. Exempt turnover ₹30 lakh, total turnover ₹1.2 crore. No non-business use. ITC to be reversed under Rule 42 (₹).

quiz.q: For Rule 42, exports are treated as
quiz.why: Section 16 of the IGST Act treats zero-rated supplies as taxable for ITC purposes.

quiz.q: Reversal for non-business use of common credit
quiz.why: Rule 42 deems five percent of common credit attributable to non-business purposes when used partly so.

quiz.q: Credit used exclusively for exempt supplies is
quiz.why: Section 17(2) disallows credit attributable to exempt supplies.

lessons.title: Lab: Utilisation of ITC and cash payment

scenes.text: Output: IGST ₹50,000, CGST ₹30,000, SGST ₹30,000. Credit ledger: IGST ₹80,000, CGST ₹10,000, SGST ₹15,000. How much cash is payable?
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Order of utilisation (s.49(5), s.49A, Rule 88A)
steps.body: IGST credit must be used first: against IGST, then against CGST and SGST/UTGST in any order and proportion. Only after IGST credit is fully used can CGST and SGST credit be used. CGST credit: against CGST, then IGST. SGST credit: against SGST, then IGST. CGST credit can never pay SGST and vice versa.

steps.title: Worked example (optimal)
steps.body:
Step 1: IGST credit 80,000 → IGST liability 50,000 (balance 30,000).
Step 2: Use remaining IGST credit 30,000 — first see what CGST and SGST credits can cover: CGST gap 30,000 − 10,000 = 20,000; SGST gap 30,000 − 15,000 = 15,000. Allocate IGST 20,000 to CGST and 10,000 to SGST.
Step 3: CGST credit 10,000 → CGST (fully paid). SGST credit 15,000 → SGST; SGST remaining 30,000 − 10,000 − 15,000 = 5,000.
Cash payable: SGST ₹5,000 only.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body:
Output: CGST 40,000, SGST 40,000, IGST 10,000. ITC: CGST 60,000, SGST 20,000, IGST nil.
CGST credit: 40,000 to CGST, then 10,000 to IGST; balance 10,000 carried forward. SGST credit: 20,000 to SGST → SGST cash 20,000. Cash payable ₹20,000 (CGST surplus cannot pay SGST).

steps.title: Ledgers and interest
steps.body: Electronic cash ledger (deposits via PMT-06), electronic credit ledger, electronic liability register. Interest on delayed payment u/s 50: 18% p.a. on the net cash liability for the period of delay; on ITC wrongly availed and utilised: 18% as notified.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using CGST credit for SGST; using CGST/SGST credit before exhausting IGST credit; paying RCM via credit.

activity.prompt: Output: IGST ₹20,000, CGST ₹45,000, SGST ₹45,000. ITC: IGST ₹30,000, CGST ₹20,000, SGST ₹25,000. Minimum total cash payable (₹).

quiz.q: Which credit must be exhausted first?
quiz.why: Section 49A requires IGST credit to be utilised fully before CGST or SGST credit.

quiz.q: CGST credit can pay
quiz.why: Section 49(5)(b) allows CGST credit for CGST and then IGST only.

quiz.q: Interest rate on delayed tax payment u/s 50(1)
quiz.why: The notified rate on net cash liability paid late is eighteen percent per annum.

questions.why: Section 2(62) includes IGST charged on import of goods.

questions.why: Section 16(2)(aa) requires the details to be communicated through the auto-drafted statement.

questions.why: Section 16(3) bars ITC on the tax component if depreciation is claimed on it.

questions.why: Further supply of such vehicles is an exception to the block.

questions.q: ITC on construction of the factory building
questions.why: Section 17(5)(d) blocks credit on construction of immovable property on own account.

questions.q: Canteen services mandatory under the Factories Act: ITC
questions.why: Credit is allowed where providing the service is obligatory under a law.

questions.q: Common ITC ₹50,000; exempt turnover 10%, no non-business use. Eligible common ITC
questions.why: Ten percent, ₹5,000, is reversed, leaving ₹45,000.

questions.q: SGST credit can be used against
questions.why: Section 49(5)(c) allows SGST credit for SGST and then IGST.

questions.q: Output CGST ₹10,000, SGST ₹10,000; ITC CGST ₹25,000, SGST ₹0. SGST cash payable
questions.why: CGST credit cannot discharge SGST, so ₹10,000 is paid in cash.

questions.why: Section 17(5)(i) blocks credit of tax paid under section 74.

questions.why: Section 17(5)(h) blocks credit on goods destroyed.

questions.why: IGST credit of ₹40,000 covers part of CGST and SGST, leaving ₹20,000 in cash.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Registration, Invoicing, E-way Bills, Returns & Compliance
courses.summary: Threshold and compulsory registration, tax invoice, credit and debit notes, e-invoicing, e-way bill rules, the return cycle (GSTR-1, GSTR-3B, QRMP, GSTR-9/9C), payment, interest and late fees, refunds, TDS/TCS under GST, assessment, audit, offences and appeals.
outcomes: Decide when registration is required by threshold or compulsorily
Prepare a compliant tax invoice and credit/debit note
Apply e-way bill and e-invoicing rules
Plan the monthly and annual return calendar
Outline refunds, demands, penalties and the appeal ladder

scenes.text: A Jaipur bakery's turnover will cross ₹40 lakh this year. A customer in Delhi also wants regular supplies.
When must it register?

steps.title: Threshold (s.22)
steps.body: Aggregate turnover in a financial year exceeding ₹20 lakh (₹10 lakh in specified special category states). For persons exclusively supplying goods, the limit is ₹40 lakh in most states (states could opt; several north-eastern and hill states kept ₹20 lakh). Aggregate turnover = all-India value of taxable, exempt, export and inter-state supplies of the same PAN, excluding inward RCM supplies and taxes. Apply within 30 days of becoming liable.

steps.title: Compulsory registration (s.24)
steps.body: Regardless of turnover: inter-state taxable supply of goods (services suppliers up to the threshold are exempted by notification); casual taxable persons; persons liable under reverse charge; e-commerce operators and suppliers through them who must collect TCS (with relaxations for some small suppliers); non-resident taxable persons; persons deducting TDS under GST; Input Service Distributors; online information and database access services from outside India to unregistered persons.

steps.title: Process and other points
steps.body: Form REG-01 on the portal with PAN, Aadhaar authentication, business details, bank account; GSTIN issued in REG-06. Registration is state-wise; separate verticals may be registered. Voluntary registration is allowed. Cancellation by officer or on application (REG-16); revocation within the prescribed period. Non-registration when liable attracts penalty and tax demand.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Bakery: taxable sales ₹36 lakh, exempt bread (assume exempt) ₹6 lakh, so aggregate turnover ₹42 lakh. Step 1: Goods-only supplier in Rajasthan — limit ₹40 lakh. Step 2: 42 > 40 → registration required. Step 3: Separately, inter-state supply of goods to Delhi requires compulsory registration from the first such supply.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Excluding exempt supplies from aggregate turnover; computing turnover state-wise instead of PAN-wise all-India.

a.text: A designer in Pune supplies services worth ₹15 lakh, partly to clients in Gujarat. Registration needed?

choices.label: No — inter-state service suppliers below ₹20 lakh are exempted
Yes — any inter-state supply needs registration
choices.feedback: That rule applies to goods, not services below the threshold.

b.text: A trader in Surat with turnover ₹8 lakh sells goods to a buyer in Mumbai.

choices.label: Registration required — inter-state supply of goods
Not required — below threshold
choices.feedback: Inter-state goods supply triggers compulsory registration.

c.text: You applied s.22 and s.24 correctly.

quiz.q: General threshold for services suppliers (normal states)
quiz.why: Section 22(1) sets twenty lakh rupees for normal category states.

quiz.q: Application for registration must be made within
quiz.why: Section 25(1) requires application within thirty days of becoming liable.

quiz.q: Aggregate turnover includes
quiz.why: Section 2(6) includes exempt supplies in aggregate turnover.

lessons.title: Invoices, credit/debit notes, e-invoicing and e-way bills

scenes.text: A lorry with goods worth ₹1,20,000 is stopped for inspection; the driver has an invoice but no e-way bill.
The goods can be detained under s.129.

steps.title: Tax invoice (s.31, Rule 46)
steps.body: Goods: before or at removal/delivery. Services: within 30 days of supply (45 days for banks and insurers). Mandatory particulars: name, address, GSTIN of supplier; serial number unique for the FY (up to 16 characters); date; recipient name, address and GSTIN (if registered); HSN/SAC; description; quantity; taxable value; rate and amount of CGST/SGST/IGST; place of supply with state name for inter-state supply; whether tax is payable on reverse charge; signature. Bill of supply for exempt or composition supplies.

steps.title: Credit and debit notes (s.34)
steps.body: Credit note when taxable value or tax charged is excessive, goods are returned, or services are deficient; must be declared not later than 30 November following the end of the FY or annual return date, whichever is earlier. Debit note when value or tax charged is deficient.

steps.title: E-invoicing
steps.body: Mandatory for B2B invoices of taxpayers with aggregate turnover above ₹5 crore in any year from 2017-18. The invoice is reported to the Invoice Registration Portal, which returns an IRN and signed QR code; data auto-populates GSTR-1 and the e-way bill.

steps.title: E-way bill (Rule 138)
steps.body: Required for movement of goods of consignment value exceeding ₹50,000 (inter-state; for intra-state, as per state notification), generated on the EWB portal: Part A (invoice details) and Part B (vehicle). Validity: 1 day per 200 km for normal cargo (20 km per day for over-dimensional cargo). Exempted goods and specified modes are excluded.

steps.title: Worked example: validity
steps.body: Distance 850 km by road (normal cargo). Step: 850 ÷ 200 = 4.25 → 5 days of validity (each part of 200 km adds a day).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Including GST in deciding the ₹50,000 limit wrongly — consignment value includes the tax but excludes value of exempt goods; issuing service invoices after 30 days.

activity.prompt: E-way bill validity for normal cargo travelling 1,120 km (days).

quiz.q: E-way bill threshold (consignment value)
quiz.why: Rule 138(1) requires an e-way bill where consignment value exceeds fifty thousand rupees.

quiz.q: E-invoicing turnover threshold (current)
quiz.why: From 1 August 2023 the threshold was reduced to five crore rupees.

quiz.q: Service invoice should be issued within
quiz.why: Rule 47 requires a service invoice within thirty days of the supply.

lessons.title: Lab: Returns, payment and the compliance calendar

scenes.text: An accountant's month revolves around two dates: GSTR-1 on the 11th and GSTR-3B on the 20th.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Main returns
steps.body: GSTR-1: outward supplies — monthly by the 11th of next month; quarterly by the 13th for QRMP taxpayers (with optional IFF for B2B invoices in the first two months). GSTR-2B: auto-drafted ITC statement, generated on the 14th. GSTR-3B: summary return and payment — monthly by the 20th; quarterly by the 22nd or 24th (state-wise) for QRMP, with PMT-06 monthly payments by the 25th. GSTR-4: composition annual. GSTR-7: TDS deductors by the 10th. GSTR-8: e-commerce TCS by the 10th. GSTR-9: annual return by 31 December; GSTR-9C reconciliation statement (self-certified) for aggregate turnover above ₹5 crore. QRMP eligibility: aggregate turnover up to ₹5 crore.

steps.title: Late fee and interest
steps.body: Late fee for GSTR-3B/GSTR-1: ₹50 per day (₹25 CGST + ₹25 SGST), ₹20 per day for nil returns, subject to caps notified by turnover. Interest u/s 50: 18% p.a. on net cash liability.

steps.title: Worked example: interest
steps.body: GSTR-3B for June due 20 July; filed on 9 August with net cash liability ₹1,20,000. Delay = 20 days. Interest = 1,20,000 × 18% × 20/365 = ₹1,184 (approx.). Late fee = 20 × ₹50 = ₹1,000.

steps.title: Refunds, TDS and TCS
steps.body: Refunds (s.54): exports and supplies to SEZ (with or without payment of IGST), inverted duty structure, excess cash balance — apply within 2 years from the relevant date (RFD-01). TDS (s.51): government departments and notified bodies deduct 2% (1% CGST + 1% SGST, or 2% IGST) on contracts above ₹2.5 lakh. TCS (s.52): e-commerce operators collect on net taxable supplies at notified rates (reduced to 0.5% IGST / 0.25% + 0.25% from 10 July 2024).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Computing interest on gross liability instead of net cash liability; missing GSTR-1 which blocks the buyer's ITC.

activity.prompt: GSTR-3B filed 15 days late; net cash liability ₹73,000. Interest @18% p.a. using 365 days (₹, nearest rupee).

quiz.q: GSTR-3B monthly due date
quiz.why: Monthly filers must file GSTR-3B by the twentieth of the following month.

quiz.q: GSTR-9C applies when aggregate turnover exceeds
quiz.why: The reconciliation statement is required above five crore rupees.

quiz.q: QRMP scheme is available up to turnover of
quiz.why: Registered persons with aggregate turnover up to five crore rupees may opt for QRMP.

scenes.text: A trader receives a notice for excess ITC claimed in FY 2022-23. Was it fraud or an honest error?
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Assessment and audit
steps.body: Self-assessment (s.59); provisional (s.60); scrutiny of returns (s.61, ASMT-10); best judgement for non-filers (s.62) and unregistered persons (s.63); summary (s.64). Audit by department (s.65) and special audit by a CA/CMA (s.66).

steps.title: Demand and recovery (s.73, s.74, s.74A)
steps.body: For periods up to FY 2023-24: s.73 for non-fraud cases (penalty 10% of tax or ₹10,000, whichever higher; nil if paid before notice) and s.74 for fraud or suppression (penalty equal to tax; reduced if paid early). From FY 2024-25, s.74A applies a single time limit: notice within 42 months and order within 12 months thereafter, with penalty 10% (non-fraud) or 100% (fraud).

steps.title: Offences and penalties (ss.122, 132)
steps.body: Offences include supplying without invoice, issuing invoices without supply, availing ITC without receipt of goods or services, collecting tax and not paying it beyond three months. Prosecution under s.132 depends on the tax amount; arrest provisions apply to serious cases above ₹5 crore as specified. Compounding is available for some offences.

steps.title: Appeals
steps.body: Adjudicating authority → Appellate Authority (s.107, within 3 months, pre-deposit 10% of disputed tax) → GST Appellate Tribunal (s.112, pre-deposit further 10%) → High Court (substantial question of law) → Supreme Court. Advance Ruling (s.97) on classification, valuation, ITC and similar questions.

steps.title: Worked example: pre-deposit
steps.body: Disputed tax ₹8,00,000 (not admitted). Step 1: Appeal to Appellate Authority — pre-deposit 10% = ₹80,000 (plus full admitted amount). Step 2: Appeal to the Tribunal — further 10% of the amount in dispute after the first appeal order (if still ₹8,00,000) = ₹80,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Going straight to the High Court without the statutory appeal; ignoring the 3-month limit.

activity.prompt: Disputed tax in an order ₹12,50,000, admitted tax nil. Pre-deposit for first appeal under s.107 (₹).

quiz.q: Time limit for first appeal
quiz.why: Section 107(1) allows three months from communication of the order.

quiz.q: Scrutiny of returns is under
quiz.why: Section 61 empowers the officer to scrutinise returns and seek explanation in ASMT-10.

quiz.q: Penalty in a non-fraud case (s.73) when tax is paid after notice
quiz.why: Section 73(9) and s.122 provide ten percent or ten thousand rupees, whichever is higher.

questions.q: Goods-only supplier threshold in most states
questions.why: Notification 10/2019-CT raised the limit to forty lakh rupees for exclusive goods suppliers in states that adopted it.

questions.q: Casual taxable person must register
questions.why: Section 24(ii) requires compulsory registration for casual taxable persons.

questions.q: Invoice serial number maximum length
questions.why: Rule 46 allows up to sixteen characters.

questions.q: Credit note for FY 2025-26 must be declared by
questions.why: Section 34(2) uses 30 November after the end of the financial year or annual return date if earlier.

questions.q: E-way bill Part B contains
questions.why: Part B records transport and vehicle details.

questions.q: E-way bill validity for 380 km normal cargo
questions.why: Up to 200 km is one day and each additional 200 km or part adds one day.

questions.q: Annual return due date
questions.why: Section 44 with Rule 80 sets 31 December following the end of the financial year.

questions.q: Late fee per day for a non-nil GSTR-3B
questions.why: The notified late fee is ₹25 CGST plus ₹25 SGST per day.

questions.q: TDS under GST is deducted at
questions.why: Section 51 provides deduction at two percent of payment.

steps.title: Output tax
steps.body: Intra-state: CGST 90,000 + SGST 90,000. Inter-state: IGST 72,000. Exempt: nil. Total output = ₹2,52,000.

steps.title: Eligible ITC
steps.body: Intra-state purchases: CGST 54,000 + SGST 54,000. Inter-state: IGST 36,000. Car: blocked. (For simplicity, common credit apportionment is ignored here because all purchases relate to taxable sales.) Total ITC = ₹1,44,000.

steps.title: Utilisation
steps.body: IGST credit 36,000 → IGST liability 72,000 → IGST balance 36,000. CGST credit 54,000 → CGST 90,000 → CGST balance 36,000. SGST credit 54,000 → SGST 90,000 → SGST balance 36,000. Cash payable: IGST 36,000 + CGST 36,000 + SGST 36,000 = ₹1,08,000.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Total output 2,52,000 − total ITC 1,44,000 = 1,08,000 ✔ — when no credit is stranded the shortcut works.

uni-bcom-income-tax.title: Income Tax Law & Practice (India)
uni-bcom-income-tax.description: Computation of income and tax for individuals under the Income-tax Act 1961 for AY 2026-27 (FY 2025-26): residential status, the five heads of income, deductions, new vs old regime, TDS and return filing. Assumptions stated in every unit. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Com programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Basic Concepts, Residential Status & Exempt Incomes
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Income Tax Law & Practice)
courses.summary: Assumptions: Income-tax Act 1961 as applicable to assessment year 2026-27 (previous year 2025-26), individual assessees. The Income-tax Act 2025 is due to replace the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026 for later years — section numbers here refer to the 1961 Act. Covers key definitions, residential status, scope of total income and agricultural income.
outcomes: Define person, assessee, previous year, assessment year and income
Determine residential status of an individual from day counts
Apply the scope of total income for ROR, RNOR and NR
Identify agricultural income and its partial integration
List major exempt incomes under section 10

lessons.title: Key definitions and the structure of the Act

scenes.text: Priya joined a firm in July 2025. Her friend says she must file 'this year's' return.
Which year is 'this year'? Income of FY 2025-26 is assessed in AY 2026-27.

steps.title: Basic terms
steps.body: Person (s.2(31)): individual, HUF, company, firm, AOP/BOI, local authority, artificial juridical person. Assessee (s.2(7)): person by whom tax is payable. Previous year (s.3): the financial year immediately preceding the assessment year — 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026. Assessment year (s.2(9)): the 12 months starting 1 April in which income of the previous year is assessed — AY 2026-27. Income (s.2(24)) is an inclusive definition covering profits, dividends, gifts above limits, winnings etc.

steps.title: Five heads of income (s.14)
steps.body: (1) Salaries; (2) Income from house property; (3) Profits and gains of business or profession; (4) Capital gains; (5) Income from other sources. Gross total income = sum of heads after set-off; total income = GTI − Chapter VI-A deductions. Tax is then computed at slab or special rates, less rebate, plus surcharge (if applicable) and 4% health and education cess.

steps.title: Exceptions to 'previous year income taxed next year'
steps.body: Income of a non-resident shipping business, persons leaving India permanently, AOP formed for a short purpose, persons likely to transfer assets to avoid tax, discontinued business — these may be assessed in the same year.

steps.title: Rounding
steps.body: Total income is rounded off to the nearest multiple of ₹10 (s.288A) and tax to the nearest ₹10 (s.288B).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Writing 'AY 2025-26' for FY 2025-26 income; forgetting cess; treating capital receipts as income without a specific provision.

activity.prompt: Which head of income?

items.text: Profit on sale of listed shares held 2 years

quiz.q: Income of FY 2025-26 is assessed in
quiz.why: The assessment year is the year immediately following the previous year, so FY 2025-26 maps to AY 2026-27.

quiz.q: How many heads of income are there?
quiz.why: Section 14 classifies income under five heads.

quiz.q: Health and education cess rate
quiz.why: Cess is levied at four percent of income tax plus surcharge.

lessons.title: Lab: Residential status of an individual

scenes.text: Mr Lee, a foreign national, stayed in India for 75 days in FY 2025-26.
Over the four previous years he stayed 400 days. Is he resident?

steps.title: Basic conditions (s.6(1))
steps.body: An individual is resident if (a) in India for 182 days or more in the previous year, OR (b) 60 days or more in the previous year AND 365 days or more in the four preceding years. Otherwise non-resident. In condition (b) the 60 days is replaced by 182 for an Indian citizen leaving India for employment or as crew, and for an Indian citizen or person of Indian origin visiting India; for such a visitor with Indian income (other than foreign sources) above ₹15 lakh, the figure is 120 days. An Indian citizen with such income above ₹15 lakh not liable to tax in any other country is deemed resident (s.6(1A)).

steps.title: ROR or RNOR (s.6(6))
steps.body: A resident is 'not ordinarily resident' if he was non-resident in 9 out of 10 preceding years, OR in India for 729 days or less in the 7 preceding years. Visitors covered by the 120-day rule, and deemed residents under s.6(1A), are RNOR.

steps.title: Worked example 1: Mr Lee
steps.body: Step 1: 182-day test — 75 < 182, fails. Step 2: 60 + 365 test — 75 ≥ 60 and 400 ≥ 365, passes. Step 3: Resident. Step 4: Suppose he was non-resident in all 10 preceding years — he is RNOR.

steps.title: Worked example 2: Indian citizen working abroad
steps.body: Ravi, an Indian citizen employed in Dubai, visits India for 150 days; Indian income ₹8 lakh. Step 1: 182-day test fails. Step 2: As a citizen visiting India with Indian income ≤ ₹15 lakh, the 60 days become 182, so test (b) fails. Step 3: Non-resident.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Counting only full days — both the day of arrival and departure are generally counted; applying the 60-day rule to visiting Indian citizens.

a.text: Foreign national: 190 days in India this year. Resident?

choices.label: Yes — 182 days or more
choices.feedback: Right: the first basic condition is met.

choices.label: No — not a citizen
choices.feedback: Citizenship is not the test for basic conditions.

b.text: He was non-resident in 9 of the 10 preceding years. ROR or RNOR?

choices.label: ROR
choices.feedback: Non-resident in 9 of 10 years makes him RNOR.

c.text: Status determined: Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident.

quiz.q: 60 days + 365 days in preceding
quiz.why: Section 6(1)(c) looks at 365 days in the four years preceding the previous year.

quiz.q: A visiting Indian citizen with Indian income of ₹20 lakh: the 60 days become
quiz.why: For such visitors with Indian income above fifteen lakh rupees, the period is 120 days.

quiz.q: RNOR if in India for at most how many days in 7 preceding years?
quiz.why: Section 6(6)(a) treats 729 days or less in the preceding seven years as not ordinarily resident.

story.title: Three statuses, one set of incomes

scenes.text: An individual has income in India and abroad. How much is taxed depends on status.
Let us compute it three ways.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: ROR: income received or deemed received in India + accruing or deemed to accrue in India + accruing and received outside India (global income). RNOR: first two + income accruing outside from a business controlled in, or profession set up in, India. NR: only income received/deemed received in India or accruing/deemed to accrue in India. Past untaxed foreign income brought into India is not income.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Incomes: (a) salary received in India ₹4,00,000; (b) profit from a London business controlled from London ₹3,00,000, received in London; (c) profit from a Dubai business controlled from India ₹1,50,000, received in Dubai; (d) rent from a Mumbai flat received in Singapore ₹2,00,000.
ROR: a + b + c + d = ₹10,50,000.
RNOR: a + c + d = ₹7,50,000.
NR: a + d = ₹6,00,000 (d accrues in India).

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Draw a table with incomes as rows and ROR / RNOR / NR as columns; tick or cross each cell; then add columns.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Excluding Indian rent received abroad for an NR — it accrues in India so it is taxable; adding foreign business income for RNOR when the business is controlled abroad.

activity.prompt: Using the worked-example incomes, but suppose (c) is ₹2,50,000 instead. Total income of an RNOR (₹).

quiz.q: For a non-resident, foreign income received abroad is
quiz.why: A non-resident is taxed only on income received or accruing in India.

quiz.q: An RNOR is taxed on foreign income only if
options: it is from a business controlled in or profession set up in India
quiz.why: Section 5(1) proviso brings such foreign income within an RNOR's total income.

quiz.q: Global income is taxable for
quiz.why: Only a resident and ordinarily resident individual is taxed on worldwide income.

scenes.text: Suresh earns ₹6 lakh from business and ₹2 lakh from paddy fields.
Agricultural income is exempt — but it still affects his tax rate under the old regime.

steps.title: Agricultural income (s.2(1A), s.10(1))
steps.body: Rent or revenue from land in India used for agriculture; income from agricultural operations including processing to make the produce marketable; income from a farm building used for these purposes. Exempt under s.10(1). Not agricultural: dividend from a tea company, income from dairy or poultry, purchased produce, interest on a loan to a farmer. Composite incomes: tea grown and manufactured — 40% business income, 60% agricultural (Rule 8).

steps.title: Partial integration
steps.body: Applies to individuals and HUFs when net agricultural income exceeds ₹5,000 and non-agricultural income exceeds the basic exemption limit. Tax = tax on (non-agri + agri income) − tax on (agri income + basic exemption limit). Exams usually test it under the old regime slabs, as done here.

steps.title: Other common exemptions (s.10)
steps.body: Share of profit from a firm (s.10(2A)); leave travel concession (10(5)); gratuity (10(10)), commuted pension (10(10A)), leave encashment (10(10AA)) within limits; life insurance maturity subject to conditions (10(10D)); PPF interest and maturity (10(11)); scholarships (10(16)). Several s.10 exemptions such as LTC and HRA are not available under the new regime.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating income from foreign agricultural land as exempt (only land in India); forgetting to subtract the second tax in partial integration.

activity.prompt: Old regime, age 40: non-agricultural income ₹7,00,000, agricultural income ₹1,00,000. Tax before cess using partial integration (₹).

quiz.q: Income from poultry farming is
quiz.why: Poultry does not involve cultivation of land, so it is not agricultural income.

quiz.q: Tea grown and manufactured: agricultural portion
quiz.why: Rule 8 treats sixty percent of such income as agricultural.

quiz.q: Partial integration applies only when agri income exceeds
quiz.why: Net agricultural income must exceed five thousand rupees for aggregation.

questions.q: Previous year for AY 2026-27
questions.why: The previous year is the financial year before the assessment year.

questions.q: Which is NOT a 'person' under s.2(31)?
questions.why: A branch is part of a person, not a separate person.

questions.q: Foreign national: 100 days this year, 300 days in previous 4 years. Status:
questions.why: He fails 182 days and fails 365 days in the four preceding years.

questions.q: Foreign national: 65 days this year, 500 days in previous 4 years. Status:
questions.why: He satisfies 60 days in the year and 365 days in the four preceding years.

questions.q: Indian citizen leaving India for a job abroad in Sept 2025 after 160 days in India this year:
questions.why: For such a citizen the 60 days are replaced by 182 days, and 160 is below both tests.

questions.q: NR's rent from a Delhi house received in London is
questions.why: Income from property in India accrues in India and is taxable for all assessees.

questions.q: Total income is rounded to the nearest
questions.why: Section 288A rounds total income to the nearest multiple of ten rupees.

questions.q: Dividend from a tea company is
questions.why: Dividend is income from shareholding, not from land.

questions.q: Old regime partial integration: non-agri ₹5,00,000, agri ₹1,00,000. Tax before cess:
questions.why: Tax on ₹6,00,000 is ₹32,500 and tax on ₹3,50,000 is ₹5,000, so the tax is ₹27,500.

questions.q: Share of profit from a partnership firm received by a partner is
questions.why: Section 10(2A) exempts a partner's share of the firm's total income.

questions.q: RNOR is taxed on income from a business controlled from India but accruing abroad?
questions.why: Section 5(1) proviso includes such income for an RNOR.

questions.q: The Income-tax Act 2025 is intended to apply from
questions.why: It is due to replace the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026, so AY 2026-27 computations still use the 1961 Act.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Income from Salaries
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Income Tax Law & Practice)
courses.summary: Assumptions: AY 2026-27, resident individual below 60, Income-tax Act 1961. Covers the employer–employee relationship, basis of charge, allowances (HRA), perquisites, retirement benefits (gratuity, leave encashment, pension), standard deduction and complete salary computation under both the default new regime (s.115BAC) and the old regime.
outcomes: State the basis of charge under s.15 and the meaning of salary under s.17(1)
Compute HRA exemption under s.10(13A)
Value common perquisites and compute gratuity exemption
Apply deductions under s.16 under each regime
Compute taxable salary and tax under the new and old regimes

scenes.text: Neha's slip shows basic, DA, HRA, conveyance and a special allowance.
Which parts are taxable — and does it matter that she pays ₹30,000 a month as rent in Mumbai?

steps.title: Basis of charge (s.15)
steps.body: Salary is taxable on due basis or receipt basis, whichever is earlier: salary due from an employer in the previous year (paid or not), salary paid in the previous year before it became due, and arrears paid in the previous year if not taxed earlier. An employer–employee relationship is essential; salary of an MP or MLA is taxed under 'other sources'. Salary (s.17(1)) includes wages, annuity, pension, gratuity, fees, commission, perquisites, advance salary, leave encashment and employer contributions to specified funds above limits.

steps.title: HRA exemption (s.10(13A), Rule 2A) — old regime only
steps.body: Least of: (1) actual HRA received; (2) rent paid minus 10% of salary; (3) 50% of salary in Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, 40% elsewhere. Here salary = basic + DA forming part of retirement benefits + commission as a fixed percentage of turnover, for the period of residence in rented accommodation.

steps.title: Other allowances
steps.body: Fully taxable: dearness allowance, city compensatory, overtime, lunch, special allowance. Partly exempt in the old regime: children education ₹100 per month per child (max two), hostel ₹300 per month per child. Under the new regime, exemptions are limited — e.g. transport allowance for specially-abled employees and conveyance for official duty remain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Including HRA itself or special allowance in 'salary' for the HRA formula; claiming HRA exemption under the new regime; using 50% for a non-metro city such as Bengaluru (40%).

activity.prompt: Old regime. Basic + DA (forming part) ₹5,00,000; HRA received ₹1,80,000; rent paid in Pune ₹1,50,000. HRA exemption (₹).

quiz.q: HRA metro limit percentage
quiz.why: Rule 2A allows fifty percent of salary for Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata and Chennai.

quiz.q: Salary of a Member of Parliament is taxed under
quiz.why: There is no employer–employee relationship, so it falls under income from other sources.

quiz.q: Advance salary is taxed
quiz.why: Section 15(b) taxes salary paid in advance in the year it is received.

scenes.text: Mr Iyer retires after 20 years and 7 months with last salary ₹52,000 a month.
He receives ₹8,00,000 gratuity. How much is exempt?

steps.title: Perquisites (s.17(2))
steps.body: Rent-free or concessional accommodation; benefit to a specified employee (e.g. car, servants, utilities); obligations of the employee met by employer; life insurance premium paid by employer; ESOP value at exercise; employer contribution to PF, NPS and superannuation together above ₹7.5 lakh. Valuation rules are in Rule 3. Tax-free perquisites include medical treatment in employer's hospital, refreshments during office hours, telephone/mobile, and training.

steps.title: Gratuity (s.10(10))
steps.body: Government employees: fully exempt. Covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act: least of (a) actual gratuity, (b) 15/26 × last drawn salary (basic + DA) × completed years (part exceeding 6 months counted as a full year), (c) ₹20,00,000. Not covered: least of actual, ½ month's average salary of the last 10 months × completed years (fractions ignored), ₹20,00,000.

steps.title: Worked example: covered employee
steps.body: Last drawn basic + DA ₹52,000 per month; service 20 years 7 months → 21 years. Step 1: 15/26 × 52,000 × 21 = ₹6,30,000. Step 2: Limit ₹20,00,000; actual ₹8,00,000. Step 3: Exempt = ₹6,30,000; taxable = ₹1,70,000.

steps.title: Leave encashment and pension
steps.body: Leave encashment on retirement (non-government): least of actual, 10 months' average salary, cash equivalent of leave (max 30 days per year of service), and ₹25,00,000. Commuted pension: non-government employee — one-third of full commuted value exempt if gratuity also received, else one-half. Uncommuted pension is fully taxable as salary.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Rounding service down for covered employees (more than 6 months rounds up); using 15/30 instead of 15/26 for covered employees.

activity.prompt: Covered employee: last drawn basic + DA ₹39,000 per month, service 14 years 8 months, gratuity received ₹4,00,000. Exempt gratuity (₹).

quiz.q: Gratuity exemption ceiling
quiz.why: Section 10(10) caps the exemption for non-government employees at twenty lakh rupees.

quiz.q: For a covered employee, 25 years 7 months counts as
quiz.why: A part year exceeding six months is treated as a full year under the Payment of Gratuity Act.

quiz.q: Leave encashment exemption ceiling for non-government employees
quiz.why: The limit was raised to twenty-five lakh rupees from 1 April 2023.

lessons.title: Deductions u/s 16 and the two regimes

scenes.text: From AY 2024-25, the new regime is the default. Salaried employees may opt out every year when filing.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Section 16 deductions
steps.body: New regime (s.115BAC): standard deduction ₹75,000 (AY 2026-27); no entertainment allowance or professional tax deduction. Old regime: standard deduction ₹50,000; entertainment allowance for government employees (least of ₹5,000, 1/5 of basic, actual); professional tax paid.

steps.title: New regime slabs (AY 2026-27)
steps.body: Up to ₹4,00,000 nil; 4–8 lakh 5%; 8–12 lakh 10%; 12–16 lakh 15%; 16–20 lakh 20%; 20–24 lakh 25%; above 24 lakh 30%. Rebate u/s 87A up to ₹60,000 where total income ≤ ₹12,00,000 (not on special-rate incomes like s.111A/112A), with marginal relief just above.

steps.title: Old regime slabs (below 60)
steps.body: Up to ₹2,50,000 nil; 2.5–5 lakh 5%; 5–10 lakh 20%; above 10 lakh 30%. Senior citizen (60–80) exemption ₹3,00,000; super senior (80+) ₹5,00,000. Rebate u/s 87A up to ₹12,500 where total income ≤ ₹5,00,000.

steps.title: Worked example: rebate
steps.body: Gross salary ₹12,75,000 under new regime. Step 1: 12,75,000 − 75,000 = ₹12,00,000. Step 2: Tax = 20,000 + 40,000 = 60,000. Step 3: Rebate 87A ₹60,000 → tax nil.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Applying old slabs to the new regime; deducting 80C under the new regime (not allowed, except employer NPS 80CCD(2)).

courses.title: Unit 3 · House Property & Profits of Business or Profession
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Income Tax Law & Practice)
courses.summary: Assumptions: AY 2026-27, Income-tax Act 1961. Annual value and deductions for let-out and self-occupied property; computation of business income with admissible and inadmissible expenses; depreciation on block of assets; presumptive taxation u/s 44AD, 44ADA and 44AE.
outcomes: Compute gross and net annual value of a let-out property
Apply s.24 deductions and self-occupied property rules under each regime
Adjust net profit as per P&L to taxable business income
Compute depreciation on a block of assets including the half-rate rule
Apply presumptive taxation schemes

scenes.text: Kavya lets out a flat at ₹30,000 a month; municipal value ₹3,20,000, fair rent ₹3,40,000, standard rent ₹3,50,000.
She paid municipal tax ₹20,000 and home-loan interest ₹1,50,000.

steps.title: Charge (s.22)
steps.body: Annual value of a building or land appurtenant, owned by the assessee, not used for own business or profession. Composite rent and sub-letting income go to other sources or business as appropriate.

steps.title: Gross annual value of let-out property (s.23(1))
steps.body: Step A: Expected rent = higher of municipal value and fair rent, but not exceeding standard rent (Rent Control Act). Step B: GAV = higher of expected rent and actual rent received or receivable (after unrealised rent, subject to conditions); if lower actual rent is due to vacancy, actual rent is taken. NAV = GAV − municipal taxes paid by the owner during the year.

steps.title: Deductions (s.24)
steps.body: (a) Standard deduction 30% of NAV; (b) interest on borrowed capital — actual for let-out property; pre-construction interest allowed in five equal instalments from the year of completion. Self-occupied property: annual value nil (up to two houses); interest deduction up to ₹2,00,000 (old regime) for acquisition/construction completed within five years; under the new regime, interest on self-occupied property is not allowed, and HP loss cannot be set off against other heads.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Deducting municipal tax that is unpaid or paid by the tenant; computing 30% on GAV instead of NAV; setting off HP loss beyond ₹2,00,000 against other heads under the old regime (excess is carried forward 8 years).

activity.prompt: Let-out house: municipal value ₹2,40,000, fair rent ₹2,70,000, standard rent ₹2,60,000, actual rent ₹2,50,000 p.a., municipal tax paid ₹10,000, interest on loan ₹60,000. Income from house property (₹).

quiz.q: Standard deduction under s.24(a)
quiz.why: Section 24(a) allows thirty percent of the net annual value.

quiz.q: Interest limit on self-occupied property (old regime)
quiz.why: Section 24(b) caps interest on a self-occupied house at two lakh rupees when conditions are met.

quiz.q: Pre-construction interest is allowed in
quiz.why: It is deductible in five equal annual instalments starting from the year of completion.

lessons.title: Business income: admissible and inadmissible items

scenes.text: A trader's P&L shows a net profit of ₹8,00,000, but it includes income-tax paid, donations and a cash payment to a supplier.
The tax computation adjusts each item.

steps.title: Charge (s.28) and general deduction (s.37)
steps.body: Profits of any business or profession carried on during the previous year are taxable. Expenses wholly and exclusively for business, not capital, not personal, are allowed under s.37(1). Specific deductions: rent, repairs, insurance (s.30–31), depreciation (s.32), scientific research (s.35), bad debts written off (s.36(1)(vii)), employer's contribution to PF (s.36(1)(iv)).

steps.title: Disallowances
steps.body: s.40(a): failure to deduct or pay TDS — 100% for payments to non-residents, 30% for residents. s.40(b): partner's remuneration and interest beyond limits (interest max 12% p.a.). s.40A(2): excessive payments to relatives. s.40A(3): cash payments exceeding ₹10,000 to a person in a day (₹35,000 for transporters). s.43B: certain expenses allowed only on actual payment (tax, bonus, employer PF, leave encashment, interest to banks; payments to micro/small enterprises beyond the time limit of the MSMED Act). Income tax, penalties for offences and personal expenses are never deductible.

steps.title: Worked example: adjusted profit
steps.body:
Net profit per P&L ₹8,00,000. Debited: income tax ₹40,000; donation to a charitable trust ₹10,000; cash purchase ₹25,000 in a single payment; depreciation per books ₹60,000 (tax depreciation ₹75,000). Credited: dividend ₹12,000.
Add: 40,000 + 10,000 + 25,000 + 60,000 = 1,35,000 → 9,35,000.
Less: dividend 12,000 (other sources) and tax depreciation 75,000 → ₹8,48,000 business income. (Donation may be claimed under s.80G subject to conditions under the old regime.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Disallowing only the excess over ₹10,000 for cash payment (the whole payment is disallowed); forgetting to replace book depreciation with tax depreciation.

activity.prompt: Allowed or disallowed while computing business income?

items.text: Salary to staff with TDS deducted and paid
Cash payment of ₹18,000 to a supplier in one day

quiz.q: Cash payment limit u/s 40A(3) (non-transporter)
quiz.why: Payments exceeding ten thousand rupees in a day otherwise than by banking channels are disallowed.

quiz.q: Disallowance for not deducting TDS on payment to a resident
quiz.why: Section 40(a)(ia) disallows thirty percent of the sum when TDS is not deducted or paid on resident payments.

quiz.q: Bonus to employees is allowed on
quiz.why: Section 43B allows bonus only when actually paid, generally by the return due date.

lessons.title: Lab: Depreciation on block of assets (s.32)

scenes.text: A manufacturer buys a machine for ₹4,00,000 on 10 December 2025 and puts it to use at once.
It is used for less than 180 days in the year — only half the rate applies.

steps.title: Block concept
steps.body: Depreciation is on the written-down value of a block of assets (same class and rate). WDV at year end = opening WDV + actual cost of additions − sale proceeds of assets sold (not below nil). If an asset is put to use for less than 180 days in the year of acquisition, depreciation is 50% of the normal rate on that addition. Common rates: building (residential) 5%, other building 10%, furniture 10%, plant and machinery 15%, computers and software 40%, intangible assets (other than goodwill) 25%.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Plant and machinery block (15%): opening WDV ₹10,00,000; addition ₹4,00,000 used < 180 days.
Step 1: Depreciation on opening WDV = 10,00,000 × 15% = 1,50,000.
Step 2: On the addition = 4,00,000 × 7.5% = 30,000.
Step 3: Total = ₹1,80,000; closing WDV = ₹12,20,000.

steps.title: Additional depreciation (s.32(1)(iia))
steps.body: Manufacturing assessees get an extra 20% of actual cost of new plant and machinery (10% if used < 180 days, balance next year), not available under s.115BAA/115BAB companies or the individual new regime.

steps.title: Short-term capital gain on block (s.50)
steps.body: If sale proceeds exceed opening WDV + additions, the excess is short-term capital gain. If all assets of the block are sold and proceeds are less, the shortfall is short-term capital loss.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Charging depreciation asset-by-asset; forgetting the half-rate rule; treating block STCG as LTCG even for old assets.

activity.prompt: Furniture block (10%): opening WDV ₹2,00,000; addition ₹60,000 in October (used ≥ 180 days); sale of one item ₹20,000. Depreciation for the year (₹).

quiz.q: Depreciation rate on computers
quiz.why: Computers including software are depreciated at forty percent under Appendix I.

quiz.q: Asset put to use for 150 days in the year of purchase gets
quiz.why: The second proviso to s.32(1) restricts depreciation to fifty percent for use under 180 days.

quiz.q: Sale proceeds exceeding block WDV plus additions give
quiz.why: Section 50 deems such excess to be short-term capital gain.

scenes.text: A grocer with turnover ₹1.4 crore, mostly digital receipts, does not want to maintain detailed books.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: 44AD — eligible business
steps.body: Resident individual, HUF or firm (not LLP). Turnover up to ₹2 crore, or up to ₹3 crore if cash receipts are not more than 5% of total receipts. Deemed profit: 8% of turnover, or 6% of turnover received by digital/banking modes. No further deduction for expenses or depreciation. Opting out within 5 years bars the scheme for the next 5 years.

steps.title: 44ADA — professionals
steps.body: Resident professionals (legal, medical, engineering, architecture, accountancy, technical consultancy, interior decoration and other notified) with gross receipts up to ₹50 lakh, or ₹75 lakh if cash receipts ≤ 5%. Deemed profit 50% of gross receipts.

steps.title: 44AE — goods carriages
steps.body: Not more than 10 goods carriages at any time in the year. Heavy goods vehicle (over 12 tonnes): ₹1,000 per tonne of gross vehicle weight per month or part; other vehicles: ₹7,500 per vehicle per month or part.

steps.title: Worked example: 44AD
steps.body: Turnover ₹1,40,00,000 of which ₹1,25,00,000 digital and ₹15,00,000 cash. Step 1: Eligible (≤ ₹2 crore). Step 2: 6% × 1,25,00,000 = 7,50,000; 8% × 15,00,000 = 1,20,000. Step 3: Presumptive income ₹8,70,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Allowing depreciation over and above presumptive income; applying 44AD to commission agents or professionals.

activity.prompt: Doctor under 44ADA: gross receipts ₹42,00,000 (all digital). Presumptive income (₹).

quiz.q: 44AD deemed profit on digital receipts
quiz.why: The rate is six percent for turnover received through banking or digital modes.

quiz.q: 44ADA deemed profit
quiz.why: Section 44ADA presumes profit at fifty percent of gross receipts.

quiz.q: 44AE applies to owners of up to
quiz.why: The scheme is for assessees owning not more than ten goods carriages at any time in the year.

questions.why: Section 22 excludes property used for the owner's business or profession.
Expected rent is capped at standard rent of ₹1,90,000, which exceeds actual rent.

questions.q: Annual value of one self-occupied house
questions.why: Section 23(2) treats the annual value of up to two self-occupied houses as nil.

questions.q: Excess HP loss (old regime) can be carried forward for
questions.why: Section 71B permits carry forward for eight assessment years.

questions.q: Interest on partner's capital is allowed up to
questions.why: Section 40(b) limits allowable interest to twelve percent simple interest per annum.

questions.q: Income tax paid debited to P&L is
options: allowed if paid by due date
questions.why: Section 40(a)(ii) prohibits deduction of tax levied on profits.

questions.q: P&M opening WDV ₹5,00,000, addition ₹2,00,000 used 100 days. Depreciation @15%:
questions.why: ₹75,000 on opening WDV plus 7.5 percent of ₹2,00,000, which is ₹15,000.

questions.q: Computer block WDV ₹1,00,000, sold all for ₹1,30,000. Result:
questions.why: Section 50 treats proceeds over the block value as short-term capital gain.

questions.q: 44AD turnover ₹90 lakh all in cash. Presumptive income:
questions.why: Eight percent of ₹90 lakh is ₹7,20,000.

questions.q: 44AE: one heavy goods vehicle of 15 tonnes held for 12 months. Income:
questions.why: One thousand rupees per tonne per month gives 15 × 12 × 1,000 = ₹1,80,000.

questions.why: Section 115BAC denies s.24(b) interest for self-occupied property.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Capital Gains & Income from Other Sources
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Income Tax Law & Practice)
courses.summary: Assumptions: AY 2026-27; transfers on or after 23 July 2024 follow the Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 rates (LTCG 12.5% without indexation; listed equity STCG 20%; s.112A exemption ₹1.25 lakh). Covers capital asset, transfer, holding period, computation, exemptions u/s 54, 54EC, 54F, and income from other sources including gifts and winnings.
outcomes: Classify capital assets as short-term or long-term
Compute STCG and LTCG for listed shares and immovable property
Compare the 12.5% and the 20%-with-indexation option for land/buildings
Apply exemptions under s.54, 54EC and 54F
Compute income from other sources, including taxable gifts

lessons.title: Capital asset, transfer and holding period

scenes.text: Rohit sold listed shares held 14 months and a plot held 3 years.
Are both long-term? The holding period differs by asset type.

steps.title: Capital asset (s.2(14))
steps.body: Property of any kind held by the assessee, whether or not connected with business, including securities held by FIIs. Excludes: stock-in-trade, personal effects (but jewellery, paintings, drawings, sculptures, archaeological collections are capital assets), rural agricultural land in India, specified gold bonds and deposit schemes.

steps.title: Holding period (for transfers on or after 23 July 2024)
steps.body: Listed securities (shares, units of equity funds, listed bonds) — long-term if held more than 12 months. All other assets including unlisted shares, land and building, gold — long-term if held more than 24 months. Otherwise short-term. Specified mutual funds and market-linked debentures are always short-term (s.50AA).

steps.title: Transfer (s.2(47))
steps.body: Sale, exchange, relinquishment, extinguishment of rights, compulsory acquisition, conversion into stock-in-trade, and part-performance possession under s.53A of the Transfer of Property Act. Not transfer (s.47): gift or will, distribution on partition of HUF, transfer between holding and wholly-owned Indian subsidiary, conversion of bonds into shares.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating a gifted asset as acquired on the date of gift — under s.49 the cost and the holding period of the previous owner are included; assuming a gift of shares is a transfer.

activity.prompt: Short-term or long-term (transfer in 2025-26)?

items.text: Equity mutual fund units held 10 months

quiz.q: Listed shares become long-term after
quiz.why: Listed securities are long-term if held for more than twelve months.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a capital asset?
quiz.why: Section 2(14) excludes stock-in-trade.

quiz.q: A gift of property to a relative is
quiz.why: Section 47(iii) excludes transfer under gift or will.

scenes.text: Meera bought a plot in FY 2015-16 for ₹20,00,000 and sold it in September 2025 for ₹80,00,000, paying ₹1,00,000 brokerage.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Format (s.48)
steps.body: Full value of consideration − expenditure on transfer = net consideration; − cost of acquisition − cost of improvement = capital gain. For land/building, if stamp duty value exceeds consideration by more than 10%, stamp value is taken (s.50C).

steps.title: Rates
steps.body: STCG on listed equity/equity funds (STT paid) u/s 111A: 20%. Other STCG: slab rates. LTCG on listed equity u/s 112A: 12.5% on gains above ₹1,25,000 in a year. Other LTCG u/s 112: 12.5% without indexation. Resident individuals/HUFs transferring land or building acquired before 23 July 2024 may instead pay 20% with indexation, whichever is lower. Cost Inflation Index: 2015-16 = 254, 2025-26 = 376.

steps.title: Worked example: Meera — two options
steps.body:
Net consideration = 80,00,000 − 1,00,000 = 79,00,000.
Option 1 (12.5%, no indexation): LTCG = 79,00,000 − 20,00,000 = 59,00,000; tax = ₹7,37,500.
Option 2 (20% with indexation): indexed cost = 20,00,000 × 376/254 = 29,60,630; LTCG = 49,39,370; tax = ₹9,87,874.
Meera chooses option 1: ₹7,37,500 (plus cess).

steps.title: Worked example: listed shares
steps.body: Listed shares bought for ₹2,00,000 in 2023, sold for ₹5,00,000 in 2025 with STT paid. Step 1: LTCG = 3,00,000. Step 2: Exempt ₹1,25,000 → taxable 1,75,000. Step 3: Tax @12.5% = ₹21,875 (no 87A rebate on 112A gains).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Applying indexation to shares; forgetting the ₹1.25 lakh exemption is per year, not per transaction; using 10% (the pre-23 July 2024 rate).

activity.prompt: Listed equity shares (STT paid) held 3 years: cost ₹4,00,000, sale ₹9,00,000, no other 112A gains. Tax u/s 112A before cess (₹).

quiz.q: STCG on listed shares with STT u/s 111A
quiz.why: From 23 July 2024 the s.111A rate is twenty percent.

quiz.q: s.112A annual exemption
quiz.why: The Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 raised the threshold to one lakh twenty-five thousand rupees.

quiz.q: In Meera's case the better option is
quiz.why: Tax of ₹7,37,500 is less than ₹9,87,874 under the indexation option.

story.title: Selling to buy a bigger home

scenes.text: Vikram sells his house with LTCG ₹40 lakh and buys a new house for ₹30 lakh within a year.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: s.54 — house to house
steps.body: Individual/HUF; long-term residential house transferred; new residential house in India purchased 1 year before or within 2 years after, or constructed within 3 years. Exemption = lower of LTCG and cost of new house, capped at ₹10 crore. Option of two houses once in a lifetime if LTCG ≤ ₹2 crore. Unutilised amount before return due date must be deposited in the Capital Gains Account Scheme. Selling the new house within 3 years reverses the exemption.

steps.title: s.54EC and s.54F
steps.body: 54EC: LTCG from land or building invested within 6 months in specified bonds (NHAI, REC, PFC, IRFC) — maximum ₹50 lakh in a financial year; lock-in 5 years. 54F: LTCG on any asset other than a residential house; invest net consideration in a residential house; exemption = LTCG × amount invested ÷ net consideration, capped at ₹10 crore; assessee must not own more than one other house on the date of transfer.

steps.title: Worked example: 54 and 54F
steps.body:
54: Vikram's LTCG 40,00,000; new house 30,00,000. Exempt = 30,00,000; taxable LTCG = 10,00,000.
54F: Shares sold for net consideration 60,00,000 with LTCG 24,00,000; house bought for 45,00,000. Exempt = 24,00,000 × 45/60 = 18,00,000; taxable LTCG = 6,00,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: In 54F, comparing cost of the new house with LTCG (the proportion uses net consideration); exceeding ₹50 lakh in 54EC bonds.

activity.prompt: s.54F: net consideration on sale of gold ₹50,00,000; LTCG ₹20,00,000; new house cost ₹35,00,000. Exempt amount (₹).

quiz.q: Maximum 54EC investment in a financial year
quiz.why: The proviso to s.54EC caps investment at fifty lakh rupees in a year.

quiz.q: Cap on s.54 exemption (from AY 2024-25)
quiz.why: The Finance Act 2023 capped the cost of new house considered at ten crore rupees.

quiz.q: s.54F applies to transfer of
options: any long-term asset other than a residential house
quiz.why: Section 54F covers long-term capital assets other than a residential house.

scenes.text: At her wedding, Anu receives ₹3,00,000 from friends. Last year a friend gifted her ₹70,000 on her birthday.
Which gift is taxable?

steps.title: Residual head (s.56)
steps.body: Income not taxable under any other head. Specific items: dividends (taxable in shareholders' hands; interest to earn it deductible up to 20% of dividend, s.57), interest on securities and deposits, family pension (deduction 1/3 or ₹25,000 under new regime / ₹15,000 old, whichever is less), rental of machinery or plant, winnings from lotteries, crosswords, games (taxed at 30% u/s 115BB with no deduction), and gifts u/s 56(2)(x).

steps.title: Gifts u/s 56(2)(x)
steps.body: Money received without consideration exceeding ₹50,000 in aggregate in a year is fully taxable. Immovable property without consideration with stamp duty value above ₹50,000, or for inadequate consideration where the difference exceeds the higher of ₹50,000 and 10% of consideration, is taxable. Exempt: gifts from relatives, on marriage, under a will or inheritance, in contemplation of death, from a local authority, charitable trusts.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Anu: wedding gifts ₹3,00,000 — exempt (on marriage). Birthday gift ₹70,000 from a friend — aggregate exceeds ₹50,000, so the whole ₹70,000 is taxable. Lottery ₹1,00,000 — taxable at 30%: ₹30,000 + cess ₹1,200.

steps.title: Worked example: family pension
steps.body: Family pension ₹2,40,000 under new regime. Deduction = least of 1/3 (80,000) and ₹25,000 = ₹25,000. Taxable = ₹2,15,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Taxing only the excess over ₹50,000 (the whole amount becomes taxable); allowing basic exemption against lottery winnings.

activity.prompt: Gifts in cash from friends during the year: ₹20,000, ₹25,000 and ₹15,000. Amount taxable u/s 56(2)(x) (₹).

quiz.q: Tax rate on lottery winnings
quiz.why: Section 115BB taxes such winnings at thirty percent without deduction.

quiz.q: A gift of ₹5 lakh from one's brother is
quiz.why: Gifts from relatives as defined are excluded from s.56(2)(x).

quiz.q: Interest deduction against dividend income is limited to
quiz.why: Section 57 restricts interest expense to twenty percent of the dividend income.

scenes.text: Sunil lost ₹3 lakh in his business but earned ₹2 lakh short-term capital gain.
Can the business loss wipe out the capital gain?

steps.title: Clubbing (ss.60–64)
steps.body: Income of others included in the assessee's income: transfer of income without asset (s.60); revocable transfer (s.61); income of spouse from concern where the individual has substantial interest, or from assets transferred without adequate consideration (s.64(1)); income of minor child clubbed with the parent having higher income, with exemption ₹1,500 per child (s.10(32)), except income from the minor's own skill or a disabled minor.

steps.title: Set-off rules
steps.body: Intra-head first (s.70), then inter-head (s.71). Exceptions: LTCL only against LTCG; STCL against STCG or LTCG; speculation loss only against speculation income; loss from owning race-horses only against such income; lottery winnings cannot absorb any loss; business loss cannot be set off against salary; HP loss against other heads up to ₹2,00,000 (old regime only).

steps.title: Carry forward
steps.body: Business loss — 8 years against business income (return filed in time). Speculation loss — 4 years. Capital losses — 8 years, with same character rules. HP loss — 8 years. Unabsorbed depreciation — indefinitely. Return must be filed by the due date for carry forward of business and capital losses (s.80).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Salary 6,00,000; business loss (non-speculative) 3,00,000; STCG 2,00,000; LTCL 50,000.
Step 1: Business loss cannot be set off against salary; set off against STCG 2,00,000 (inter-head allowed) → remaining loss 1,00,000 carried forward.
Step 2: LTCL 50,000 cannot be set off against salary or STCG → carried forward.
Step 3: GTI = salary 6,00,000 (before standard deduction already applied as per regime).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Setting off business loss against salary; setting off LTCL against STCG.

a.text: STCL ₹80,000 and LTCG ₹1,20,000 in the same year. Can they be set off?

No

choices.label: Yes
choices.feedback: Winnings are taxed in full at 30%.

c.text: Good — you know the special set-off rules.

quiz.why: Section 32(2) has no time limit for unabsorbed depreciation.

steps.title: Main deductions (old regime)
steps.body: 80C (with 80CCC, 80CCD(1)) — max ₹1,50,000: PPF, EPF employee share, ELSS, life insurance premium, principal of housing loan, tuition fees for two children, 5-year bank FD, NSC, Sukanya Samriddhi. 80CCD(1B) — extra ₹50,000 for NPS. 80D — health insurance: self/family ₹25,000 (₹50,000 if senior) plus parents ₹25,000 (₹50,000 if senior); preventive check-up up to ₹5,000 within these. 80E — interest on education loan, 8 years, no cap. 80G — donations at 50% or 100%, some with qualifying limit of 10% of adjusted GTI; cash donations above ₹2,000 not allowed. 80TTA — savings interest up to ₹10,000 (non-senior). 80TTB — deposits interest up to ₹50,000 for seniors.

steps.title: Under the new regime
steps.body: Most Chapter VI-A deductions are not allowed. Allowed: 80CCD(2) employer's NPS contribution (up to 14% of salary for all employers from AY 2025-26), 80CCH (Agniveer corpus), 80JJAA (new employment, for business).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Old regime: PPF 80,000; LIC premium 30,000; children's tuition 60,000; NPS own 50,000; mediclaim self 22,000 and senior parents 38,000; savings interest 14,000.
80C: 80,000 + 30,000 + 60,000 = 1,70,000 → capped 1,50,000.
80CCD(1B): 50,000.
80D: 22,000 + 38,000 = 60,000.
80TTA: 10,000.
Total = ₹2,70,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Claiming 80TTA on FD interest (only savings accounts); claiming 80D for premium paid in cash (only check-up may be in cash); claiming 80C under the new regime.

activity.prompt: Old regime: EPF ₹72,000; ELSS ₹50,000; home-loan principal ₹60,000; NPS own ₹40,000 (claim fully under 80CCD(1B)); mediclaim self ₹18,000. Total Chapter VI-A deduction (₹).

steps.title: New regime
steps.body:
Salary 12,00,000 − 75,000 = 11,25,000. HP 88,000. Other sources 55,000. Total income ₹12,68,000.
Slab tax = 20,000 + 40,000 + 68,000 × 15% (10,200) = ₹70,200.
Rebate 87A: not available (income > ₹12 lakh), BUT marginal relief: tax cannot exceed income above ₹12,00,000 = ₹68,000. Tax = ₹68,000.
Cess 2,720 → ₹70,720.

steps.title: Decision
steps.body: The new regime saves about ₹87,780. Note marginal relief: without it, tax would have been ₹70,200 + cess.

steps.title: Marginal relief test
steps.body: Just above ₹12 lakh under the new regime: tax payable (before cess) = lower of normal slab tax and (total income − 12,00,000). Relief stops at around ₹12,75,000 where slab tax equals the excess.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting marginal relief; applying 87A to special-rate capital gains; adding FD interest to 80TTA.

steps.title: Advance tax (ss.207–211)
steps.body: Payable if tax liability after TDS is ₹10,000 or more. Instalments (cumulative): 15% by 15 June, 45% by 15 September, 75% by 15 December, 100% by 15 March. Presumptive (44AD/44ADA) assessees may pay 100% by 15 March. Resident seniors without business income are exempt.

steps.title: Interest
steps.body: 234A: delay in filing return — 1% per month on unpaid tax. 234B: advance tax paid less than 90% of assessed tax — 1% per month from April. 234C: deferment of instalments — 1% per month (3 months for each of the first three instalments, 1 month for the last). Late fee u/s 234F: ₹5,000 (₹1,000 if total income ≤ ₹5 lakh).

steps.title: TDS and returns
steps.body: Key TDS: s.192 salary (slab average rate), 194A interest other than securities, 194C contractors (1%/2%), 194J professional fees (10%; 2% technical), 194I rent, 194H commission. Form 16 for salary; Form 26AS / AIS show credits. Return forms: ITR-1 (resident, total income ≤ ₹50 lakh, salary, one HP, other sources, LTCG u/s 112A up to ₹1.25 lakh), ITR-2 (capital gains, more HP), ITR-3 (business), ITR-4 (presumptive). Due date for non-audit individuals: 31 July of the AY; belated or revised return by 31 December.

steps.title: Worked example: instalments
steps.body: Estimated tax ₹1,20,000, no TDS. Cumulative due: 15 June ₹18,000; 15 Sept ₹54,000; 15 Dec ₹90,000; 15 March ₹1,20,000. Second instalment alone = 54,000 − 18,000 = ₹36,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating instalment percentages as separate rather than cumulative; using ITR-1 when there is business income.

scenes.text: The CEO of a snack company asks: should we launch a new flavour, and at what price?
Financial statements tell her what happened last year; management accounting helps her decide what to do next.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: Management accounting is the presentation of accounting information in a way that helps management in **planning, decision-making and control**. It draws on financial accounting, cost accounting, statistics and economics.

steps.title: Functions and tools
steps.body:
**Functions**: planning and forecasting, organising data, interpreting, controlling, communicating, motivating, coordinating.

**Tools**: financial statement analysis, ratio analysis, fund and cash flow statements, marginal costing and CVP, budgetary control, standard costing, responsibility accounting, decision accounting.

steps.title: MA vs FA
steps.body:
| Basis | Financial accounting | Management accounting |
|---|---|---|
| Users | external | internal managers |
| Compulsion | statutory | voluntary |
| Focus | past | future |
| Format | prescribed | flexible |
| Precision | exact | estimates acceptable |
| Audit | required | not required |

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying management accounting replaces management – it only supports decisions.
- Claiming it must follow GAAP formats.
- Forgetting its limitations: depends on the quality of underlying data, can be costly, and involves personal judgement.

activity.prompt: Financial accounting or management accounting?

quiz.q: Management accounting mainly serves:
quiz.why: It provides information for managers' planning, decisions and control.

quiz.q: Management accounting is:
quiz.why: No law requires it; firms adopt it for their own needs.

quiz.q: Which is a tool of management accounting?
quiz.why: Budgetary control is a planning and control tool used by managers.

quiz.q: Management accounting focuses mainly on:
quiz.why: It uses past and present data to support future decisions.

scenes.text: A retailer's sales grew 25% this year.
A comparative statement reveals that cost of goods sold grew even faster, squeezing margins.

steps.title: Method (horizontal analysis)
steps.body:
Place two or more years side by side; compute:
- **Absolute change** = Current − Previous
- **% change** = Absolute change ÷ Previous × 100

Applies to the income statement and the balance sheet.

steps.title: Solved: comparative income statement
steps.body:
| Item | 2024 | 2025 | Change | % |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sales | 10,00,000 | 12,50,000 | +2,50,000 | +25.0 |
| COGS | 6,00,000 | 7,80,000 | +1,80,000 | +30.0 |
| Gross profit | 4,00,000 | 4,70,000 | +70,000 | +17.5 |
| Operating expenses | 2,40,000 | 2,70,000 | +30,000 | +12.5 |
| Operating profit | 1,60,000 | 2,00,000 | +40,000 | +25.0 |

**Interpretation**: costs rose faster than sales, so gross margin fell; tighter control of operating expenses preserved operating profit growth.

steps.title: Comparative balance sheet
steps.body: Look for: growth in fixed assets financed by long-term funds or short-term borrowings; changes in working capital; changes in owners' equity versus debt.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing the change by the current year instead of the base (previous) year.
- Reporting % changes on a negative base without comment.
- Drawing conclusions from absolute figures alone.

activity.prompt: Net profit was ₹1,60,000 last year and ₹2,00,000 this year. Percentage increase?

quiz.q: Comparative statements are an example of:
quiz.why: They compare the same items across periods, which is horizontal analysis.

quiz.q: If COGS rises faster than sales, the gross profit ratio:
quiz.why: A larger share of sales is consumed by cost, so gross margin falls.
