quiz.why: Change is measured relative to the starting figure.

scenes.text: An analyst compares a ₹500 crore chain with a ₹5 crore shop.
Converting each item to a percentage of sales or total assets makes them comparable.

steps.title: Method (vertical analysis)
steps.body:
- Common-size income statement: each item as **% of sales (revenue)**
- Common-size balance sheet: each item as **% of total assets** (or total equity and liabilities)

Useful for inter-firm and inter-period comparison of structure.

steps.title: Solved: common-size income statement (2025)
steps.body:
Sales 12,50,000 = 100%
- COGS 7,80,000 = **62.4%**
- Gross profit 4,70,000 = **37.6%**
- Operating expenses 2,70,000 = **21.6%**
- Operating profit 2,00,000 = **16.0%**

For 2024: COGS 60%, GP 40%, opex 24%, operating profit 16% – same operating margin despite the lower gross margin.

steps.title: Solved: common-size balance sheet
steps.body:
Total assets 20,00,000: fixed assets 12,00,000 (**60%**), inventories 3,00,000 (**15%**), receivables 4,00,000 (**20%**), cash 1,00,000 (**5%**).
Funded by equity 10,00,000 (**50%**), long-term debt 6,00,000 (**30%**), current liabilities 4,00,000 (**20%**).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total expenses as the base for the income statement.
- Comparing common-size percentages without noting different accounting policies.
- Forgetting that both sides of a common-size balance sheet total 100%.

scenes.text: An investor wants to see whether a company's growth is steady or erratic.
Trend percentages set the first year at 100 and show every later year relative to it.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
**Trend % = Current year figure ÷ Base year figure × 100**

Choose a normal base year. Compare trends of related items: sales vs receivables, sales vs inventory, sales vs net profit.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
| Year | Sales | Trend | Receivables | Trend |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | 8,00,000 | 100 | 1,00,000 | 100 |
| 2024 | 10,00,000 | 125 | 1,40,000 | 140 |
| 2025 | 12,50,000 | 156.25 | 2,00,000 | 200 |

**Interpretation**: receivables are growing much faster than sales – collection may be weakening or credit terms loosening.

steps.title: Pros and limits
steps.body: Trend analysis shows direction over many years quickly. It does not adjust for inflation, and an abnormal base year distorts all later percentages.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the previous year as base for each year (that is year-on-year growth, not a trend %).
- Choosing an abnormal year as base.
- Interpreting a trend in isolation without related items.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Ratio analysis
courses.summary: Meaning, uses and limitations of ratio analysis, liquidity ratios (current and quick), solvency ratios (debt–equity, proprietary, interest coverage), activity or turnover ratios (inventory, receivables, payables, assets), profitability ratios (gross, net, operating, ROCE, ROE, EPS) and working back from ratios to missing figures.
outcomes: Compute and interpret liquidity ratios
Compute and interpret solvency ratios

Compute profitability ratios including ROCE and ROE
Derive missing balance sheet figures from given ratios

story.title: Can we pay next month's bills?

scenes.text: A supplier is deciding whether to give a wholesaler 60 days' credit.
It checks how easily the wholesaler's current assets cover its current liabilities.

steps.title: Ratios
steps.body:
- **Current ratio** = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities (conventional norm about 2:1)
- **Quick (acid-test) ratio** = Quick assets ÷ Current liabilities, where quick assets = current assets − inventories − prepaid expenses (norm about 1:1)
- **Absolute liquid (cash) ratio** = (Cash + marketable securities) ÷ Current liabilities

Norms are rules of thumb and differ by industry.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Current assets 4,00,000 including inventory 1,50,000 and prepaid expenses 10,000; current liabilities 2,00,000.

- **Current ratio = 2:1**
- Quick assets = 4,00,000 − 1,50,000 − 10,000 = 2,40,000
- **Quick ratio = 1.2:1**

steps.title: Solved: working back
steps.body:
Current ratio 2.5; working capital ₹1,20,000.

- CA − CL = 1,20,000 and CA = 2.5 CL → 1.5 CL = 1,20,000
- **CL = 80,000; CA = 2,00,000**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving inventory in quick assets.
- Including bank overdraft in quick liabilities when the question defines liquid liabilities excluding it (read the definition).
- Assuming a very high current ratio is always good – it may signal idle cash or excess stock.

activity.prompt: Current assets ₹3,60,000 including inventory ₹1,20,000 (no prepaid expenses); current liabilities ₹1,60,000. Quick ratio (as a number, e.g. 1.5)?

quiz.q: Quick assets exclude:
quiz.why: Inventories are not quickly convertible to cash, so they are excluded.

scenes.text: A bank considers a five-year loan to a manufacturer.
It looks at how much the owners have put in compared with borrowings, and how comfortably profits cover interest.

steps.title: Ratios
steps.body:
- **Debt–equity** = Long-term debt ÷ Shareholders' funds (conservative norm 2:1 or lower)
- **Proprietary ratio** = Shareholders' funds ÷ Total assets
- **Total debt ratio** = Total debt ÷ Total assets
- **Interest coverage** = EBIT ÷ Interest on long-term debt
- **Debt service coverage** = (PAT + depreciation + interest) ÷ (interest + principal instalment)

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Shareholders' funds 6,00,000; long-term debt 3,00,000; current liabilities 2,00,000; total assets 11,00,000; EBIT 1,80,000; interest 30,000.

- **Debt–equity = 0.5:1**
- **Proprietary ratio = 6 ÷ 11 = 0.55**
- **Interest coverage = 6 times**

steps.title: Trading on equity
steps.body: If ROCE exceeds the interest rate on debt, using more debt raises return on equity (favourable financial leverage). If ROCE falls below the interest rate, leverage hurts equity holders.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including current liabilities in 'debt' when the formula uses long-term debt.
- Using PAT instead of EBIT for interest coverage.
- Ignoring preference capital classification (treat as per question – usually part of shareholders' funds).

activity.prompt: EBIT ₹3,00,000; interest on debentures ₹60,000. Interest coverage ratio (times)?

quiz.q: Debt ₹8,00,000; equity ₹4,00,000. Debt–equity ratio:
A higher proprietary ratio indicates:
quiz.why: More of the assets are financed by owners, which protects creditors.

quiz.q: Interest coverage uses:
quiz.why: Profit before interest and tax measures what is available to pay interest.

quiz.q: Favourable trading on equity occurs when:
quiz.why: Borrowed funds earning more than their cost increase equity returns.

scenes.text: A mobile phone dealer's warehouse holds last season's models.
Turnover ratios show how quickly stock and receivables are converted into sales and cash.

steps.title: Ratios
steps.body:
- **Inventory turnover** = COGS ÷ Average inventory; holding period = 365 ÷ turnover
- **Receivables (debtors) turnover** = Net credit sales ÷ Average receivables (debtors + B/R); collection period = 365 (or 360, or 12 months) ÷ turnover
- **Payables turnover** = Net credit purchases ÷ Average payables; payment period similarly
- **Fixed asset turnover** = Net sales ÷ Net fixed assets
- **Working capital turnover** = Net sales ÷ Working capital

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
COGS 7,20,000; inventory opening 1,40,000, closing 1,60,000.
- Average inventory = 1,50,000 → **turnover 4.8 times**; holding period ≈ 76 days

Credit sales 9,00,000; average receivables 1,50,000.
- **Receivables turnover 6 times**; collection period = 12 ÷ 6 = **2 months** (≈ 61 days on 365)

steps.title: Operating cycle
steps.body: Operating cycle ≈ inventory holding period + receivables collection period − payables payment period. A shorter cycle needs less working capital.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total sales instead of credit sales for receivables turnover.
- Using sales instead of COGS for inventory turnover (unless the question says so).
- Using closing figures when opening and closing are both given.

activity.prompt: Credit sales ₹7,20,000; debtors at start ₹1,00,000 and at end ₹1,40,000. Average collection period in days (use a 360-day year)?

quiz.q: Inventory turnover = COGS ÷
quiz.why: Average inventory best represents stock held during the period.

quiz.q: Receivables turnover 8 times. Collection period (360 days):
Sales ₹30,00,000; net fixed assets ₹10,00,000. Fixed asset turnover:
A lower inventory turnover usually indicates:
quiz.why: Stock sitting longer means it turns over fewer times.

scenes.text: Two companies each earn ₹1 crore profit; one uses ₹5 crore of capital, the other ₹20 crore.
Profitability ratios relate profit to sales and to capital employed.

steps.title: Ratios
steps.body:
- **Gross profit ratio** = GP ÷ Net sales × 100
- **Net profit ratio** = NP ÷ Net sales × 100
- **Operating ratio** = (COGS + operating expenses) ÷ Net sales × 100; operating profit ratio = 100 − operating ratio
- **ROCE** = EBIT ÷ Capital employed × 100 (capital employed = shareholders' funds + long-term debt, or fixed assets + working capital)
- **ROE** = PAT (less preference dividend) ÷ Equity shareholders' funds × 100
- **EPS**, **P/E** = Market price ÷ EPS, **dividend payout** = DPS ÷ EPS

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
EBIT 1,80,000; interest 30,000; tax 30%; equity 6,00,000; long-term debt 3,00,000.

- Capital employed = 9,00,000 → **ROCE = 20%**
- PBT 1,50,000; tax 45,000; PAT 1,05,000 → **ROE = 17.5%**
- With 60,000 equity shares: **EPS = ₹1.75**; market price ₹28 → **P/E = 16**

steps.title: DuPont view
steps.body: ROE = Net profit margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier (total assets ÷ equity). It shows whether returns come from margins, efficiency or leverage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using PAT in ROCE (ROCE uses EBIT).
- Forgetting to deduct preference dividend in ROE and EPS.
- Including non-operating income in operating profit ratio.

activity.prompt: EBIT ₹2,70,000; shareholders' funds ₹12,00,000; long-term debt ₹6,00,000. ROCE (%)?

quiz.why: ROCE measures return to all long-term providers of capital before interest and tax.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Cash flow statement (AS 3) and funds flow
courses.summary: Cash and cash equivalents, classification of cash flows into operating, investing and financing activities under AS 3, the indirect and direct methods for operating cash flow, computing investing and financing flows from balance sheet changes, preparing the full statement, and how a funds flow statement differs.
outcomes: Classify cash flows into operating, investing and financing activities
Compute cash from operations by the indirect method
Derive purchases and sales of fixed assets from ledger data
Compute operating receipts and payments by the direct method
Prepare a complete cash flow statement and reconcile it with cash balances

scenes.text: A growing electronics distributor reports record profit but struggles to pay salaries.
A cash flow statement shows where cash came from and where it went.

steps.title: Key definitions (AS 3)
steps.body:
- **Cash**: cash on hand and demand deposits with banks
- **Cash equivalents**: short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible to known cash amounts with insignificant risk of value change – generally with **original maturity of three months or less**
- **Operating activities**: principal revenue-producing activities
- **Investing activities**: acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and investments not included in cash equivalents
- **Financing activities**: changes in the size and composition of owners' capital and borrowings

steps.title: Special items
steps.body:
For a **non-financial company**:
- Interest and dividends **received** → investing
- Interest and dividends **paid** → financing
- Income-tax paid → operating, unless specifically identified with investing or financing

For a **financial enterprise** (bank, NBFC), interest paid and received are operating.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a 6-month fixed deposit as a cash equivalent.
- Classifying dividend paid as operating for a trading company.
- Treating depreciation as a cash flow (it is added back only in the indirect method).

activity.prompt: Classify each cash flow for a manufacturing company under AS 3.

quiz.q: Cash equivalents generally have original maturity of:
quiz.why: AS 3 treats investments maturing within three months of acquisition as cash equivalents.

quiz.q: For a manufacturing company, interest paid on debentures is:
quiz.why: It is a cost of obtaining finance, so it is a financing outflow.

quiz.q: For a bank, interest received is:
quiz.why: Lending is a bank's principal revenue activity, so interest is operating.

quiz.q: Purchase of a patent is:
quiz.why: Acquiring a long-term intangible asset is an investing outflow.

scenes.text: Profit of ₹1,20,000 includes depreciation and a loss on sale – neither uses cash this year.
The indirect method adjusts profit for non-cash items and working-capital changes.

steps.title: Format
steps.body:
Net profit before tax and extraordinary items
**+** depreciation, amortisation, loss on sale of assets, interest paid (financing), provisions
**−** profit on sale of assets, interest/dividend received (investing)
= **Operating profit before working capital changes**
**+** decrease in current assets / increase in current liabilities
**−** increase in current assets / decrease in current liabilities
= Cash generated from operations
**−** income-tax paid
= **Net cash from operating activities**

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Net profit before tax 1,20,000; depreciation 30,000; loss on sale of machinery 5,000; debtors increased 20,000; inventory decreased 10,000; creditors increased 8,000; tax paid 25,000.

- Operating profit before WC changes = 1,20,000 + 30,000 + 5,000 = **1,55,000**
- WC changes: −20,000 + 10,000 + 8,000 → **1,53,000**
- Less tax 25,000 → **Net cash from operating activities = ₹1,28,000**

steps.title: Finding profit before tax
steps.body: If only the change in P&L balance is given: Net profit before tax = Closing surplus − Opening surplus + transfer to reserves + proposed/paid dividend (as per question) + provision for tax made during the year.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reversing signs for working capital (an increase in debtors uses cash, so it is deducted).
- Starting from profit after tax and then deducting tax paid again.
- Including interest received in operating cash for a non-financial company.

activity.prompt: Net profit before tax ₹2,00,000; depreciation ₹40,000; profit on sale of investments ₹10,000; inventory increased ₹30,000; creditors increased ₹15,000; debtors decreased ₹5,000; no tax paid. Net cash from operating activities (₹)?

quiz.q: An increase in trade receivables is:
quiz.why: More sales are tied up in receivables, so less cash was collected.

quiz.q: Depreciation in the indirect method is:
quiz.why: It reduced profit without using cash, so it is added back.

quiz.q: Profit on sale of machinery is:
quiz.why: The full sale proceeds appear in investing, so the profit element is removed from operating.

quiz.q: A decrease in trade payables is:
quiz.why: Paying suppliers reduces cash, so it is deducted.

story.title: Where did the new machine come from?

scenes.text: The machinery balance rose by ₹1.5 lakh even after depreciation and a sale.
Rebuilding the machinery account reveals how much was actually bought.

steps.title: Reconstructing asset accounts
steps.body:
Machinery (at WDV):
**Purchases = Closing + Depreciation + Book value of asset sold − Opening**

Sale proceeds appear as investing inflow; profit or loss on sale is adjusted in operating activities.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Machinery: opening 5,00,000; closing 6,50,000; depreciation 60,000; a machine with book value 40,000 sold for 35,000.

- Purchases = 6,50,000 + 60,000 + 40,000 − 5,00,000 = **2,50,000**
- **Investing: −2,50,000 + 35,000 = −2,15,000**
- (Loss 5,000 added back in operating)

Financing: shares issued 2,00,000; debentures redeemed 1,00,000; dividend paid 50,000; interest paid 20,000.
- **Financing: +2,00,000 − 1,00,000 − 50,000 − 20,000 = +30,000**

steps.title: Non-cash transactions
steps.body: Transactions not involving cash – e.g. machinery acquired by issuing shares, conversion of debentures into shares – are **excluded** from the statement and disclosed in a note.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using closing − opening as purchases without adding back depreciation and disposals.
- Showing a non-cash share issue for an asset as both inflow and outflow.
- Treating premium on shares issued separately – total cash received is the inflow.

activity.prompt: Machinery: opening ₹4,00,000; closing ₹5,20,000; depreciation for the year ₹50,000; a machine with book value ₹30,000 was sold. Machinery purchased during the year (₹)?

quiz.q: Sale of machinery for ₹35,000 is shown as:
quiz.why: Proceeds from disposal of long-term assets are investing inflows.

quiz.q: Machinery bought by issuing shares worth ₹1,00,000 is:
quiz.why: No cash moved, so it is a non-cash transaction disclosed separately.

quiz.q: Shares of ₹10 issued at ₹12 for 10,000 shares. Financing inflow:
quiz.why: Total cash received including premium is ₹1,20,000.

quiz.q: Repayment of a long-term loan is:
quiz.why: Repaying borrowings changes the size of financing.

lessons.title: Direct method, full statement and funds flow

scenes.text: The finance team must present one statement explaining the fall in cash from ₹1,00,000 to ₹43,000.
Operating, investing and financing flows add up exactly to that change.

steps.title: Direct method
steps.body:
Shows gross receipts and payments:
- Cash from customers = Sales + Opening receivables − Closing receivables
- Cash to suppliers = Purchases + Opening payables − Closing payables
- Cash paid for expenses = Expense + Opening outstanding − Closing outstanding (adjust prepaid similarly)

AS 3 encourages the direct method; the indirect method is widely used in practice.

steps.title: Solved: direct method items
steps.body:
Sales 10,00,000; receivables opening 1,20,000, closing 1,50,000 → **cash from customers 9,70,000**.
Purchases 6,00,000; payables opening 80,000, closing 1,00,000 → **cash to suppliers 5,80,000**.

steps.title: Solved: complete statement
steps.body:
From the earlier lessons:
- Operating +1,28,000
- Investing −2,15,000
- Financing +30,000
- **Net decrease = −57,000**
- Opening cash and cash equivalents 1,00,000 → **closing 43,000** ✓

steps.title: Funds flow statement (contrast)
steps.body: A funds flow statement explains changes in **working capital** (funds = net working capital) between two balance sheets through sources and applications of funds. A cash flow statement explains changes in **cash and cash equivalents** only. Funds flow is no longer a mandatory statement but still appears in many syllabi.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that a rise in receivables lowers cash collected.
- Mixing funds-flow logic (working capital) into the cash flow statement.
- Not reconciling net change with opening and closing cash.

activity.prompt: Total sales ₹8,00,000; trade receivables at start ₹90,000 and at end ₹70,000. Cash received from customers (₹)?

quiz.why: Net change −10,000 so closing cash = ₹30,000.

quiz.q: AS 3 encourages the use of the:
quiz.why: AS 3 encourages the direct method because it shows gross receipts and payments.

questions.q: Cash flow statements are governed (non-Ind AS) by:
questions.why: AS 3 deals with cash flow statements.

questions.why: Its original maturity is within three months.

questions.q: Dividend received by a manufacturing company is:
questions.why: For non-financial companies, dividends received are investing inflows.

Goodwill amortised ₹10,000 is, in the indirect method:

questions.why: No cash moves on conversion.

questions.why: AS 3 treats taxes as operating unless specifically identifiable with other activities.

questions.q: Sales ₹5,00,000; receivables rose by ₹40,000. Cash from customers:
Net cash from operating ₹2,00,000; investing −₹3,50,000; financing +₹1,00,000. Net change:
Interest paid by a bank on deposits is:
questions.why: For financial enterprises, interest paid is part of operations.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Marginal costing, CVP analysis and decisions
courses.summary: Marginal versus absorption costing, contribution and the P/V ratio, break-even point, margin of safety and target profit, the two-period method, and decision-making with marginal costing: key factor, special orders, make or buy, and shutting down a segment.
outcomes: Compute contribution, P/V ratio and explain profit differences between marginal and absorption costing
Compute break-even point, margin of safety and sales for a target profit
Derive P/V ratio and fixed cost from two periods' data
Rank products under a limiting factor and evaluate special orders
Evaluate make-or-buy and shut-down decisions using relevant costs

scenes.text: A factory produced 12,000 units but sold only 10,000, and its absorption-costing profit looked surprisingly good.
Marginal costing shows that part of the 'profit' was fixed overhead carried forward in closing stock.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Marginal cost** = variable cost of one more unit (DM + DL + direct expenses + variable overheads)
- Under marginal costing, **fixed costs are period costs** – charged in full to P&L; stock is valued at variable cost
- **Contribution** = Sales − Variable cost = Fixed cost + Profit
- **P/V ratio** = Contribution ÷ Sales × 100

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Selling price ₹50; variable cost ₹30; fixed costs ₹2,00,000.

- Contribution per unit = **₹20**; P/V ratio = **40%**
- At 15,000 units: contribution 3,00,000 − fixed 2,00,000 = **profit ₹1,00,000**

steps.title: Solved: marginal vs absorption profit
steps.body:
Production 12,000 units; sales 10,000; no opening stock; fixed production overhead ₹1,80,000 (absorbed at ₹15 per unit).

- Closing stock 2,000 units carries 2,000 × 15 = 30,000 of fixed overhead under absorption costing
- **Absorption profit exceeds marginal profit by ₹30,000**

Rule: production > sales → absorption profit higher; production < sales → marginal profit higher; equal → same.

- Calling contribution 'profit'.

lessons.title: Break-even, margin of safety and target profit

scenes.text: A café chain's new outlet has fixed costs of ₹2 lakh a month.
The owner needs to know how many cups cover costs, and how many give a ₹60,000 profit.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **BEP (units)** = Fixed cost ÷ Contribution per unit
- **BEP (₹)** = Fixed cost ÷ P/V ratio
- **Margin of safety** = Actual sales − BEP sales; MOS ratio = MOS ÷ Actual sales
- **Profit** = MOS × P/V ratio
- **Sales for target profit** = (Fixed cost + Target profit) ÷ P/V ratio (or ÷ contribution per unit for units)

steps.title: Break-even chart
steps.body: In a break-even chart, total cost line starts at the fixed cost level and the sales line starts at zero; they cross at BEP. The angle between them is the **angle of incidence** – a wider angle means profit grows fast once BEP is passed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing fixed cost by selling price instead of contribution.
- Computing MOS ratio on BEP instead of actual sales.
- Forgetting to add target profit to fixed cost.

activity.prompt: Fixed costs ₹1,50,000; P/V ratio 30%. Break-even sales (₹)?

lessons.title: Key factor, special orders and make or buy

scenes.text: A toy maker's moulding machine is fully booked; it can make either robots or cars.
The right choice depends on contribution per machine hour, not per unit.

steps.title: Key (limiting) factor
steps.body:
When a resource is scarce (machine hours, labour hours, material, demand), rank products by **contribution per unit of the key factor**.

Product A: contribution ₹30, 3 machine hours → ₹10/hour
Product B: contribution ₹24, 2 machine hours → **₹12/hour** → produce B first.

steps.title: Solved: special order
steps.body:
Spare capacity exists. A buyer offers ₹35 per unit for 2,000 units; variable cost ₹30; normal price ₹50; fixed costs unchanged.

- Incremental contribution = (35 − 30) × 2,000 = **₹10,000** → accept, provided regular customers and prices are not affected.

steps.title: Solved: make or buy
steps.body:
Component made at DM ₹20, DL ₹12, variable OH ₹6 = ₹38; apportioned fixed OH ₹8 (unavoidable). Supplier price ₹42.

- Relevant cost of making = ₹38 < ₹42 → **make**; saving ₹4 per unit
- If capacity freed by buying could earn other contribution, include that opportunity cost.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ranking by contribution per unit when a key factor exists.
- Including unavoidable fixed costs in make-or-buy.
- Accepting a special order below variable cost.

scenes.text: A department store's toy section shows a loss after its share of rent and head-office costs.
Closing it would remove its contribution but not the rent – so the store would lose more.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body:
Close or drop a segment only if the **contribution lost < avoidable fixed costs saved** (plus any other benefit, e.g. renting the space).

Apportioned fixed costs that will continue anyway are **irrelevant**.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Department C: sales 3,00,000; variable cost 2,40,000 → contribution 60,000; apportioned fixed costs 80,000 (all unavoidable) → shows loss 20,000.

- If closed, contribution 60,000 is lost and fixed costs stay
- **Overall profit falls by ₹60,000 → keep C**

steps.title: Solved: product mix
steps.body:

- **Choose mix 2** (if within capacity and demand).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Closing a segment because its 'net profit' is negative after apportioned costs.
- Forgetting avoidable fixed costs when they exist.
- Ignoring qualitative factors: customer loyalty, employee morale, complementary sales.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Budgetary control and standard costing
courses.summary: Budgets and budgetary control, functional budgets (sales, production, material purchase), flexible budgets and cash budgets, zero-based and performance budgeting, standard costing with material and labour variances including idle time, overhead variances and basic sales variances.
outcomes: Prepare production and material purchase budgets
Prepare a flexible budget and cost at a different activity level

scenes.text: A footwear maker expects to sell 10,000 pairs next quarter.
From that sales budget it works out how many to produce and how much leather to buy.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Budget**: a quantitative plan for a future period
- **Budgetary control**: setting budgets, comparing actuals, analysing variances and taking corrective action
- **Principal (key/limiting) budget factor**: the factor limiting activity, usually sales demand – budgeting starts with it
- **Master budget**: summary of all functional budgets (budgeted P&L and balance sheet)
- Requirements: budget committee, budget manual, budget period, clear responsibility centres

steps.title: Functional budgets
steps.body:
- **Production (units)** = Budgeted sales + Closing finished stock − Opening finished stock
- **Material usage** = Production × material per unit
- **Material purchases** = Usage + Closing material stock − Opening material stock
- Labour, overhead, selling and cash budgets follow

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Sales 10,000 units; finished stock opening 1,500, closing 2,000; 2 kg material per unit; material stock opening 3,000 kg, closing 4,000 kg.

- Production = 10,000 + 2,000 − 1,500 = **10,500 units**
- Usage = **21,000 kg**
- Purchases = 21,000 + 4,000 − 3,000 = **22,000 kg**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding opening stock instead of subtracting in the production budget.
- Computing purchases from sales instead of production.
- Starting the budgeting process with production when sales is the limiting factor.

quiz.why: The master budget consolidates all functional budgets.

lessons.title: Flexible budgets, cash budgets and modern approaches

scenes.text: Actual output was 80% of capacity, but the fixed budget was for 60%.
A flexible budget restates allowed costs for the actual level, so the comparison is fair.

steps.title: Flexible budget
steps.body:
A budget designed to change with the level of activity. Separate costs into fixed, variable and semi-variable; recompute for each level.

Compare actual costs with the flexible budget for **actual** output, not with the original fixed budget.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Variable cost ₹20 per unit; semi-variable ₹30,000 fixed + ₹5 per unit; fixed ₹50,000.

At 8,000 units:
- Variable 1,60,000; semi-variable 70,000; fixed 50,000
- **Total ₹2,80,000; ₹35 per unit**

At 6,000 units: 1,20,000 + 60,000 + 50,000 = 2,30,000 (₹38.33 per unit).

steps.title: Cash budget and other approaches
steps.body:
**Cash budget**: opening balance + expected receipts − expected payments = closing balance, month by month; shows when borrowing is needed. E.g. opening 20,000 + receipts 1,50,000 − payments 1,65,000 = **5,000**.

- **Zero-based budgeting**: every activity justified from zero each period
- **Performance budgeting**: links budgets to outputs and performance measures (common in government)
- **Rolling budget**: a new period added as each period ends

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Keeping fixed costs per unit constant across levels.
- Treating the whole semi-variable cost as variable.
- Including depreciation in a cash budget.

activity.prompt: Using the same cost structure (variable ₹20 per unit; semi-variable ₹30,000 + ₹5 per unit; fixed ₹50,000), what is the total budgeted cost at 9,000 units (₹)?

quiz.q: Depreciation in a cash budget is:
quiz.why: Depreciation is not a cash outflow.

quiz.q: Zero-based budgeting requires:
options: justification of each activity from zero
quiz.why: ZBB starts from zero and every expense must be justified afresh.

lessons.title: Standard costing: material and labour variances

scenes.text: The buyer got steel below standard price, but production used more than allowed.
Variance analysis separates the buyer's saving from the shop floor's overuse.

steps.title: Material variances
steps.body:
SQ = standard quantity for actual output; AQ = actual quantity; SP, AP = standard and actual price.
- **Cost variance** = SQ × SP − AQ × AP
- **Price variance** = AQ × (SP − AP)
- **Usage variance** = SP × (SQ − AQ)
- Check: Cost = Price + Usage

Positive = Favourable (F); negative = Adverse (A).

steps.title: Labour variances
steps.body:
SH = standard hours for actual output; AH paid; AH worked; SR, AR.
- **Cost** = SH × SR − AH paid × AR
- **Rate** = AH paid × (SR − AR)
- **Idle time** = Idle hours × SR (always adverse)
- **Efficiency** = SR × (SH − AH worked)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using standard quantity for the budgeted rather than actual output.
- Using actual price in the usage variance.
- Using hours paid in the efficiency variance when there is idle time.

activity.prompt: Standard quantity for actual output 500 kg; actual quantity used 520 kg; standard price ₹25 per kg. Material usage variance in ₹ (enter the amount; it is adverse)?

quiz.why: The price difference applies to the quantity actually bought or used.

scenes.text: A plant produced 9,000 units against a budget of 10,000, while rent and salaries stayed the same.
The volume variance shows the cost of the under-used capacity.

steps.title: Fixed overhead variances (output basis)
steps.body:
Standard rate per unit = Budgeted FOH ÷ Budgeted output.
- **FOH cost variance** = Absorbed (actual output × rate) − Actual FOH
- **Expenditure (budget) variance** = Budgeted FOH − Actual FOH
- **Volume variance** = Absorbed FOH − Budgeted FOH

**Variable overhead cost variance** = Actual output × standard VOH rate − Actual VOH.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body:
Budgeted FOH 50,000 for 10,000 units (₹5 per unit). Actual output 9,000; actual FOH 52,000.

- Absorbed = 45,000
- **Cost variance = 7,000 A**
- **Expenditure = 2,000 A**
- **Volume = 5,000 A** (2,000 + 5,000 = 7,000 ✓)

VOH standard ₹2 per unit; actual VOH 19,000 → **1,000 A**.

steps.title: Solved: sales variances (turnover method)
steps.body:
Budget: 10,000 units at ₹50. Actual: 9,500 units at ₹48.

- **Sales price variance** = 9,500 × (48 − 50) = **19,000 A**
- **Sales volume variance** = 50 × (9,500 − 10,000) = **25,000 A**
- Total sales value variance = 4,56,000 − 5,00,000 = 44,000 A ✓

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using budgeted output instead of actual output for absorbed overheads.
- Mixing turnover-basis and profit-basis sales variances.
- Forgetting that expenditure + volume = FOH cost variance.

story.title: One sheet to rule them all

scenes.text: Ishita condenses five units into one sheet the night before her exam.

steps.title: Analysis and ratios
steps.body:
- % change = (Current − Base) ÷ Base × 100; Trend % = Year ÷ Base year × 100
- Common-size: P&L on sales; balance sheet on total assets
- Current = CA ÷ CL; Quick = (CA − inventory − prepaid) ÷ CL
- D/E = LT debt ÷ Equity; Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ Interest
- Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ Avg inventory; Debtors turnover = Credit sales ÷ Avg debtors
- ROCE = EBIT ÷ (Equity + LT debt); ROE = (PAT − Pref. div.) ÷ Equity; EPS; P/E

steps.title: Cash flow (AS 3)
steps.body:
- Cash equivalents: ≤ 3 months original maturity
- Indirect: PBT + non-cash charges − non-operating gains ± working capital changes − tax paid
- Non-financial company: interest/dividend received → investing; paid → financing
- Asset purchases = Closing + Depreciation + BV of sales − Opening

steps.title: CVP, budgets, variances
steps.body:
- Contribution = S − V; P/V = C ÷ S
- BEP units = F ÷ C per unit; BEP ₹ = F ÷ P/V
- MOS = Sales − BEP; Profit = MOS × P/V
- Two-period: P/V = ΔProfit ÷ ΔSales
- Key factor: rank by contribution per scarce unit
- Production = Sales + Closing FG − Opening FG
- MPV = AQ(SP − AP); MUV = SP(SQ − AQ)
- LRV = AH paid (SR − AR); Idle = Idle h × SR; LEV = SR(SH − AH worked)
- FOH expenditure = Budget − Actual; Volume = Absorbed − Budget

scenes.text: Sales of an air cooler model have slowed; marketing proposes a 10% price cut.

steps.title: Data
steps.body: Selling price ₹120; variable cost ₹72; fixed costs ₹4,80,000; current sales 15,000 units.

steps.title: Step 2: 10% price cut
steps.body:
- New price ₹108; contribution ₹36; P/V 33.3%
- New BEP = 4,80,000 ÷ 36 = **13,334 units** (13,333.3 rounded up)
- Units to keep profit at ₹2,40,000 = 7,20,000 ÷ 36 = **20,000 units** – a 33% rise in volume

Decision: recommend the cut only if market research supports at least a one-third increase in volume.

steps.title: Variation to try

steps.body:

steps.title: Q1: Cash flow statement (15 marks)
steps.body: Plan: (1) working notes for fixed assets, investments, tax and dividend accounts, (2) operating activities by indirect method, (3) investing, (4) financing, (5) net change reconciled to opening and closing cash, (6) note on non-cash transactions.

steps.title: Q2: Ratios from given ratios (10 marks)

steps.title: Q4: Short note – limitations of ratio analysis (5 marks)
steps.body: Points: based on historical data; ignores qualitative factors; affected by window dressing; different accounting policies hamper comparison; no single standard norm; price-level changes ignored.
